earnings.headline: Intuit grew sales 14 percent in its last quarter and full year, but expects slower growth next year.
points: Sales (revenue) for the year rose 14 percent to $21.4 billion. The last quarter also grew 14 percent, to $4.4 billion.
Profit per share (EPS) rose 20 percent to $16.46 for the year. Its newer 'Big Bets' products grew 34 percent.
Their own forecast (guidance) for next year is sales up 9% to 10%, slower than this year's 14 percent.
Weak spots: U.S. TurboTax users fell to 39.0 million from 39.9 million. Mailchimp sales are expected flat to slightly down.
Intuit sells TurboTax (taxes), Credit Karma (credit and loans), QuickBooks (business accounting) and Mailchimp (email marketing).
Credit Karma sales rose 20 percent to $2.6 billion. TurboTax grew more slowly, up 7 percent to $5.3 billion.
It spent $5.5 billion buying back its own stock, up 96 percent. It holds $7.2 billion in cash but owes $7.7 billion in debt.
Risks they name: competition, the government doing taxes itself, keeping up with AI, hacking and fraud, and a restructuring plan.
Several headlines say the stock has been falling, including one drop of 7% before its next earnings report.
One article ties the drop to fears that a new AI finance tool could compete with TurboTax.
The next earnings report is set for November 19.

takeaways: The business grew well last year: sales and profit both rose, and it passed $20 billion in yearly sales.
Growth is expected to slow next year, and fewer people used TurboTax this year than last year.
Investors are worried AI tools could take tax customers away. Intuit says AI is central to its own plan.

earnings.headline: Coca-Cola sold more drinks, grew sales 7%, grew profit faster, and raised its own full-year forecast.
points: Sales grew 7% to $13.4 billion. People bought 5% more drinks worldwide, led by India, China, Mexico and Brazil.
Operating income (profit from running the business) grew 12%. Earnings per share (profit per share) rose 8% to $0.93.
They raised their full-year guidance (their own forecast), but the forecast numbers were not in the text we read.
Weak spots: North America drink volume was flat, sports drinks fell 3%, and they lost market share in Europe, Middle East & Africa.
They own big drink brands like Coca-Cola, Sprite, fairlife and Powerade, sold in more than 200 countries via bottling partners.
In 2025, $28.8 billion of their sales came from outside the United States, so swings in the dollar can lift or cut results.
Named risks: new laws on plastic, water use and climate could raise their costs or force them to change some recipes.
They warn some brand and investment values may need write-downs (impairment charges) if future cash forecasts fall short.
Many headlines say the stock hit record highs after a 95% run.
Some writers worry the price is high: Barron's says its valuation (price compared to profits) is the highest in 25 years.
Writers disagree on what comes next. These are opinion pieces, not official company news.

takeaways: The quarter was mostly good: more drinks sold, higher sales, and wider profit margins than a year ago.
Not every part grew: North America volume was flat, sports drinks slipped, and they lost share in one big region.
A weaker dollar helped results this quarter. The company's own report warns that currency swings can also hurt.

earnings.headline: Sales more than doubled to $159.0 million and the loss shrank to $5.2 million, but Angel still lost money.
points: Sales (revenue) were $159.0 million, up 107.7% from a year ago. Guild memberships brought in $115.6 million of that.
Still losing money, but less: net loss was $5.2 million, down from $38.5 million a year earlier.
Their own forecast (guidance) is unchanged: an Adjusted EBITDA loss (a cleaned-up loss) of less than $25 million for 2026.
Paying members hit 2.94 million. But cash fell to $45.6 million from $63.3 million a year ago, and they owe $75.5 million in notes.
They earn from Guild memberships, a cut of movie ticket sales, licensing shows to Amazon, Apple and Netflix, and merchandise.
At the end of 2025 they had about 2.0 million paying members and held about 303.1 bitcoins as a company savings asset.
They raised cash by selling new shares: about $55.0 million in September 2025, plus a plan to sell up to $150,000,000 more.
Risks they name: a history of losses, hits are hard to predict, movies need big upfront marketing, and a long patent lawsuit.
Headlines say Q3 showed a loss, but sales beat what analysts expected.
The stock was added to the Russell 2000 and 3000 indexes (big lists of US companies that many funds follow).

takeaways: Fast growth: sales and paying members are rising quickly, and the cost to win members is a smaller share of sales than a year ago.
Not profitable yet: the company still lost money this quarter and expects a loss for the full year.
Watch cash and shares: cash is lower than a year ago, it owes money, and selling new shares can shrink each owner's slice.

earnings.headline: Palantir's sales grew 96% from a year ago to $2.313 billion, and it raised its own forecast for the full year.
points: Sales (revenue) were $2.313 billion, up 96% from a year ago. It was the first quarter ever above $2 billion.
Profit (GAAP net income) was $1.128 billion, a 49% margin, so it kept about half of each sales dollar as profit.
Guidance (their own forecast): Q4 sales of $2.649 - $2.653 billion, and full-year 2026 sales of $8.530 - $8.534 billion.
Weaker spot: new contracts signed (TCV) were $2.918 billion, up only 6% from a year ago, far slower than sales growth.
They rent out software (Foundry, Gotham, Apollo, AIP) that helps governments and companies use their data and AI.
In 2025, sales were $4.5 billion, up 56% from $2.9 billion in 2024. Customers grew from 711 to 954.
Risk they name: many contracts can be canceled "for convenience," so future deal value is not certain to turn into sales.
Other named risks: wars, interest rates, currency swings and tariffs could hurt them or their customers.
Many headlines ask why the stock keeps falling even though the business is growing fast.
One headline cites a 25% drop from an October high. Others debate whether the price is too high for the growth.

takeaways: The business is growing very fast and is now very profitable, with $10.4 billion in cash and U.S. Treasury securities.
New contract signings grew much more slowly than sales. That is worth watching.
A fast-growing company is not the same as a cheap stock. The headlines show the share price fell anyway.

earnings.headline: Broadcom's sales hit $29.6 billion this quarter, up 86 percent from a year ago, mostly from chips used for AI.
points: Sales (revenue) were $29.6 billion, up 86 percent. AI chip sales alone were $16.7 billion, up 221% from a year ago.
Profit per share (EPS) under standard accounting rules was $2.68, up from $0.85 in the same quarter last year.
Their own forecast (guidance) for next quarter: about $34.8 billion in sales, up 93 percent. It is only an estimate and could miss.
'Adjusted' profit of $20.1 billion leaves out real costs, like stock paid to workers. Software sales grew much slower than chips.
They make money two ways: computer chips (a lot of them for AI data centers) and business software, like VMware's cloud tools.
In fiscal 2025 the business brought in $27,537 million of cash and paid $11,142 million to shareholders as dividends.
They also spent $2,450 million buying back their own stock that year.
Risks they name: losing big customers, AI demand cooling, relying on a few suppliers, and a large amount of debt to repay.
The stock has swung hard lately: one headline says it fell 22% in a month, another says it jumped 18.2% in a week.
One report says well-known investor David Tepper sold all his Broadcom shares last quarter.
Several headlines tie Broadcom's moves to other AI chip makers, like Nvidia.

takeaways: Broadcom is growing very fast right now, mostly because big tech firms are buying its AI chips.
That growth leans on a small group of huge customers; if they cut spending, sales could fall.
The company pays a $0.65 per share dividend each quarter, but its stock price has been swinging a lot.

earnings.headline: McDonald's grew its profit faster than its sales this quarter, but fewer customers visited its U.S. restaurants.
points: Same-store sales rose 1.5% worldwide but fell 0.2% in the U.S., where fewer customers came in, though each spent more.
Profit grew: operating income (profit from running the business) rose 7%, and earnings per share rose 10% to $3.51.
Total sales at all its restaurants, including franchise-owned ones, grew 4% to over $38 billion.
No new forecast was given. The CEO said U.S. results got better through the quarter after a push on cheaper value deals.
Several articles debate whether the stock price already looks high after a 24% rise in a month.
One piece asks if rising food costs in 2027 could squeeze margins (the share of each sale McDonald's keeps as profit).
Other news covers delivery growth with Uber and a marketing push on Discord aimed at GTA 6 game players.

takeaways: McDonald's earned more profit this quarter, helped by higher fees from franchise owners and other income.
The U.S., its home market, was the weak spot: fewer visits, though spending per visit went up.
It is raising its dividend (cash paid to shareholders) 4% to $1.93 a share, and booked $56 million in reorganizing costs.

earnings.headline: Sales grew 11% to $2.8 billion, but profit fell sharply because of big one-time costs from buying other companies.
points: Sales (revenue) rose 11% to $2.8 billion. Newer drugs grew 49% to $1.26 billion, helped by drugs bought with Apellis.
Older multiple sclerosis (MS) drug sales fell 13% to $919 million, and copycat drug (biosimilar) sales fell 16%.
Adjusted profit per share fell 46% to $2.62. By official (GAAP) rules they lost money, mostly from $284 million in deal costs.
Their own forecast (guidance) for 2026 profit per share went up at the low end: now $12.20 to $13.00, from $12.00 to $13.00.
They sell medicines for brain and nerve diseases like MS, SMA and ALS, and share Alzheimer's drug LEQEMBI with Eisai.
Cash and investments rose to about $4.2 billion at the end of 2025, up from about $2.4 billion a year earlier.
Cash from everyday business fell 23.3% in 2025, partly from higher tax payments and payments for deals.
Risks they name: cheap generic copies of TECFIDERA and a rival copy of TYSABRI keep cutting sales; tariffs add uncertainty.
Headlines focus on new two-year data saying their early Alzheimer's drug diranersen slowed decline.
Eisai and Biogen shared three-year real-world LEQEMBI data showing slower Alzheimer's progression.
Results from two big lupus drug trials are expected in the first half of December 2026.

takeaways: The company is growing again: newer drugs are selling fast enough to make up for older MS drugs losing ground.
Profit took a hit this quarter, mostly from one-time costs of buying companies, and total debt is about $7.7 billion.
Several big drug trial results are due over the next 12 months. They could help or hurt; nothing is certain.

earnings.headline: Sales jumped and the company raised its own yearly forecast, but its official operating profit shrank sharply.
points: Revenue (sales) grew 39% from a year ago to $3.44 billion, which the CEO called a record first quarter.
Operating income (official profit from running the business) fell to $96 million, from $309 million a year ago.
Net income (profit after all costs) rose to $482 million, or $0.57 per share, from $334 million a year ago.
Guidance (their own forecast) was raised: full-year sales of $14.52 billion to $14.57 billion, up 26% to 27%.
They sell cybersecurity: firewalls, cloud and AI protection, and tools that guard logins, mostly as subscriptions.
Big change: after buying CyberArk, they say the business got much bigger and that brought new risks and rivals.
Risks they name: tough competition, including cloud giants and AI firms that offer their own security tools.
Other risks: a hack or a flaw in their own products could hurt their name, and past growth may not continue.
Headlines say they agreed to buy AI startup Applied Compute for $4.5 billion.
Several stories say the stock rose after results topped what Wall Street analysts expected.
Other stories tie demand to AI-driven cyberattacks becoming a bigger threat.

takeaways: Sales and signed future contracts are growing fast, and the company expects more growth this year.
Official operating profit shrank a lot even as sales grew, which means costs grew faster than sales.
They keep buying other companies (CyberArk, and now plans for Applied Compute). Deals like these can pay off or cause problems.

earnings.headline: Record quarter: sales rose 65% to $10.2 billion, topping the company's own forecast.
points: Sales (money from customers) were $10.2 billion, up 65%. Without buyouts and currency effects, growth was 37%.
Profit per share (EPS) was $0.79, up 61%. New orders hit a record $12.2 billion, more than they shipped (1.19:1).
Their own forecast (guidance) for next quarter: sales of $10.3 to $10.5 billion. For all of 2026: $36.9 billion to $37.1 billion.
Caution: they're paying about $1.6 billion for four companies, partly with borrowed money (debt). Forecasts may not come true.
They make connectors, cables, antennas and sensors that link electronics together, built in about 40 countries.
Biggest unit, Communications Solutions, was 52% of 2025 sales. Harsh Environment was 26%. Interconnect and Sensor was 22%.
They estimate their whole market was worth about $500 billion in 2025.
The full risk list wasn't in the text we read. The company warns that results could differ a lot from its forecasts.
Several articles debate whether the stock price is already too high for the company's growth.
One article asks what happens to Amphenol if spending on AI data centers slows down.
One headline says the stock fell 3.41% on Nov 16.

takeaways: Sales and profit grew fast this quarter and beat the company's own forecast.
They're sharing cash with owners: a 20% bigger dividend and a new $4 billion plan to buy back their own shares.
Much of the growth comes from data-center demand and buyouts partly paid with debt. If that demand slows, growth could slow too.

earnings.headline: Sales grew 39% to $782.5 million, their fastest growth in nearly four years, but the official loss got bigger and margins slipped.
points: Sales (revenue) were $782.5 million, up 39% from a year ago. The CEO called it their best quarter ever.
Official (GAAP) loss grew to $34.1 million from $1.3 million. Adjusted profit, which skips stock pay and some other costs, was $143.7 million.
Gross margin (what's left of each sales dollar after direct costs) slipped to 71.2% from 74.0% a year ago.
Their own forecast (guidance): $845.0 to $846.0 million in sales next quarter, and $2,963.0 to $2,964.0 million for the full year.
They make money mostly from subscriptions. Businesses pay monthly or yearly to use their network for security and speed.
Sales were $2,167.9 million in 2025, up from $1,669.6 million in 2024.
They have lost money every year since they began. The loss for 2025 was $102.3 million.
Risks they name include slower growth, tariffs raising equipment costs, and a weak economy cutting customer spending.
Most headlines cover the stock jumping after results, citing faster sales growth and a raised full-year forecast.
Some stories link the growth to customers using Cloudflare's AI platform to build apps.
Not all one way: one headline asks why the stock fell on a Tuesday after the big run-up.

takeaways: Sales are growing fast, up 39% in a year, and the company's own forecast for the year went up.
It still loses money under official accounting, and that loss got bigger this quarter.
The company plans to cut part of its workforce as it leans harder on AI. That brings one-time costs.

earnings.headline: Joby raised its sales forecast and made progress on FAA approval, but it still spends far more cash than it brings in.
points: Sales (revenue) were $55 million in Q3 2026, mostly from Blade, its passenger flight service, which flew 44,000+ people.
No profit number is given. They expect to use $385 million to $415 million of cash in the second half of 2026.
Their own forecast (guidance) for 2026 sales rose 15%, to $135 million to $140 million.
Surprise: its J208 plane flew itself across the U.S., and Air Force contracts grew to ~$37 million. It plans to buy Resonant Sciences.
Joby is building an electric air taxi for a pilot and up to four passengers. It plans to run rides, sell aircraft and do defense work.
In August 2025 Joby bought Blade, a passenger air charter service in New York and Southern Europe.
Joby has lost money every year since 2009. Its total past losses (accumulated deficit) were $2,785.6 million at the end of 2025.
Biggest named risks: FAA approval could be late or never come, government shutdowns, crowded airspace, and rivals getting there first.
Headlines say the stock is still down 56% in 2026, even though it rose after the Q3 results.
Several stories focus on how much cash Joby is burning and say its biggest hurdle is still ahead.
Other articles guess how far the stock could rise or fall. These are opinions, not company facts.

takeaways: Joby does not sell air taxi rides yet. Almost all of its sales today come from Blade.
It still spends far more than it earns, but it has $2.2 billion in cash and short-term investments to fund the work.
The key thing to watch is FAA approval. It is in the fifth and final stage, and the company warns it could take longer than planned.

earnings.headline: Match Group says Q3 met its own targets and Tinder's daily users grew again in September, but the release gives no sales or profit figures.
points: Tinder's daily users grew vs. a year ago in September, the first time in three and a half years.
Hinge grew users, sales, and paying users by double digits vs. last year.
Tinder's sales are not growing yet. The company says it hopes to turn better user trends into sales growth in 2027.
They cut the number of shares by 4% in a year and 10% since early 2025, and will pay a $0.20 per share dividend on January 21, 2027.
Most money comes from people paying directly in apps like Tinder and Hinge (subscriptions and extras). Ads bring in some too.
Apple and Google take fees on in-app purchases, a big cost. The company names cutting these fees as a risk it may not achieve.
They renamed their main profit measure to "Adjusted EBITDA" (profit before some costs). The number itself did not change.
They carry debt, with $450 million due December 15, 2027. Named risks include losing users, competition, and cyberattacks.
Headlines discuss the Q3 results and a raised guidance (the company's own forecast).
A company director bought 2,500 shares, according to one report.
The finance chief will speak at UBS and Nasdaq London conferences in December.

takeaways: Tinder, the biggest app, is showing early signs of getting more users again, but its sales have not caught up yet.
Hinge is the clear bright spot, growing in users and sales.
The company returns cash to owners through a dividend and fewer shares, but it also carries a lot of debt.

earnings.headline: Apple had a record September quarter with sales of $114.5 billion, up 12 percent, though iPad and wearables sold less.
points: Sales (money coming in) were $114.5 billion, up 12 percent from a year ago. iPhone and Services set records.
Profit per share was $2.10, up 14 percent. $0.05 of that came from tariff refunds (import taxes paid back).
Worse: iPad sales fell to $6,229 million from $6,952 million. Wearables and Home fell to $8,300 million from $9,013 million.
No sales forecast (guidance) was given here. Leaders are counting on new iPhones and the all-new Siri AI for the holidays.
iPhone is the main earner: $254,098 million of $478,834 million in sales this year. Services added $123,301 million.
Spending on research rose to $45,765 million from $34,550 million. Unsold goods (inventory) jumped to $14,541 million from $5,718 million.
About 60% of sales go through other sellers, like phone carriers, rather than Apple's own stores.
Big risks they name: tariffs and trade fights, a weak economy, and relying on factories mostly in Asia for key parts.

takeaways: Apple had its best year ever for sales, mostly thanks to iPhones and Services like the App Store and iCloud.
Not everything grew: iPads and wearables sold less, and part of the profit boost came from tariff refunds.
Apple says trade fights, tariffs and supply problems in Asia could hurt the business in the future.

earnings.headline: AbbVie's sales grew and it raised its own full-year forecast, but older drugs like Humira kept shrinking.
points: Sales (revenue) were $17.404 billion, up 10.3 percent. Skyrizi ($5.776 billion) and Rinvoq ($2.706 billion) led the way.
Profit per share (EPS) was $2.37 under standard accounting rules, or $3.82 adjusted (leaving out some special costs).
Weak spots: Humira sales fell 31.2 percent, Imbruvica fell 26.1 percent, and the beauty (aesthetics) unit fell 1.4 percent.
Guidance (their own forecast) for 2026 adjusted EPS rose to $13.95 - $13.99. The dividend goes up 5.2 percent in 2027.
AbbVie makes and sells medicines for immune diseases, brain and nerve conditions and cancer, plus beauty products like Botox.
Two drugs, Skyrizi and Rinvoq, made up about 42% of total sales in 2025, so a lot rides on them.
Biggest risk they name: when patents (legal protection) end, cheaper copies called generics or biosimilars can cut sales fast.
They also warn that rivals and governments may challenge their patents early, which could hurt sales and earnings.
Headlines say the stock hit new 52-week highs, and one analyst firm raised its price target after the latest results.
Some articles ask what happens if Skyrizi and Rinvoq growth slows, since so much of the business depends on them.
Others debate whether the stock's price is fair compared with the company's cash flow and raised forecast.

takeaways: Most of the growth comes from two newer immune drugs, Skyrizi and Rinvoq, so the company leans heavily on them.
Older drugs like Humira and Imbruvica are shrinking fast, and cheaper copies are a risk the company names itself.

earnings.headline: Abbott's sales grew 14.5 percent, but much of that jump came from buying cancer-test maker Exact Sciences; it kept its profit forecast.
points: Sales (money coming in) rose 14.5 percent. Without the Exact Sciences purchase and currency swings, growth was 7.0 percent.
Profit per share was $0.53 by standard accounting rules, or $1.42 after removing one-off items the company excludes.
Guidance (their own forecast): full-year profit per share of $5.50 to $5.55, and sales growth of about 6.0 percent.
Weak spots: Neuromodulation sales fell 1.2 percent, and U.S. Structural Heart sales fell 11.1 percent.
Abbott sells medical devices, lab tests, baby and adult nutrition drinks, and brand-name generic drugs sold outside the U.S.
In 2025, glucose monitor sales hit $7.6 billion, up from $6.4 billion. COVID test sales fell to $297 million.
Diagnostics sales fell 4.5 percent in 2025 on weaker COVID test demand and tough conditions in China.
Risks named: tariffs, currency swings, price controls, competition, and cheaper generic drugs replacing brand ones.
Most headlines are about the stock price. One mentions trial results for the Amulet 360 heart device.

takeaways: The business grew this quarter, but a big part of the jump came from buying a cancer-testing company.
The company kept its own profit forecast steady and has raised its dividend (cash paid to owners) for 54 years in a row.
Not everything grew: some heart and nerve-device sales slipped, and nutrition sales are down 1.3 percent this year so far.

earnings.headline: Sales grew 23% to $342 million, but profit fell to $54 million from $72 million a year earlier.
points: Sales (revenue) were $342 million in the third quarter, up 23% from $279 million a year ago.
DAYBUE, a Rett syndrome drug, sold $140 million, up 39%. NUPLAZID sold $202 million, up 14%.
Profit fell: net income was $54 million, down from $72 million, as selling and office costs rose to $159 million.
Guidance (their own forecast) for 2026 DAYBUE sales rose to $505–$520 million. They also lowered their research spending forecast.
Acadia makes money selling two drugs: NUPLAZID for Parkinson's disease psychosis and DAYBUE for Rett syndrome.
Sales of the two drugs were $1,071.5 million in 2025, up from $957.8 million in 2024.
It pays partner Neuren royalties (a cut of sales) on DAYBUE, from 10% up to 15% in North America.
Big risk: copycat (generic) drugs. One legal deal lets a generic NUPLAZID launch February 27, 2038, or earlier in some cases.
The stock hit a 52-week low (its lowest price in a year) at 18.24 USD.
A court fight over NUPLAZID's patent could mean protection until 2038, or only 2030, depending on an appeal.
Other stories cover the raised sales forecast and the lower research spending forecast.

takeaways: Sales are growing, led by DAYBUE, but quarterly profit was lower than last year.
The company raised its DAYBUE forecast and had $976 million in cash and investments.
Patent fights and drug trials are the big unknowns; losing the appeal could let copycats in sooner.

points: Several headlines are about a takeover deal between Aurora Cannabis and Organigram, another cannabis company.
Headlines also say Curaleaf and Tilray were talked about as possible bidders; one says Curaleaf is unlikely to buy Aurora.
Some headlines report the stock fell on Friday and Monday and did worse than the overall market.

takeaways: Aurora may be bought by Organigram. A takeover means one company buys another, which can change who runs the business.
Writers disagree on what other cannabis companies might do, so the final outcome is still not settled.
This summary is based only on news headlines, not Aurora's own official reports, so it leaves out sales and profit facts.

earnings.headline: Archer moved closer to flying air taxis in LA and to closing a big Boeing deal, but it still makes almost no sales.
points: Sales: the letter gives no sales total for the quarter. The company is still mostly spending, not selling.
Profit: none yet. A cost measure (adjusted EBITDA) matched their own forecast. Money on hand: $1.4B.
Next: they expect to close buying Wisk, Insitu and SkyGrid from Boeing soon. Only one of nearly 20 approvals is left.
Surprise: the FAA cleared Midnight to start flying in LA soon. Full safety approval (type certification) is not done yet.
They make almost no money yet. The plan: sell air taxis, run air taxi rides in cities, and sell aircraft tech for defense.
They took control of Hawthorne Airport near LA and began renting hangar space. That rent is their first revenue (sales).
Losses: they lost $618.2 million in 2025 and about $2.3 billion since starting. They expect losses to continue.
Biggest risks: FAA approval may be delayed, building planes at scale is hard, and investors could lose part or all of their money.
Many headlines ask whether the stock is worth its price after it fell 46% this year.
One report says the loss got bigger this quarter. Others focus on how fast the company is spending its cash.
Writers also discuss Boeing becoming Archer's biggest shareholder once the deal closes.

takeaways: Archer is still building its product. It spends far more than it earns, and losses keep coming.
There is real progress: an FAA permit, LA flights soon, and a deal for Insitu, a drone maker with over $200 million in yearly sales.
Its big goals depend on approvals and deadlines, like the LA28 Games in 2028. The company itself warns that delays could happen.

earnings.headline: Sales grew 18% and profit grew even faster in the third quarter, both ahead of the company's own expectations.
points: Sales (revenue) rose 18% to $1,381.9 million, up from $1,172.5 million a year earlier.
Profit (net income) rose 36% to $378.4 million. Profit per share rose 45% to $5.66, from $3.91.
They raised their own forecast (guidance): about $5.35 billion in sales for 2026, growth of 18%.
They repurchased 1.9 million of their own shares for $747 million this quarter, which lowers the share count.
They earn fees when businesses pay bills, use company cards, pay for fuel and tolls, book hotels, or send money abroad.
Sales in 2025 rose to $4,528.4 million from $3,974.6 million. Corporate Payments grew to 36% of all sales.
One part got worse: Lodging Payments (hotel bookings) sales fell to $469.5 million from $488.6 million.
Risks they name: fuel prices, exchange rates, interest rates, hacking, and a lawsuit from the FTC (a US regulator).
Most headlines are about the raised forecast and the stock rising 6 straight days, up 14%.
One analyst firm, Cantor Fitzgerald, raised its price target (its guess for the share price).

takeaways: The business grew strongly this quarter and did better than its own plan.
Not every part grew: hotel payment sales shrank last year, and profit margins slipped a little.
Forecasts can change. The company says results may differ, and it faces a government lawsuit.

earnings.headline: Campbell's had a weak fourth quarter: sales and profit fell, and it cut its dividend to pay down debt faster.
points: Sales fell 8% to $2.1 billion. Part of that drop is because last year's quarter had an extra week.
Profit dropped hard: adjusted EBIT (profit before interest and taxes) fell 25% to $242 million, hurt by higher costs and tariffs.
They cut the dividend (cash paid to owners) by 36%, to $0.25 a share each quarter from $0.39, to pay off debt faster.
Their own forecast for fiscal 2027 (their business year): adjusted profit per share of $1.65 to $1.80, down from $2.17.
They make and sell packaged foods: soups, sauces, drinks and snacks like Campbell's, Rao's, Goldfish and Pepperidge Farm.
Full-year sales fell 5% to $9.7 billion. The Snacks side shrank more than the soups and meals side.
They bought 49% of La Regina, which makes Rao's pasta sauces: $146 million paid, $140 million more due in 2027.
Risks they name: tariffs and rising costs, store brands competing on price, and new rules on 'ultra-processed' foods.
Headlines focus on the dividend and on Campbell's being seen as a steady 'defensive' food company in shaky markets.
Some articles point out the stock has fallen a lot over the past 5 years.
A Rao's film about families and friends sharing fewer meals together also got attention.

takeaways: Campbell's is selling less and earning less, mostly because ingredient, shipping and tariff costs went up.
The dividend cut means less cash for owners now, but more money goes to paying down the company's debt.
They plan $500 million in cost savings by fiscal 2030, but still expect lower profit in fiscal 2027.

earnings.headline: Sales grew 7% to $10.0 billion, but costs, including a warehouse fire in Korea, turned last year's profit into a loss.
points: Sales (revenue) were $10.0 billion, up 7% from last year, or 11% if you remove currency swings.
They lost 501 million dollars vs a 95 million profit last year; without a July warehouse fire, the loss was 321 million.
Cash left after spending on the business (free cash flow) was negative 409 million dollars over the past year.
Newer businesses grew sales 23% to $1.6 billion, and their losses shrank by $23 million.
They sell goods and groceries online, deliver restaurant food, stream video, and offer payments, under brands like Coupang and Farfetch.
In Korea, Rocket Delivery offers free next-day delivery on millions of items, even for orders placed just before midnight.
In November 2025 outsiders got into customer accounts (a data incident). They name fines and investigations as risks.
They pay no dividend (cash paid to owners) and don't plan one, but they buy back shares under a $1 billion plan.
South Korea fined Coupang $220M over its food delivery practices, per a Seeking Alpha headline.
Headlines say the stock fell 6 days in a row and is down 15%.

takeaways: Sales are still growing, but the company went from a profit to a loss this quarter.
A warehouse fire, a customer data incident, and a government fine are real costs and risks.
The newer businesses grow fastest, but they still lose money every quarter.

earnings.headline: Copart's sales grew a little last quarter, but its profit fell because costs rose faster than sales.
points: Sales (revenue) were $1.2 billion, up 2.4% from the same quarter last year.
Profit (net income) fell 17.4% to $327.4 million. Profit per share dropped to $0.35 from $0.41.
Costs grew faster than sales: running its lots rose 7.7% and office (admin) costs rose 16.6%.
No forecast (guidance) was given. Interest earned on its cash fell 20.5%, and it spent heavily buying back its own shares.
Copart runs online car auctions. It mostly sells wrecked or total-loss cars for insurance companies and earns fees per sale.
Insurers supplied 79% of its cars in fiscal 2026, down from 81% the year before.
Full-year sales were $4.7 billion, up just 0.4%. Profit was $1.5 billion, down 4.4%.
The full risk list wasn't in the text we have. The company warns real results could differ a lot from its plans.
Most headlines are about the stock price and analyst forecasts, not new business events.
One headline says the next earnings report is due Nov. 20.
A Seeking Alpha opinion piece argues the company's current problems are short-term.

takeaways: Copart still makes a lot of money, but it earned less this year than last year.
Sales are barely growing while costs are climbing faster.
Its cash pile shrank this year, largely because it spent a lot buying back its own stock.

earnings.headline: Charles River beat its own forecast and raised its 2026 outlook, though total sales dipped after it sold some businesses.
points: Revenue (sales) was $982.7 million, down 2.2% from a year ago, mainly because they sold some businesses in May 2026.
Leaving out the sold businesses, sales grew 4.7%. Adjusted profit per share rose 27.2% to $3.09.
Official profit per share was $6.86, but $5.06 of it came from a one-time tax reserve reversal, not everyday business.
They raised their guidance (own forecast) for 2026: adjusted profit per share of $11.35 – $11.55, up from $11.15 – $11.45.
This part of the annual report covers rules for insider stock trading and a code of ethics for all staff and directors.
A risk they name: outsiders have gotten into their computer systems before and could do it again.
The board's audit committee watches cyber risk. Tech leaders meet with it generally at least quarterly.
This excerpt does not explain in detail how the company makes money.
Several headlines say the stock has risen a lot (95% to 106% runs) and may already be fully priced.
A finance executive gave up 649 shares to pay taxes on stock awards that vested.
Other headlines cover the 2026 Q3 earnings call and daily stock moves, both up and down.

takeaways: The core business grew again: sales rose 4.7% without the sold units, the second quarter in a row of growth.
The huge official profit jump is mostly a one-time tax gain. The adjusted $3.09 per share is the cleaner number.
Not everything improved: the research-models unit's organic sales fell 0.6% and its adjusted margin slipped to 24.4%.

earnings.headline: Salesforce grew sales 11% from a year ago and raised its own full-year forecast, helped partly by a company it bought.
points: Sales (revenue) were $11.3 billion, up 11% from a year ago. $456 million came from Informatica, a company they bought.
Profit per share was $4.29, up 119%. Cash the business brought in was $1.3 billion, up 71%.
They raised their own forecast (guidance) for the year to $46.1 billion to $46.4 billion in sales.
A stronger U.S. dollar cost $100M of the raise, and $200 million of it depends on two deals that haven't closed yet.
They mostly rent business software online (subscriptions). That made up about 95 percent of sales.
Last year (fiscal 2026) sales were $41.5 billion, up ten percent. Profit per share rose to $7.80 from $6.36.
They bought Informatica for about $9.6 billion and cut staff, offices and data centers to lower costs.
Biggest risks they name: hacks or outages, tough rivals, deals that don't pay off, new AI rules and currency swings.
Recent headlines report new job cuts at Salesforce and a cyberattack, and the stock had its worst week since April.
One report says the stock fell 9.2% after a new partnership called Copilotforce was formed.
Some headlines raise worries about the company's debt (leverage), while others debate whether the stock is cheap.

takeaways: The latest quarter grew in sales, profit and cash, and the company raised its forecast for the year.
Part of the growth comes from buying other companies, and the new forecast depends on two deals closing.
Recent news is negative: job cuts, a reported cyberattack and a falling stock. Weigh that next to the results.

earnings.headline: Cronos had record sales in Q3 2026, but its bottom-line profit fell compared with a year ago.
points: Sales (revenue) hit $63.5 million in Q3 2026, a record, up 73% from a year ago on a like-for-like basis.
Profit after all costs (net income) fell to $17.8 million from $28.3 million, mainly from lower other income and taxes.
Core operating profit (Adjusted EBITDA, which leaves out some costs) rose to $17.1 million. Spending on running the business also rose.
They gave no forecast (guidance). In October 2026 they finished buying CanAdelaar, a Dutch cannabis company.
Cronos grows and sells cannabis: for adults in Canada (Spinach brand), medical in Israel (PEACE NATURALS), and other countries.
Changes named in the report: a deal to buy Dutch firm CanAdelaar, and leaving the U.S. hemp product business.
They warn they have lost money before, with negative operating cash flow in four of the last six years.
Other risks: an Israeli probe into cheap Canadian imports, the Middle East conflict, strict rules, and Altria's big influence.
One headline says shares rose after Q3 results beat what analysts expected.
Another notes the stock had a 93% run; several others report days when it fell.
A Motley Fool article compares the balance sheets (cash and debts) of 5 cannabis companies.

takeaways: Sales are growing fast, led by Israel, Germany and Canada, and hit new records.
Bottom-line profit was lower than last year, so not every number got better.
Real risks remain: an Israel trade probe, conflict in the region, tough cannabis rules, and past losses.

earnings.headline: Carpenter had its most profitable first quarter ever, but heavy spending on a plant expansion left its free cash flow negative.
points: Sales were $798.2 million, up 9 percent from $733.7 million a year ago, but lower than the quarter before.
Operating income (profit from running the business) was $196.4 million: up 28 percent on the year, down 5 percent from last quarter.
Free cash flow (cash left after paying for plants) was negative $24.8 million, worse than negative $3.4 million a year ago.
Their own forecast (guidance): $192 million to $197 million operating income next quarter, $850 million to $880 million for the year.
They make special metals like titanium, nickel and cobalt alloys. Aerospace and defense was 65% of sales last year.
Yearly sales rose to $3,124.2 million from $2,877.1 million. Operating income rose to $702.0 million from $521.8 million.
Not everything grew: medical sales shrank to $278.4 million from $351.2 million.
Risks they name: raw metal supply and price swings, and key plants in Pennsylvania and Alabama with few backups if equipment fails.
The stock hit a 52-week low at 270.44 USD. Articles say investors are reacting to a softer near-term outlook.
A law firm posted a notice aimed at investors who lost money on the stock.
Other headlines cover new leadership appointments and a debate over whether the stock's price is reasonable.

takeaways: The company is earning more than a year ago, helped by strong orders from the airplane industry.
It is spending heavily to grow, so the cash left over this quarter was negative.
The stock is near a yearly low and faces a law-firm notice, even though the company kept its full-year forecast.

earnings.headline: Sales of its gene-editing treatment grew fast, but the company still lost slightly more money than a year ago.
points: CASGEVY sales (its sickle cell and thalassemia treatment) were $99 million, up 30% from last quarter and nearly six times a year ago.
Net loss (spent more than it earned) was $111.4 million, a bit worse than the $106.4 million loss a year earlier.
Research spending rose to $71.9 million from $58.9 million. Cash grew to $2,276.6 million, mostly from new borrowing.
Next: heart drug CTX310 data at a medical meeting November 9, 2026. The FDA gave it a status that can speed its review.
They earn money mainly from CASGEVY, a one-time gene-editing treatment, splitting profits and costs 60/40 with partner Vertex.
CASGEVY became the world's first approved CRISPR gene-editing treatment in 2023. Most other drugs are still in early testing.
Biggest risk they name: they have lost money since the start, expect more losses, and may need to raise more money.
Other risks: gene editing is new, regulators are cautious, side effects, patent fights, and Vertex controls CASGEVY.
Several headlines note the share price has slid, with one citing a 50% fall over five years.
Other headlines cover early trial results for CTX310 (cholesterol and blood fats) and zugo-cel (immune diseases).

takeaways: Sales of its one approved treatment are growing fast, but the company still loses money every quarter.
It has a large cash cushion, partly from borrowing, to keep paying for research.
Much depends on early trials. Early good results do not always hold up in bigger, later tests.

earnings.headline: CrowdStrike called this its best quarter ever: sales grew 26% and it turned a small official profit after a loss a year ago.
points: Sales (revenue) were $1.47 billion, up 26% from $1.17 billion in the same quarter last year.
Official (GAAP) profit was a small $5.3 million, up from a $70.2 million loss. Core operations still lost $33.2 million.
They raised their own forecast (guidance): full-year sales of $5,991.1 - $6,011.1 million, ending January 31, 2027.
Cash from running the business hit a record $530.3 million. Yearly subscription sales (ARR) grew 25% to $5.84 billion.
They sell cybersecurity by subscription: one cloud platform, Falcon, protects computers, cloud systems and logins from hackers.
Falcon uses AI trained on real attacks. They say more customer data makes it smarter for every customer.
Top named risk: the July 19 Incident, a 2024 update that crashed some Windows computers, still hurts sales and reputation.
Other named risks: tough competition, long and unpredictable sales cycles, a history of losses, and being a hacker target.
Headlines follow big stock swings: one notes a 10% selloff, another asks why the stock surged.
Many headlines are price forecasts and TV or bank opinions. Those are opinions, not facts from the company.

takeaways: The business is growing fast and brought in more cash than ever this past quarter.
Official profit is still thin: $5.3 million on $1.47 billion of sales, and core operations still lost money.
Fallout from the 2024 crash is still a named risk, and the forecasts are the company's own. They may not come true.

earnings.headline: Sales jumped and the company raised its own forecast, but its loss got much bigger because of rising debt costs.
points: Sales (revenue) were $3,661 million this quarter, up from $1,365 million in the same quarter a year earlier.
It still lost money: the net loss grew to $709 million from $110 million, as interest on its debt rose to $846 million.
They raised their own forecast (guidance) for 2026 sales to $13.0 billion to $13.3 billion.
Surprise: about $132.5 billion in signed future work (backlog), but they plan to spend $37 billion to $39 billion this year.
They rent out powerful computers built for AI, plus software tools, to AI labs and big companies.
They grew to 43 data centers using over 850 MW (megawatts, a unit of power) at the end of 2025, up from 32 a year before.
Big risks they name: getting enough electricity, relying on a few large customers, and carrying a lot of debt.
They also warn they need much more money to keep building, and only a few suppliers make key parts.
Shares rose more than 24% after the report, their best day since April 2025, according to CNBC.
Other headlines say shares fell 5% when Nvidia signaled caution about financing for AI cloud firms.
Several outlets say the results eased worries about an AI slowdown and about CoreWeave's debt.

takeaways: The business is growing fast and has a lot of signed future work from customers.
It still loses money, and the loss got bigger, mostly because of interest on its borrowing.
Its future depends on continued AI demand, enough electricity, and its ability to keep raising money.

earnings.headline: Cisco's sales (revenue) grew 24% to $18.5 billion, its fastest growth in over 15 years, and it raised its own full-year forecast.
points: Sales hit $18.5 billion, up 24% from a year ago. Networking gear jumped 43%, but services grew only 1%.
Profit (net income) was $4.6 billion, up 59%. Earnings per share (profit split per share) were $1.14, up 58%.
Worse: the part of each sale kept after making the product (gross margin) fell to 63.7% from 65.5% a year ago.
Their own forecast (guidance): $18.0 billion to $18.2 billion next quarter, a bit below this one; full year now $74.8 billion to $75.8 billion.
Cisco sells network gear, software and security tools that help businesses connect and protect their computer systems.
In fiscal 2026 sales grew 12% to $63.3 billion and profit grew 30%. Product sales rose 16%; services were flat.
Big cloud companies (hyperscalers) buying AI gear were about 6% of sales, up from less than 2% the year before.
Risks they name: leaning on a few big AI customers, tight supply and higher costs for memory chips, and trade policy.
Headlines focus on Cisco beating expectations and saying its AI infrastructure sales will double this fiscal year.
Some analysts cut their price targets even after the strong quarter, so not every outside view got more upbeat.

takeaways: Cisco is growing much faster than usual, driven mostly by networking gear for AI data centers.
It expects $9B in AI sales from big cloud firms in FY27, more than double FY26, but that leans on a few customers.
Not everything improved: it keeps less of each sale as gross profit, and its services business barely grew.

earnings.headline: CoStar had record sales and its biggest profit in years, and it raised its own forecast for 2026.
points: Sales (revenue) were $952 million this quarter, up 14% from $834 million a year ago.
It made a profit (net income) of $74 million, versus a loss of $31 million in the same quarter last year.
It raised its own forecast (guidance): 2026 sales of $3.75 billion to $3.77 billion. Q4 growth slows to about 10%.
Cash fell from $1,633 million to $500 million this year, after spending on buying companies and its own shares.
It earns mostly from subscriptions: real estate data (CoStar) and listing sites like Apartments.com and Homes.com.
In 2025 sales rose 19% to $3.2 billion, but profit (net income) fell 95% to $7 million as costs grew faster.
Big buys (Matterport, Domain) added sales, but costs for its Richmond, Virginia campus weighed on results.
Risks they name: tough competition, a real estate slowdown, losing search traffic, debt, and deals that don't pay off.
Some headlines say the stock dropped and lagged the market on a recent Wednesday.
Director John Hill sold shares worth $92,049, per one report.
Apartments.com launched a 'Free Rent for a Year' sweepstakes as a marketing push.

takeaways: The company is selling more and has turned last year's losses into real profit by cutting costs.
Its cash pile shrank a lot because it spent big on buying other companies and its own shares.
Its future depends on the real estate market and on beating strong rivals; its own forecasts can be wrong.

earnings.headline: Sales grew 9% to a record-setting quarter for adjusted profit, but rising oil-based material and freight costs squeezed margins.
points: Sales (revenue) were $1.5 billion, up 9% from a year ago. Both main businesses, CCM and CWT, grew.
Adjusted profit per share hit a record $5.92, up 6%. But core profit kept per dollar of sales fell to 23.8% from 25.9%.
Oil-based materials, diesel and freight costs rose sharply. Price hikes lag costs, so margins shrank. They call it timing, not lasting.
Their own forecast (guidance) for Q4: sales up high-single-digit percent, margin flat. No new-construction recovery assumed.
They make roofing and weatherproofing products, like roof membranes and insulation, mostly for commercial buildings in North America.
Re-roofing old buildings is about 70% of their commercial roofing business. Roofs must be replaced, so demand is steady.
In 2025 sales were flat at $5,019.9 million vs $5,003.6 million. Profit per share fell to $17.16 from $18.34.
Risks they name: a few big customers, buying other companies that may not pay off, factory disruptions, and construction slumps.
Carlisle plans to acquire PermaTherm, a maker of insulated metal panels, adding to its building products line.
Analyst views are split: one sees margins recovering; another says buybacks, not business growth, are lifting per-share profit.
Some investment firms, like Virginia Retirement Systems, trimmed their holdings, per MarketBeat reports.

takeaways: The business is still growing sales, helped by steady demand to replace old roofs.
The company returns a lot of cash to owners through dividends and share buybacks, which boosts profit per share.

earnings.headline: CSX had a strong quarter: record sales of $4.02 billion and much higher profit as it moved more freight.
points: Sales (revenue) hit a record $4.02 billion, up 12% from a year ago, helped by fuel fees, more freight and higher prices.
Profit per share (EPS) was $0.57, up 54%. Leaving out a one-time $164 million write-down last year, the gain was 30%.
Operating margin (profit kept from each sales dollar) rose to 39.1%. Shipments rose 5%; container shipments rose 7%.
They gave no number forecast (guidance). The CEO said they aim for best-in-class performance in 2027.
CSX makes money moving freight by rail across 26 states. General goods (merchandise) brought in $8.8 billion, 62% of sales.
2025 was a weaker year: sales fell 3% to $14.1 billion and profit per share fell 14% to $1.54.
Coal sales fell 15%, hurt by lower world coal prices. Margin slipped to 32.1% from 36.1%.
Risks they name: competition from trucks, fuel prices, new rules, bad weather, labor trouble and cyberattacks.
Headlines say CSX stock has had a run and ask where the company's next growth will come from.
Several pieces say container (intermodal) volume and sales growth are the next big test for CSX and other railroads.

takeaways: The latest quarter clearly improved: more freight, higher sales and bigger profit than a year ago.
Part of the profit jump comes from an easy comparison: last year included a one-time $164 million write-down.
Full-year 2025 was a down year, and coal and fuel prices can swing results, so one strong quarter is not the whole story.

earnings.headline: Cintas grew sales and profit this quarter and raised its own forecast for the full year.
points: Sales (revenue) were $3.01 billion, up 10.9% from $2.72 billion a year ago.
Profit (net income) rose 12.3% to $551.7 million. Profit per share was $1.36, up from $1.20.
They raised their own forecast (guidance) for the year: sales of $12.15 billion to $12.27 billion.
Not all good: the tax rate rose to 20.0% from 17.6%, and $14.4 million in UniFirst deal costs cut into profit.
Renting and cleaning uniforms, mats and towels was 76.5% of sales, down from 77.1%. First aid and safety grew to 12.4%.
Fiscal 2026 sales were $11.3 billion, up 8.9%, mostly from selling more plus price increases, partly offset by lost customers.
They agreed to buy rival UniFirst in a deal worth about $5.5 billion. It still needs government approval.
Risks they name: the deal could fail or cost more, higher fuel, labor and medical costs, tariffs, and losing customers.
Several headlines ask what happens to Cintas if the UniFirst deal falls through.
One report says investors grew less sure the deal will close, after news of an upcoming FTC (competition regulator) meeting.
Other headlines look at whether Cintas is reasonably priced on its cash flow after the $5.5B deal.

takeaways: Cintas is still growing: more sales, more profit, and a higher forecast for the year.
The big unknown is the UniFirst purchase. Regulators are still reviewing it, and it could fall through.
Not everything improved: taxes took a bigger bite and deal costs trimmed this quarter's profit.

earnings.headline: Sales fell 9% and the company swung to a loss as Brazil got much weaker, while most other regions grew.
points: Sales fell 9% to $1.59B. Latin America dropped 31% on Brazil; North America grew 7%, Europe/Middle East/Africa 14%.
Profit turned into a loss: $(54) million this quarter vs a $60 million profit in the same quarter last year.
Their own forecast (guidance) was updated for a weaker Brazil: core profit of $1.1 to $1.125 billion for 2026.
Good news: new products sold well, and the board approved the first dividend (a cash payout to owners) since the spin-off.
They sell products that protect crops from weeds, insects and disease. The 10-K also covered their seed business.
Big change: splitting into two companies (seeds and crop protection). The split could cost more or go worse than planned.
Government approvals are getting slower and costlier. Pesticides must be re-registered every 15 years.
Pollution cleanup: $562 million set aside at the end of 2025, with up to about $553 million more possible.
Headlines say the stock fell sharply after the report, one saying 20%, blamed on Brazil's farm troubles.
The CEO said Brazil was 'materially weaker than anticipated', meaning much worse than they expected.
Analyst firm KeyBanc lowered its price target (its guess of the stock's value) after the lower outlook.

takeaways: Brazil is the main problem: farmers there are short on cash and borrowing is costly, so they bought less.
Outside Latin America, sales grew, helped by strong demand for the company's new products.
Prices fell 7% this quarter, and the company now expects a weaker year than it first hoped.

earnings.headline: This filing is an investor slide deck that promotes the company; it does not report new quarterly sales or profit numbers.
points: No fresh quarterly sales, profit, or forecast (their own outlook) is in this filing, so it can't tell us how the latest quarter went.
As of September 30, 2026 they list 1,544 properties and 48.5 M square feet of space they own.
Over five years they report 57% dividend growth and 50% growth in FFO per share (FFO = a cash-profit measure real estate firms use).
Five-year total return to shareholders was 31% for the period ended December 31, 2025. The deck is a sales pitch and highlights the good.
They make money renting storage units, mostly month-to-month, plus fees for managing 862 stores owned by others.
They grew from 631 to 662 owned stores, and space rose from 45.8 million to 48.4 million square feet.
Worse: the share of space rented (occupancy) slipped to 88.1% from 88.8%.
Risks they name: a weak economy, a slow housing market, deals that disappoint, and reliance on NY (17%), FL (14%), TX (11%), CA (10%).
Some analyst articles discussed Q3 results and storage demand coming back. These are opinions, not company filings.
An investment manager reported holding 15.4 million shares as a passive stake (an investment, not a bid to control the company).
Several headlines are about unrelated things that share the word "Cube" and say nothing about this business.

takeaways: CubeSmart rents storage units. Month-to-month leases let it change prices fast, but customers can also leave fast.
It owned more stores in 2025, but a slightly smaller share of its space was rented than the year before.
The newest filing is a sales-pitch deck with no fresh quarterly numbers, so look at the actual quarterly results before judging.

earnings.headline: Sales hit a record $353 million, up 11% from last year, but the company still lost money this quarter.
points: Sales grew 11% to $353 million. U.S. sales rose 8% and international sales rose 28%.
They lost $37.4 million this quarter, or $0.14 per share, after costs like interest, taxes and wear on equipment.
Margins slipped: they kept 48.3% of each sales dollar after product costs, down from a year ago.
Their own forecast is about $150 million in operating cash for the year. This quarter brought in $22 million.
Curaleaf offered to buy rival Aurora Cannabis, but Aurora agreed to merge with Organigram instead. Curaleaf is weighing its options.
Headlines disagree on Aurora: one doubts the deal happens, another says Curaleaf got all needed competition-law approvals.
Curaleaf keeps opening Florida stores, including a new medical cannabis shop planned in Sebring.

takeaways: Sales are growing, but the company still posted a loss of $37.4 million this quarter.
It owes much more than it holds: $636.9 million in debt versus $104.9 million in cash.
The Aurora buyout is uncertain because Aurora chose a different partner, so the outcome is still open.

earnings.headline: CVR Energy had its best quarter ever thanks to record refining profits, but its fertilizer business lost money.
points: Profit for owners was $570 million, up from $374 million a year ago. The company called it the best quarter in its history.
Adjusted EBITDA (profit before interest, taxes and wear-and-tear costs) was $582 million vs $180 million a year ago.
Fertilizer side got worse: it lost money this quarter vs a $43 million profit a year ago, partly from planned plant downtime.
An EPA waiver erased a $253 million liability (money owed). They aim to close a deal for two Marathon refineries by year end.
They make money turning crude oil into gasoline, diesel and jet fuel, and making farm fertilizer through CVR Partners.
In December 2025 they switched a renewable diesel unit back to regular oil refining because renewables weren't paying off.
Biggest risk they name: refining profits swing a lot with oil and fuel prices they can't control.
Icahn Enterprises owned about 70% of the stock. The dividend was suspended in October 2024 when cash got tight.
Headlines focus on the Marathon refinery deal; one firm, Mizuho, raised its rating on the stock after the news.
One headline says shares fell 9% on news of the debt package used to pay for the deal.
Another mentions a $1.2 billion equity raise: selling new shares, which shrinks each existing owner's slice.

takeaways: Refining had a record quarter, but the fertilizer business had a weaker one.
The company is making a big move: buying two more refineries, paid for partly with new debt and new shares.
Refining profits swing with fuel prices, so one great quarter doesn't mean the next one will be great too.

earnings.headline: CVS sold more, swung back to a profit after last year's big write-down, and raised its own forecast for 2026.
points: Sales (revenue) rose 5.4% to $108.4 billion for the quarter, helped by its drug-benefits and insurance arms.
Profit per share was $1.68, vs a loss of $3.13 a year ago, when it wrote down $5.7 billion on a clinic business.
They raised their own forecast (guidance): adjusted profit per share of at least $8.20, up from $7.90 to $8.10 before.
Weak spot: drugstore sales fell 2.0%, hurt by government drug price cuts, new cheaper generics and lower insurer payments.
CVS makes money three main ways: Aetna health insurance, managing drug benefits for employers, and about 9,000 drugstores.
Aetna covers an estimated 37 million people; its drug-benefits manager (PBM) serves about 87 million plan members.
Recent changes: it left the individual exchange insurance market in 2026 and stopped counting Omnicare in its results.
Risks they name include rising medical costs, a weaker economy, and cyberattacks, which a board committee oversees.
Shares fell 5.20% on Nov 18 and 3.26% on Nov 17, after a stretch where the stock rose 12% over 6 green days.
Several stories discuss a possible breakup of CVS that would separate the pharmacy, and the risks that brings.
Writers also debate higher medical costs at Aetna and ongoing risks to its drug-benefits (PBM) business.

takeaways: The business looks healthier than a year ago: more sales, a real profit, and better results at Aetna insurance.
Not everything improved: drugstore sales slipped, and the company itself warns medical costs remain high.
Talk of splitting up the company adds uncertainty, and the stock has moved both up and down in recent weeks.

earnings.headline: Chevron earned $9.9 billion in the third quarter of 2026, far more than a year ago but less than the quarter before.
points: Profit was $9.9 billion, up from $3,539 million a year ago, but down from $12,072 million last quarter.
Total sales weren't listed in this release. Oil sold for about $97 a barrel (Brent), up from $69 a year ago.
Output fell: 3,980 thousand barrels a day vs 4,086 a year ago, partly due to the Middle East conflict.
Debt dropped $3.5 billion. The quarterly dividend (cash paid per share) is $1.78, paid December 10, 2026.
Chevron makes money pumping oil and gas, and turning crude oil into fuels, lubricants and chemicals.
In 2025 it bought Hess, another oil company, which made up 24 percent of Chevron's total assets by year end.
Profit fell in the last quarter of 2025: $2,770 million vs $3,239 million a year earlier.
It faces several environmental cases; each could mean a penalty of $1.0 million or more.
Berkshire Hathaway still holds about $18.6 billion of Chevron stock after selling more than a third of it.
Some headlines say the stock slid on a recent day; the headlines alone don't give the reason.
Others debate whether the stock looks cheap. These are opinions, not news from the company.

takeaways: Higher oil and fuel prices lifted profit a lot versus last year, but profit dipped from last quarter.
Chevron pumped less oil and gas than a year ago, hurt in part by the Middle East conflict.
It is paying down debt and its Venezuela joint ventures plan to invest $7 billion over the next five years.

earnings.headline: Delta posted record sales on strong travel demand, but much higher fuel costs kept profit flat versus last year.
points: Sales (revenue) hit a September-quarter record of $17.6 billion, up 16 percent from a year ago (adjusted figure).
Profit was flat: adjusted pre-tax profit of $1.5 billion matched last year. Under standard accounting rules, net income fell 47%.
Fuel hurt: adjusted fuel costs were up 62 percent, and non-fuel costs per seat mile rose 7.3 percent.
Their own forecast (guidance): sales up about 20 percent next quarter, and full-year earnings of $5.10 to $5.60 per share.
Delta makes money from tickets, SkyMiles deals (American Express paid $8.2 billion in 2025), cargo, repairs and a refinery.
2025 sales rose 3%, but operating profit slipped $173 million. Premium tickets grew 7%, while Main Cabin tickets fell 5%.
Biggest risks they name: climate rules and fuel mandates that raise costs, and weak economies that cut travel demand.
They also flag currency swings, tariffs and political trouble abroad as threats to their international flights.
Most headlines track the stock's up and down days. One says it is up 24.8% in 2026, the best of the big four airlines.
One headline links falling oil prices to Delta, since fuel is one of an airline's biggest costs.
The CEO says AI fare-shopping tools are on their radar, and holiday travel demand is holding strong.

takeaways: People are still flying a lot and paying up for premium seats, so Delta's sales keep setting records.
Fuel got much more expensive, so profit stayed flat even though sales grew.
Delta plans to pay down more than $2 billion of debt in 2026, but fuel prices and the economy remain big unknowns.

earnings.headline: Sales grew 35% from a year ago to $1.20 billion, and the company brought in strong cash, but official profit stayed small.
points: Sales (revenue) rose 35% from a year ago to $1.20 billion this quarter.
Official (GAAP) profit was $75 million, a thin 6% of sales. Their adjusted view, which leaves out stock pay, shows $334 million.
Their own forecast (guidance) for next quarter is sales of $1.19 billion to $1.20 billion, about level with this quarter.
Big customers paying $100,000 or more a year grew 20%, to about 4,860 from about 4,060.
They sell monthly or yearly subscriptions to software that watches companies' apps and computer systems for problems.
Sales for 2025 were $3,427.2 million, up 28% from $2,684.3 million in 2024.
Profit fell: net income was $107.7 million in 2025, down from $183.7 million in 2024.
Risks they name: they lost money every year before 2023, a weak economy could cut tech spending, and rivals are tough.

takeaways: Sales are growing fast, and the company keeps real cash: $251 million of free cash flow (cash left after spending) this quarter.
Official profit is small because much of their pay is in stock; the 'adjusted' numbers leave that out and look much better.
Their own forecast shows next quarter's sales about flat, and they warn a weaker economy could hurt them.

earnings.headline: Deere's sales and profit grew this quarter and it raised its yearly profit forecast, but its big-farm-machine business kept shrinking.
points: Sales rose 5 percent to $12.608 billion. Profit (net income) was $1.379 billion, up from $1.289 billion a year ago.
Big farm machines did worse: sales fell 6% and profit fell 9%. Small farm gear and construction grew, with sales up 12% and 18%.
Guidance (their own forecast) for 2026 profit was raised to $4.75 billion to $5.00 billion. They think 2026 is the low point for farm gear.
For the first nine months, profit was $3.808 billion, down from $3.962 billion. Tariff recoveries added $110 million this quarter.
Deere sells farm, lawn and construction machines, and lends money to buyers. Big farm gear was 45% of equipment sales in 2025.
In 2025, weak farm markets meant fewer sales, more discounts and more unpaid loans written off. They expected some of this in 2026.
New tariffs (import taxes) cost Deere about $600 million directly in 2025. Nearly 80% of its U.S. sales are built in the U.S.
Biggest risk they name: farming goes in cycles. When farm income drops, farmers buy fewer machines.
Headlines report Deere closing plants in Iowa.
Other stories ask whether Wall Street analysts feel upbeat or worried about Deere's farm business.

takeaways: The latest quarter came in stronger than the company expected, and it raised its own profit forecast for the year.
The big-farm side is still shrinking; the growth came from small farm gear, lawn equipment and construction.

earnings.headline: Quest Diagnostics grew sales and profit in the third quarter and raised its own forecast for the full year 2026.
points: Sales were $3.10 billion, up 10.0% from 2025, as doctors, hospitals and consumers ordered more lab tests.
Profit per share was $2.78, up 28.7%. Adjusted profit per share (leaves out one-time items) was $3.00, up 15.4%.
They raised their forecast: full-year 2026 sales now expected between $12.065 billion and $12.105 billion.
Not all good: money earned per test order fell 4.2%, even though the number of test orders rose 14.5%.
They make money running lab tests. Health insurers pay 39% of sales, client payers 31, government 16 and patients 12.
Sales are partly estimates: insurers can deny or cut payments, so what they actually collect can change later.
About half of all their costs are worker pay and benefits.
They name cyberattacks and data leaks as a key risk. They say no cyber incident hurt operations in 2025.
Headlines say the stock hit an all-time high of 261.58 USD and the company declared its quarterly cash dividend.
One headline says a company officer sold US$3.02 million in stock.
Other stories compare Quest with rival lab company Labcorp and say it is doing better than other medtech firms.

takeaways: The business is growing: more test orders, higher sales and profit, and the company raised its own forecast.
Some things got worse: they earn less per test order, and long-term debt rose to $5,540 million from $5,167 million.
The release lists an 'incident' from an October 22, 2026 filing as a risk, without details here. Worth watching.

earnings.headline: Profit fell 18% as high mortgage rates and weak demand hurt home sales, though the company raised its dividend 11%.
points: Sales (revenue) were $9.4 billion this quarter. They closed on 22,915 homes, down 2% from a year ago.
Profit fell 18% to $741.8 million. That includes a $91.4 million write-down on nine apartment projects.
New orders fell 7% to 18,619 homes. Cancellations rose to 23% of orders, up from 20% a year ago.
Their own forecast (guidance) for fiscal 2027 is sales of $30.0 billion to $32.0 billion, below this year's $33.0 billion.
They mostly build and sell homes, which made up 93% of $33.0 billion in sales. The average home sold for $363,600.
Yearly profit fell to $2.9 billion from $3.6 billion. Profit per dollar of sales (margin) slipped to 11.8% from 13.8%.
To keep homes affordable, they gave bigger discounts (incentives), like paying down buyers' mortgage rates.
Biggest risks they name: high mortgage rates, a weaker economy, and buyers backing out of signed contracts.
Most headlines are analyst opinions and price forecasts about the stock, not new company news.
One report says a fund manager (Pictet) cut its stake and the stock remains under pressure.
Some headlines are about DHI Group (DHX), a different company with a similar name.

takeaways: The company still makes a profit, but it shrank this year as fewer people could afford new homes.
They expect a tougher year ahead: fewer homes (79,000 to 84,000) and discounts staying high.
They hold plenty of cash ($7.2 billion), carry little debt, and raised the dividend (cash paid to owners) to $0.50 a share.

earnings.headline: Danaher's sales and profit rose and came in better than expected, and it raised its full-year profit forecast.
points: Sales (revenue) rose 8.5% from a year ago to $6.6 billion, but core sales, which leave out deals and currency, grew only 3.0%.
Profit was $1.2 billion, or $1.71 per share, up 34.5%. Adjusted profit per share (their cleaned-up measure) rose 11.5% to $2.11.
They raised their full-year forecast (guidance) for adjusted profit per share to $8.57 to $8.62, up from $8.45 to $8.60.
Weak spot: falling sales of respiratory (cold, flu, COVID) tests will slow next quarter; core sales are seen up only about 3.0%.
Danaher sells lab tools, tests and equipment used to study disease, make medicines and diagnose patients.
In 2025, sales grew 3.0% and core sales grew 2.0%. About 59% of sales came from customers outside the United States.
Sales in China fell in 2025, and Life Sciences core sales dropped, while Biotechnology and Diagnostics grew.
Risks they name: tariffs, debt taken on to buy Masimo, tough competition, heavy regulation, and fast changes from AI.
Big investor Dodge & Cox added 9,821,403 Danaher shares to its funds, according to a fund-tracking report.
Coverage focuses on Danaher's growth plan: buying other companies, using AI, and pushing deeper into diagnostics.
Some stories point out Danaher is a key supplier of bioprocessing gear, used to make biologic medicines.

takeaways: The quarter beat the company's own expectations, and it raised its forecast for yearly profit.
Underlying growth is slower than the headline: core sales rose 3.0%, and fading respiratory test sales are a drag.
Borrowing to buy Masimo means more interest to pay: quarterly interest expense was 135 vs 67 a year ago (in millions).

earnings.headline: Disney's quarterly sales rose 16% to $25.9 billion, though an extra week in the quarter helped the numbers.
points: Revenue (sales) grew 16% to $25.9 billion, up from $22.5 billion a year earlier.
For the full year, profit per share fell 18% to $5.63 from $6.85, because last year had large one-time tax gains.
Guidance (their own forecast): double-digit growth in adjusted EPS (profit per share) in fiscal 2027, not counting the extra week.
The dividend (cash paid to owners) rises to $2.00 a share, 33% more than the $1.50 paid in fiscal 2026.
Disney makes money in three parts: Entertainment (movies, TV, Disney+, Hulu), Sports (ESPN) and Experiences (theme parks).
Full-year sales rose 8% to $102.3 billion, but net income (profit) fell to $9.9 billion from $12.4 billion.
Restructuring and write-down costs rose to $1,456 million from $819 million, including severance (job-cut) pay.
Biggest risks they name: a weaker economy, inflation, a strong U.S. dollar and changes in how people watch shows.
Most headlines say the stock rose after results came in better than expected.
One headline points to a worry: profit margins (profit kept from each dollar of sales) got squeezed.
Writers are weighing Disney's 2027 outlook and its plans for new shows and movies.

takeaways: Disney's parks, streaming and sports all grew, but an extra week in the year made the numbers look a bit bigger.
Full-year profit per share was lower than last year, mostly because last year had one-time tax gains.
Disney is paying owners more cash and expects growth next year, but a weaker economy could hurt parks and ads.

earnings.headline: Healthpeak's cash profit per share dipped from last year, but it raised its full-year forecast and signed many new leases.
points: Profit (net income) was $0.02 per share, up from a loss in the same quarter last year.
FFO as Adjusted (a cash-profit measure for property owners) fell to $0.44 per share, down from 0.46 a year ago.
Their own forecast (guidance) for yearly FFO rose to $1.76 - $1.78, but the yearly profit forecast was cut to $0.39 - $0.41.
Senior housing arm Janus Living grew sales (revenue) 78% to $268 million; income from the same lab buildings slipped 0.7%.
Healthpeak owns and rents out healthcare buildings: doctors' offices, lab space for drug research, and senior housing.
This year it planned to split senior housing into a separate public company, Janus Living, while keeping a majority stake.
Risks they name: cuts to research grants, drug pricing rules, tariffs, and higher interest rates hurting lab tenants.
Medicaid cuts and expired health insurance help could hurt the hospitals and doctors who rent their buildings.
A company officer, the treasurer, sold $127,069 worth of shares, per recent headlines.
Other headlines discuss what Wall Street analysts think of the stock and how safe its dividend is.

takeaways: Cash profit per share slipped a bit from last year, but the company now expects a slightly better full year.
Lab space is filling up again (occupancy up 130 bps), but research funding and policy risks are still real.
It pays a monthly dividend of $0.10167 per share, or $1.22 a year; future payments are up to the board.

earnings.headline: Agilent's sales and profit grew in the third quarter, and it raised its own forecast for the full year.
points: Sales (revenue) were $1.88 billion, up 8.1% from a year ago. All three business groups grew.
Profit was $362 million, or $1.28 per share, up 8% from a year ago.
Guidance (their own forecast) for the year is now $7.49 billion to $7.51 billion in sales, raised from before.
Part of the profit boost came from one-time tariff refunds ($17 million). Next quarter's forecast assumes no more refunds.
Agilent sells lab instruments, software, supplies and services to drug makers, medical labs and testing labs.
Sales were $6,948 million in 2025, up 7 percent, after falling 5 percent in 2024. Net income was $1,303 million.
It reorganized into three business groups. Buying BIOVECTRA added about 2 percentage points of sales growth.
Biggest risks it names: tariffs and trade rules raising costs, customers cutting spending, and price competition.
Agilent announced a quarterly cash dividend (a cash payment to shareholders) of 26.25 cents per share.
It launched a new cancer test panel, a product for its diagnostics business.
Other headlines cover routine executive share moves for taxes, not changes to the business.

takeaways: The business grew sales and profit this quarter and raised its own forecast for the year.
Some of the profit lift was a one-time tariff refund, and the company left that out of its forecast going forward.
Debt went up: long-term debt rose to 3,645 from 3,050 (in millions), and cash dipped to 1,758 from 1,789.

earnings.headline: Accenture's quarterly sales of $18.7 billion beat its own forecast and profit grew, but cash flow for the quarter fell.
points: Sales (revenue) were $18.68 billion, up 6%, above their own forecast (guidance) of $17.75 billion to $18.40 billion.
Profit per share (EPS) was $3.29, up 46% vs a year ago, when one-time job-cut costs hit; up 9% if you leave those out.
Their own forecast for next year: sales growth of 3% to 6% and EPS of $14.39 to $14.81.
Worse: cash left after spending (free cash flow) fell to $2.85 billion from $3.81 billion; clients took 50 days to pay vs 47.
They earn money by advising big companies (consulting) and running their tech and AI work (managed services), with about 814,000 people.
Full-year sales were $74.18 billion, up 6%. They gave $11.5 billion back to shareholders through dividends and buying back shares.
Worse: Asia Pacific profit fell as higher costs ate up its sales growth, and the tax rate rose to 25.1% from 23.7%.
A named risk: hacks or data leaks could bring legal, reputation and money harm. They say there has been no material impact so far.
Headlines mention a new outsourcing deal covering 850 roles, part of a big IT and AI overhaul for a client.
Some headlines note the stock fell more than the overall market on certain days.
One headline says record managed services contracts come alongside tougher rules from regulators.

takeaways: Sales and profit grew this year, and quarterly sales beat the company's own forecast.
Not everything improved: quarterly free cash flow dropped, clients paid more slowly, and Asia Pacific profit fell.
Next year's own forecast is sales growth of 3% to 6%. A forecast is the company's plan, not a promise.

earnings.headline: Adobe posted record quarterly sales and raised its full-year forecast, but profit after tax grew much more slowly than sales.
points: Sales (revenue) hit a record $6.76 billion for the quarter, up 13% from a year ago.
Profit per share (EPS) was $4.62 by standard rules, up from $4.18. Net profit rose to $1.83 billion, a smaller gain than sales.
Their own forecast (guidance) for next quarter is $6.80 billion to $6.85 billion in sales. They also raised full-year targets.
Worse spots: costs and taxes rose faster than sales, and cash on hand fell by 560 million during the quarter.
Adobe makes money mostly from subscriptions. People and businesses pay regularly for apps like Photoshop, Acrobat and Firefly.
In fiscal 2025, creative and document sales (Digital Media) grew 11% to $17.65 billion, up from $15.86 billion.
Big risk they name: AI rivals could build tools faster or better, which could pull customers away and push prices down.
They also warn their AI bets may not succeed or make money, and problems with AI could hurt their reputation.
