points: Sales (revenue) hit a record $20.1 billion, up 9% from a year ago, as card members spent more and paid more in card fees.
Profit was $3.7 billion vs $2.9 billion a year ago. Part of that came from a one-time $982 million gain from selling a stake.
Without that one-time gain, profit per share was $4.68, up 13%. With it included, it was $5.42.
Costs also rose 9% to $14.5 billion, and money set aside for legal matters went up. A lower tax rate of 18.1% vs 24.1% helped profit.
Its biggest income is the fee stores pay each time you use an Amex card. It also earns interest on card balances and yearly card fees.
In 2025, sales were $72,229 million, up 10%, and profit was $10,833 million, up 7%. Costs grew a bit faster, up 11%.
The cash dividend (cash paid to shareholders) rose to $3.28 per share from $2.80.
Biggest risks it names: a weak economy, inflation, tariffs and wars. About 41% of card spending comes from businesses.
One headline says the CEO sold $99 million of stock the day before a big drop in the share price.
Other stories cover the company buying back its own shares. The share count is down 27% since 2016.
Writers also compare Amex with Visa and Mastercard and argue about what the stock is worth after the higher forecast.

takeaways: People kept spending on Amex cards, and fewer card members failed to pay back what they owed (1.8% vs 1.9%).
Part of this quarter's profit jump came from one-time items: a gain from selling a stake and a lower tax bill.
The company does well when the economy is strong. A slowdown would likely mean less spending and more unpaid card bills.

earnings.headline: Beam lost more money than a year ago, but its gene-editing drug trials kept moving forward.
points: Net loss (money lost) grew to $134.4 million, up from $112.6 million in the same quarter a year earlier.
No sales are listed. Research costs were $110.1 million vs $109.8 million; office costs rose to $31.5 million from $26.7 million.
Cash fell to $1.0 billion from $1.2 billion. With $200 million more in planned borrowing, they expect it to last into mid-2029.
Next: they plan to ask the FDA to approve risto-cel for sickle cell disease as early as year-end 2026.
Beam builds medicines that fix a single letter of DNA (base editing). All of its drugs are still being tested.
Its sickle cell trial, BEACON, finished signing up patients, and all doses were made as of December 2025.
Risks they name: they need to raise more money, results can swing quarter to quarter, and approvals may not come.
One trial patient died four months after treatment; doctors tied it to the prep drug busulfan, not risto-cel.
Headlines say risto-cel met its main goal in a sickle cell trial, and a U.S. filing is expected by year-end.
One headline says the stock fell 7% even though the trial met its goals.
Another says analysts' forecasts have become a little darker since the latest report.

takeaways: All of Beam's medicines are still in testing, and it lost more money this quarter than a year ago.
Its first big step could be the risto-cel filing as early as year-end 2026. A filing is not an approval.
Beam says its money lasts into mid-2029, but that counts on borrowing that has conditions attached.

earnings.headline: Sales slipped and profit roughly halved as fewer new homes were started, but the company kept the middle of its yearly forecast.
points: Sales were $3.9 billion, down 2.2%, mainly because fewer new homes are being started.
Profit (net income) was $60.4 million vs $122.4 million a year ago. That is $0.56 per share vs $1.10.
Free cash flow (cash left after spending) fell 83.7% to $76.0 million, from $464.9 million a year ago.
Their own forecast (guidance) for 2026 sales is $14.2 billion to $14.6 billion. They narrowed it but kept the middle.
They make, sell and install building materials like trusses, wall panels, windows, doors and lumber for pro home builders.
They had about 585 locations in 43 states in the annual report. The latest release says about 575.
Biggest named risk: sales depend on home building, which rises and falls with interest rates, affordability and the economy.
Other named risks: lumber price swings, tariffs, and tough competition. Industry forecasters expect housing demand to fall near-term.
The company held an Investor Day in November, where its leaders presented to investors.
Several analysts kept neutral-style ratings on the stock. One headline notes the shares fell 56%.

takeaways: Fewer new homes are being built, and that hurt this company's sales and profit a lot this quarter.
Debt is heavier: net debt is 4.1x a year of adjusted EBITDA (a core profit measure), up from 2.3x a year ago.
On the plus side, they have $1.5 billion they can tap and saved about $57 million through cost cuts so far this year.

earnings.headline: BlackRock's sales and profit rose sharply from a year ago, though reported profit dipped from last quarter.
points: Sales (revenue) rose 19% from a year ago to $7,752 million, helped by markets, new client money and higher performance fees.
Profit per share was $10.57, up 25%. Leaving out one-off items ('as adjusted') it was $15.93, up 38%.
Worse: profit fell from last quarter ($1,914 million to $1,659 million), hit by a $564 million noncash charge tied to past deals.
The CEO expects a strong fourth quarter but gave no number forecast. Big institutions pulled $27 billion out of index funds.
BlackRock manages money for others, $14.0 trillion at the end of 2025, and earns fees as a percentage of that money.
It also sells software like Aladdin, a platform other firms use to manage investments and risk.
Big change: on July 1, 2025 it bought HPS Investment Partners, a large manager of loans to companies.
Risks they name: market drops shrink fees, clients can leave, tough competition, and fitting bought companies in smoothly.
BlackRock declared a $5.73 quarterly dividend (cash paid to shareholders), up from $5.21 a year earlier.
UK regulators named Aladdin a 'critical third party', meaning extra oversight because so many firms rely on it.
BlackRock was reported among the investors in a Bajaj Finance share sale.

takeaways: Clients handed BlackRock $205 billion in new money this quarter, and sales and adjusted profit grew fast from a year ago.
Reported profit fell from last quarter due to a paper charge, and taxes took a bigger bite: 29.4% vs 25.2%.
Its income moves with markets: if stocks and bonds fall, the fees it collects shrink too.

earnings.headline: Sales fell to $18.4 million, but Blink had its first-ever positive quarter on adjusted EBITDA, a profit measure that leaves out some costs.
points: Sales were $18.4 million, down 32.0% from a year ago. Some customer projects slipped, and Blink sold its car-sharing business.
Adjusted EBITDA (profit before some costs) was $0.2 million, its first positive quarter ever. Net loss was still $6.7 million.
They cut their own 2026 sales forecast to $78 million to $81 million, down from $83 million to $90 million.
A $3 million write-off for old, unusable parts pulled gross margin (money left after direct costs) down to 26.3%.
Blink sells EV chargers and runs the Blink Network. It earns from charging fees, network fees, and selling equipment.
Net loss was $83.4 million in 2025, smaller than $201.3 million in 2024, but they say losses may continue.
In December 2025 they sold 26,666,666 new shares at $0.75 each, which makes each existing share a smaller slice.
Risks they name: slow EV adoption, needing more cash, and an accumulated deficit (total past losses) of about $822 million.
StoneX cut its rating to Hold after sales came in below expectations. Needham kept its Hold rating.
Some headlines report the stock moving sharply, both up and down, around the results.

takeaways: Costs fell a lot: spending dropped 46% from a year ago. That is the main reason the profit measure turned positive.
Sales are shrinking for now, and the company lowered its own forecast. It says it hopes to grow again in 2027.
Blink has about $30.5 million in cash and no debt, but it has lost money for years and may need to raise more.

points: BioNTech plans to buy a Priority Review Voucher from Scholar Rock for $205M. It lets a future drug get a faster regulator review.
Headlines say BioNTech's sales (money from what it sells) are under pressure, which is a worry for the business.
Headlines also mention expanded patent lawsuits: court fights over who owns the rights to an invention.

takeaways: There is no new earnings report or annual report here, only headlines, so the full picture is missing.
BioNTech is paying $205M to speed up a future drug review. That only pays off if the drug works and gets approved.
Sales pressure and patent fights are real risks to watch. Headlines are opinions and news, not the company's own numbers.

earnings.headline: Profit fell to $160 million from $176.5 million last quarter: lending income grew, but fee income dropped.
points: Profit was $2.64 per share, down from $2.92. Last quarter got a one-time $30.9 million gain from swapping Visa shares.
Interest income (what they earn on loans) rose $18.1 million to $370.0 million. Their lending margin rose to 3.00% from 2.91%.
Fees fell to $188.0 million from $202.0 million. Trading income dropped $13.0 million as rising rates cut customer demand.
Loans grew $646 million to $27.7 billion. Problem loans rose to $67 million from $63 million. They gave no forecast here.
A bank in Oklahoma, Texas and nearby states. It earns from loans, deposits, wealth management, mortgages and trading.
Full-year profit rose to $578.0 million, or $9.17 a share, up from $523.6 million, or $8.14 the year before.
Problem loans rose to $66 million, up from a historic low of $42 million a year earlier.
Risks they name: competition from big banks and fintech, cyber attacks, changing rules, and a weaker economy.
A director sold $233,405 of shares and still holds 29,910 shares directly.
Headlines also cover a dividend increase and the stock being up 1.9% since the last earnings report.

takeaways: The core lending business is growing, but trading and mortgage income had a weaker quarter as rates rose.
Profit dipped mostly because last quarter had a one-time gain. Without it, last quarter would have been $156.5 million.
Bad loans are rising a little but are still low. Their capital cushion (safety buffer) slipped to 9.16% from 9.61%.

earnings.headline: Steady contract sales grew 11%, but reported profit per share fell 41% as one-off sales dropped and costs rose.
points: Sales (revenue) rose 5% to $1,669 million. Steady 'recurring' sales from ongoing contracts grew 11% to $1,083 million.
Profit fell: diluted EPS (profit per share) dropped 41% to $0.83. Adjusted EPS, which leaves out some items, rose 3% to $1.56.
They kept their own yearly forecast (guidance): 6-8% recurring sales growth and 8-12% adjusted EPS growth.
Surprise: one-off 'event' sales, like fund vote mailings, fell 41% to $67 million. They also took a $40 million loss on digital assets.
They run behind-the-scenes systems for shareholder voting and mailings, plus trading tech for banks, brokers and fund firms.
Investor communications is the bigger part, about 74% of sales. New contracts signed (closed sales) were $305.1 million this year.
Big risk: a proposed SEC rule could make email the default instead of paper, shrinking their mailing business over time.
Another risk: they rely on a few big clients. The largest was about 7% of sales, and bank mergers can shrink the client list.
Headlines discuss their dividend and whether the stock price is cheap or expensive after a recent rise.
Some stories note more options trading activity and the stock moving differently from competitors on some days.
One story says demand for proxy voting is putting the company in focus.

takeaways: Their steady, contract-based business is still growing, but profit per share fell this quarter.
Much of the profit drop came from one-off items: fewer fund votes and a loss on digital assets they hold.
Watch the SEC email-delivery rule: they expect no hit this fiscal year, but mailing sales could shrink later.

earnings.headline: Sales rose 7.4% to $1.7 billion, but growth from businesses they already owned was just 1.2% and profit per share slipped.
points: Sales (revenue) rose 7.4% to $1.7 billion, mostly from buying Accession. Growth from businesses they already had was only 1.2%.
Profit rose 5.7% to $240 million, but profit per share fell 1.5% to $0.67. Their adjusted version rose 1.9% to $1.07.
Margins got worse: they kept 18.6% of sales as profit before taxes, down from 19.4% a year ago.
No forecast (guidance) was given in this release. The CEO called insurance pricing a challenging rate environment.
They are an insurance middleman (broker). Insurance companies pay them commissions, a cut of the price customers pay.
Sales grew every year from 1993 to 2025 except 2009, when they fell 1.0%. Sales hit $5.9 billion in 2025.
The big change: they bought Accession (RSC Topco). Paying for it added debt, and they warn the benefits may come late or not at all.
Risks they name: losing key staff, cyberattacks, natural disasters, swings in insurance prices, and higher interest rates.
Most headlines are about the third-quarter results and whether the Accession purchase is paying off.
A few articles say the stock lagged similar companies on some days. Another notes an award for supporting veterans.

takeaways: Most growth this year came from buying another company, not from selling a lot more to its existing customers.
Profit is up in dollars, but they keep a smaller slice of each sales dollar than a year ago.
Debt went up after the deal: long-term debt is $7,346 million, up from $6,894 million at the end of last year.

earnings.headline: Sales grew only a little, profit fell, and after a cyberattack the company expects sales to shrink next quarter.
points: Sales (money from products sold) were $5.138 billion, up just 1.5 percent. Urology (kidney/bladder) sales fell 3.2 percent.
Official profit fell to $582 million ($0.40 per share) from $755 million ($0.51) a year ago.
Their own forecast (guidance): fourth-quarter sales to drop about 1.0 to 3.0 percent versus a year ago.
Surprise: a cyberattack first reported August 26, 2026 disrupted operations. The CEO called it a challenging year.
They make medical devices for the heart, gut, kidneys, bladder and nerves. Heart devices were $13,250 million of $20,074 million in sales.
In 2025 sales rose 19.9 percent. Buying other companies, like Axonics, helped a lot of that growth.
Total debt (money owed) rose to $11,436 million at the end of 2025, from $10,746 million.
Risks they name: trade and tariff changes, supply-chain trouble, cyberattacks, clinical trial results and competition.
Some writers are upbeat on WATCHMAN heart-device trial news. Others downgraded it, saying recovery will take longer.
Several headlines debate whether to hold or sell. These are outside opinions, not company news.
Board change: David S. Wichmann becomes lead independent director on January 1, 2027.

takeaways: The company still grew this quarter, but barely, and it earned less profit than a year ago.
A cyberattack hurt operations, and the company itself expects sales to shrink next quarter.
New product approvals and trials keep coming, but they take time to turn into sales.

earnings.headline: Sales fell 11% to $27.1 million, but Bit Digital swung to a profit, mostly because its crypto holdings rose in value.
points: Sales (revenue) were $27.1 million, down 11% from $30.5 million a year ago. Data center rental sales rose 232%.
Profit was $28.5 million vs a $107.2 million loss last quarter. About $16.3 million came from crypto gains and one-off items.
Customers have signed for about $729.0 million of future work not yet delivered; $235.1 million is expected in 2027.
Convertible debt (loans that can turn into shares) rose to $445.3 million, up from $336.2 million in June.
They hold Ethereum (a crypto coin) and earn rewards by staking it, meaning they lock it up to help run the network.
They also own most of WhiteFiber, which rents AI computers and data center space to other companies.
In June 2025 they began winding down bitcoin mining to focus on Ethereum. Mining sales fell to $2.0 million from $7.4 million.
Risks they name: a history of losses, big swings in crypto prices, and legal risks from past operations in China.
Sales came in $5.1 million below what Wall Street analysts expected.
Shares dropped in early trading before the market opened after the sales miss.
Some writers note the stock trades below the value of the $439 million in Ethereum the company holds.

takeaways: Sales shrank this quarter. The profit came mostly from crypto prices rising, and that can reverse.
Data center rentals are growing fast, and signed contracts point to more sales in coming years.
Debt went up, and results can swing a lot with Ethereum's price, so ups and downs are likely.

earnings.headline: Sales rose 11% and profit nearly doubled, though part of the profit jump came from one-time tariff refunds.
points: Sales rose 11% to $2,998 million. Sales at stores open a while (comp sales) grew only 2%, slower than 5% last year.
Profit was $184 million vs $94 million a year ago, but $55 million came from one-time tariff refunds (money back on import taxes).
They raised their own full-year forecast (guidance) to $11.77 to $11.97 profit per share, vs $10.17 last year.
Next quarter looks weaker: they expect $1.60 to $1.70 per share, below $1.80 a year ago, as they spend the refunds on lower prices.
Burlington sells brand-name clothes, shoes and home goods at up to 60% off other stores' prices. Over 99% of sales come from its stores.
It had 1,212 stores as of January 31, 2026 and aims for 2,000 long-term, opening about 100 a year on average.
Biggest named risk: its core shopper has low income, so long-lasting high prices (inflation) can cut what they spend.
They also name tariffs (import taxes), trade rules, war and a weak economy as things that could hurt sales and profit.
Several analysts downgraded the stock or lowered their expectations, with worries about competition.
The next earnings report is scheduled for Nov. 24.
One headline says the stock looks pricey after a big run; another says off-price retailers moved higher.

takeaways: Sales and profit grew, but part of the profit jump came from one-time tariff refunds, not regular business.
Growth at existing stores slowed, and the company expects next quarter's profit per share to be lower than last year's.
Much of the growth comes from opening new stores. Tough times for low-income shoppers are the main risk.

earnings.headline: Sales slipped 2.9% to $3,487 million, but profit per share rose and the company raised its own full-year profit forecast.
points: Sales fell 2.9% to $3,487 million, mainly because fewer cars were built and battery business sales dropped.
Profit per share was $1.08, up 47.9%. Leaving out one-time items, it was $1.39, up 12.1%.
Guidance (their own forecast) for adjusted profit per share rose to $5.20 to $5.35, from $5.05 to $5.30.
Full-year sales forecast is $14.0 billion to $14.2 billion, below 2025 sales of about $14.3 billion.
They make parts for gas, hybrid and electric vehicles, sold mostly to carmakers around the world.
Electric-type parts brought in about $2.6 billion, or 18% of sales; engine-based parts were $11.7 billion, or 82%.
Biggest named risk: electric car adoption could stay slower than expected, hurting returns on big investments.
A tax-refund lawsuit with PHINIA settled for $78 million, but the company still took a $40 million charge.
A quarterly dividend (cash paid to shareholders) of $0.17 per share is due Dec. 15.
Several headlines cover the company's push into power products for data centers.

takeaways: Sales are shrinking as fewer cars get built, but cost control kept profits growing.
Some profit growth came from a lower tax rate and buying back shares, not just more business.
They cut debt by $864 million and returned cash through $175 million in share buybacks.

earnings.headline: BWXT's sales rose 10% to $953.0 million this quarter and profit grew, though company overhead costs more than doubled.
points: Sales (revenue) were $953.0 million, up 10%. Commercial work grew 25%; government work grew 4%.
Profit (net income) was $102.0 million, up 24%. Earnings per share were $1.11, up from $0.89.
Their own forecast (guidance) for 2026 earnings per share narrowed to $4.72-$4.77, from $4.70 - $4.80 before.
Worse: corporate overhead costs rose 111%, and naval propulsion (submarine reactor) work had lower volume.
They build nuclear parts, reactors and fuel, mostly for U.S. Navy ships, plus parts for power plants and medical isotopes.
About 68% of 2025 sales came from U.S. Government contracts, so they depend heavily on one customer.
Big risk they name: Congress may delay or cut funding, and the government can end or change contracts at will.
A one-time contract adjustment added $29.4 million to 2025 revenue and operating income, flattering that year's results.
Headlines say the shares are near a yearly low, even after an earnings beat but missed sales expectations.
One analyst price target was cut. Analyst targets are opinions, not facts about what will happen.
The company refinanced debt: it sold new bonds and bought back older notes due in 2028 and 2029.

takeaways: Business grew this quarter: sales, profit and cash coming in were all higher than a year ago.
Most money comes from the U.S. government, so budget fights in Congress can hurt them.
They expect growth again in 2027, but that is their own forecast, and forecasts can miss.

earnings.headline: Sales kept shrinking, but they kept more of each sale and lost less money than a year ago.
points: Sales fell 8.1% to $64.5 million, mostly because they sold 10.9% fewer pounds of food.
Gross margin (the share of each sales dollar left after making the food) rose to 19.3% from 7.4%, their best in five years.
They still lost money: net loss was $82.8 million, smaller than the $97.0 million loss a year ago.
U.S. grocery sales fell 13.2%, while store sales outside the U.S. rose 13.3%, led by Europe. Sales hit the top of their own forecast.
They make plant-based versions of beef, pork and chicken, sold in grocery stores, club stores, restaurants and schools.
Sales fell 15.6% in 2025 to $275.5 million, down from $326.5 million in 2024.
2025 showed a $219.0 million profit only because of a one-time debt deal. The business itself lost $333.6 million.
Biggest risks they name: falling demand for plant-based meat, a long history of losses, and real meat being cheaper.
Recent headlines report the stock falling on several days and an outside research site cutting its rating.
The company gave hiring awards, including a $500K cash award to a manager for Europe, the Middle East and Africa.
One analysis said profit margins improved, but the sales turnaround is moving slower than needed.

takeaways: The company is shrinking: fewer people are buying its products, especially in the U.S.
It is cutting costs and keeping more of each sale, but it still loses a lot of money every quarter.
Europe is a bright spot. The open question is whether that can make up for falling U.S. sales.

earnings.headline: Cardinal Health grew sales and profit this quarter and raised its forecast for the year, but its medical products unit slipped.
points: Sales (revenue) rose 5% to $67.5 billion, up from $64.0 billion a year ago.
Profit per share (EPS) rose 27% to $2.38. Their adjusted version, which skips some one-time costs, rose 28% to $3.26.
They raised their own forecast (guidance) for adjusted EPS this year to $12.80 to $13.00, up from $12.40 to $12.60.
The medical products unit got worse: profit fell 28% to $33 million while its sales stayed flat at $3.2 billion.
Most headlines are about the stock rising after the results, with several stories on a multi-day winning streak.
Analysts at Argus and Wells Fargo raised their price targets, pointing to strong earnings and drug-business strength.
Some articles ask whether the stock is now pricey after the run-up.

takeaways: Most of the money comes from delivering medicines. That unit's profit grew 17% and carried the quarter.
Part of the per-share jump came from a lower tax rate and fewer shares after a $500 million buyback, not just more sales.
They name real risks: tariffs, the conflict with Iran, Justice Department probes, and falling generic drug prices.

earnings.headline: Sales and orders grew strongly, but a $3.1 billion write-down of its Europe business turned the official result into a big loss.
points: Sales rose 12% to $6.3 billion. Orders jumped ~35%, and orders from data centers were up ~300%.
Adjusted profit per share (leaving out one-off items) was $0.87, up from $0.67. About $0.10 of that came from IEEPA refunds.
Official (GAAP) result: a loss of $3.16 per share, from a $3.1 billion write-down of what its Europe unit is worth on the books.
Own forecast (guidance): 2026 sales now $23.8 to $24.0 billion, up from ~$23 billion. Profit per share trimmed to $2.85 to $2.90.
Carrier sells heating, cooling and cold-transport gear (Carrier, Viessmann, Toshiba) plus repair and service work.
In 2025 sales were $21.7 billion. New equipment was 72% of sales; parts and service were 28%. About 52% came from outside the U.S.
It agreed to sell its Riello business for about $430 million and reorganized into four regional and transport units.
Risks it names: tariffs, supplier problems, weather, cyber-attacks, debt, and possible write-downs of past purchases.
Most headlines are stock-price chatter and forecasts, not company news.
One headline asks what's behind a 3.1% stock pullback. It's a recap of a price drop, not new company news.

takeaways: Demand looks strong: orders rose ~35% and the order backlog (work booked but not yet delivered) is over $8.5 billion.
The big official loss came from a $3.1 billion write-down in Europe. It is a non-cash charge, but it shows that unit is worth less than they paid.
Cash came in strong: free cash flow (cash left after investment) was $674 million vs $224 million a year ago. Truck and trailer sales fell.

earnings.headline: Casey's profit jumped this quarter on strong food and fuel profits, though costs rose and gas gallons at older stores slipped.
points: Profit (net income) was $273.7 million, up 27.1%. Earnings per share were $7.37, up 27.7% from a year ago.
Sales inside stores open a year or more (same-store sales) rose 3.2%. Gas gallons at those stores fell 0.3%.
Fuel profit hit 47.8 cents per gallon. Running costs (operating expenses) rose 8.0%, partly from pay, card fees and insurance.
Their own forecast (guidance) is unchanged: a key profit measure up 8% to 10% and at least 120 new stores this year.
Casey's runs 2,944 convenience stores in 19 states, selling gas, groceries and made-in-store food like pizza.
About 71% of its stores are in towns of fewer than 20,000 people.
Last year sales rose 10.2%, mostly from buying Fikes, a chain that added 198 stores and a fuel wholesale business.
Risks they name: data hacks, food-safety scares, and rising costs for cheese, their biggest food cost.
Casey's is running 40% off any pizza on Saturdays through Jan. 2.
Next quarter's results are due soon, with a company call the morning after.
Most other headlines are stock-price commentary and forecasts, not company news.

takeaways: Profit grew much faster than sales, helped by unusually strong fuel profits that the company says can swing a lot.
Not everything improved: people bought slightly less gas at older stores, and store running costs climbed.
The company kept its yearly forecast and keeps growing by building and buying more stores.

earnings.headline: Cathay earned more this quarter and its problem loans fell, but it wrote off more bad loans and set aside more money for future losses.
points: Profit (net income) was $95.2 million, up from $92.2 million last quarter and $77.7 million a year ago.
Net interest income (loan interest earned minus deposit interest paid) hit a record $211.9 million, up 5.5%.
Money set aside for bad loans (provision) jumped to $28.6 million from $11.2 million, tied to loan growth and recent losses.
Costs rose 12.0% to $103.4 million, including an $8.0 million charity gift and a $5.4 million contract termination fee.
Cathay General owns Cathay Bank. It mainly earns the gap between the interest it charges on loans and pays on deposits.
In 2025, net interest income rose 10.1% to $742.5 million, and profit rose to $315.1 million from $286.0 million.
Loans grew 4.0% to $20.15 billion and deposits grew 6.1% to $20.89 billion in 2025.
Named risks: a weaker economy could mean more defaults and bigger bad-loan costs. Cyberattacks are also a named risk.
The company declared a dividend (a cash payment to shareholders) of 38 cents per share, payable Dec. 7, 2026.
One headline says the company raised its outlook for loan growth.

takeaways: Profit and core lending income both went up, and problem loans fell 18.0% this quarter.
The catch: the bank wrote off $25.3 million in bad loans, mostly from three borrowers, and set aside more for future losses.
Some one-time costs, like an $8.0 million charity gift, pushed expenses up 12.0% this quarter.

earnings.headline: Sales rose 1.9% and profit edged up, but core profit fell 2.2% because disaster claims were much bigger than last year.
points: Sales (premiums written, money customers paid for policies) were $15.1 billion, up 1.9% from a year ago.
Profit was $2.84 billion, up 1.5%. Core profit (leaving out one-off items) was $2.98 billion, down 2.2%.
Disaster claims jumped to $705 million from $285 million a year ago, so the insurance side earned less.
Investment income hit a record $1.89 billion. The CEO expects North America business sales to improve in future quarters.
Chubb earns money three ways: profit on the insurance it writes, income from investing premiums, and life insurance.
It offers home, car, business, health and life insurance in 54 countries and territories. 2025 premiums earned were $53.0 billion.
It now owns about 87.2 percent of Huatai Group, a Chinese insurance and money-management company.
Biggest named risks: hurricanes, fires, cyber attacks and climate change, plus claims costing more than the money set aside.
Most headlines are stock-quote pages and fund holding updates, not news about the business itself.
One headline asks whether company insiders have been unloading shares. No major business events showed up in the headlines.

takeaways: Chubb grew a little this quarter, but bigger disaster claims made its core profit dip 2.2% versus last year.
Its investments lost $4.48 billion in value this quarter, mostly from higher interest rates, even as interest income hit a record.
Over nine months results look stronger: core profit was a record $8.60 billion, up 21.0%. Disasters can swing any single quarter.

earnings.headline: Atmos earned $8.49 per share in fiscal 2026 and forecasts $9.05 - $9.25 per share for fiscal 2027.
points: No sales (revenue) total is given. Profit (net income) for the year was $1.4 billion, or $8.49 per share.
Their own forecast (guidance) for fiscal 2027 is $9.05 - $9.25 per share, which is above this year's $8.49.
They spent $4.2 billion on pipes and equipment this year, over 85% for safety, and plan about $4.5 billion next year.
The yearly dividend (cash paid to owners) is set at $4.36, a 9.0% raise. The quarterly payment is $1.09 per share.
It only sells natural gas, to about 3.4 million customers in eight states, mostly in the South. States set its prices.
It plans to spend about $29 billion from 2027 to 2031, with more than 85 percent going to safety and reliability.
Big risk: "regulatory lag". New pipes go in before states approve higher rates, and full payback is not assured.
Other named risks: pipeline leaks and repair costs, tighter safety rules, bad weather, cyber-attacks, and heavy reliance on Texas.
Several headlines cover the yearly results and the new fiscal 2027 forecast.
About $436.5M was left on Sept. 30 in a stock-sale program Atmos is replacing. New shares can thin each owner's slice.
Some "ATO" headlines are about unrelated groups (Atos Group and another ATO), not this gas company.

takeaways: The company expects profit per share to rise next year, and it is raising its dividend 9.0%.
It is spending billions on pipes. Getting that money back depends on state regulators, and that is not assured.
This is a regulated gas utility. Its main named risks are rules, safety and repair costs, weather, and its reliance on Texas.

earnings.headline: The excerpt shows BXP's size, dividend and debt ratings, but gives no sales or profit totals for the quarter.
points: The excerpt has no sales (revenue) or profit totals, so it can't show whether the quarter's results improved or got worse.
They own 162 properties covering 50.6 million square feet, and six are under construction or being rebuilt.
The dividend (cash paid to owners) is $0.70 a quarter, or $2.80 a year. That is a 4.6% yield at the $61.11 quarter-end price.
Debt is rated BBB by S&P and Baa2 by Moody's, a middle-grade credit score for borrowing money.
They make money by renting high-end office space to companies in six big cities, such as Boston and New York.
About 90% of their rent comes from downtown offices. Those were 89.8% occupied and 92.5% leased at the end of 2025.
In 2025 they signed leases on about 5.6 million square feet, but took on costs of about $138 per square foot to land them.
Risks they name: high interest rates, inflation, tariffs, clients with weak finances, and companies using less office space.
Headlines say BXP beat expectations and raised its own forecast (guidance) for 2026.
One article asks which office landlords' dividends are safest while the office market is in a slump.

takeaways: BXP is a big landlord for top offices. Its income depends on companies continuing to rent office space.
It pays a regular dividend, but that cash depends on rent coming in. It is not promised.
Office demand is still shaky and winning tenants is costly, so occupancy and leasing costs are worth watching.

earnings.headline: CACI's sales and profit grew this quarter and it raised its own forecast, but the cash it brought in was lower than a year ago.
points: Sales (revenue) were $2.5 billion, up 8.2% from a year ago. Only 2.1% came from growth of the existing business.
Profit (net income) was $130.4 million, up 4.5%. Profit per share was $5.84, up 3.7%. Higher interest and taxes held it back.
Guidance (their own forecast) for the year rose: sales now $10,700-$10,900 million, up from $10,650-$10,850 million.
Bad news: free cash flow (cash left after costs) fell to $133.5 million from $143.0 million, and customers took longer to pay.
CACI sells technology and expert staff for national security: software, data, cyber, electronic warfare, space sensors.
Almost all sales come from the U.S. government: 95.6% in fiscal 2026. The military (DoW) alone was 53.6%.
Sales for fiscal 2026 were up 10.9% from the year before.
Biggest risks they name: government budget delays or shutdowns, and the government's right to cancel contracts at any time.
A company director, Debora Plunkett, sold 235 shares at $646.31 each.
A government contract tracker reported a $25M payment to CACI.
Other headlines are stock quotes and analyst opinions, not new company news.

takeaways: The business is growing: sales are up and the company raised its own forecast for the year.
Cash coming in was weaker this quarter, so not every number improved.
CACI depends almost fully on U.S. government spending, so budget fights and shutdowns can hurt it.

earnings.headline: Sales slipped and fewer items were sold, but profit per share rose and the company kept its full-year forecast.
points: Sales fell 1.4% to $2.6 billion. Shoppers bought fewer items (volume down 2.1%), only partly offset by higher prices.
Profit per share rose 5.9% to $0.36, helped by lower costs and bigger earnings from its Ardent Mills flour joint venture.
They kept their own forecast (guidance): sales change of (3)% to (1)% and adjusted profit per share of $1.40 to $1.50.
Cash from day-to-day business went negative: $4 million used vs $121 million made a year ago, partly due to legal payments.
Conagra sells packaged food like Birds Eye, Slim Jim and Healthy Choice to stores and restaurants, mostly in the U.S.
It has four parts: Grocery & Snacks, Refrigerated & Frozen, International, and Foodservice (food made for restaurants).
A big named risk: when money is tight, shoppers switch to cheaper store brands or skip purchases.
Tariffs raised costs of ingredients and packaging, like steel for cans. The company says its fixes may not fully work.
Headlines say Conagra cut its dividend (cash paid to shareholders) by 50%.
Other reports cover a plant closure in Missouri and a planned 2027 Investor Day.
One headline says Birds Eye sweet potato sales ran nearly 175% above their yearly average before Thanksgiving.

takeaways: Fewer people are buying its food, and price increases only partly made up for that.
Profit held up, but cash coming in dropped sharply and debt is still large at $7.4 billion.
Headlines report a 50% dividend cut, so owners may get less cash from the stock than before.

earnings.headline: Caterpillar had a strong quarter: sales rose 17% to $20.7 billion and profit per share rose to $7.13 from $4.88.
points: Sales (money from customers) rose 17% to $20.7 billion, up from $17.6 billion a year ago. All three main business lines grew.
Profit per share was $7.13, up from $4.88. Operating margin (profit kept from each $1 of sales) rose to 20.4% from 17.3%.
Power Generation sales jumped 30%, mainly turbines and engines for data centers. The CEO cited strong orders and a record backlog.
Weak spots: Rail sales fell 5%, Asia/Pacific sales fell 2%, and factory costs rose $252 million in construction, partly from freight.
Cat makes construction and mining machines, engines, gas turbines and locomotives, and lends to buyers through Cat Financial.
2025 sales grew 4 percent to $67.589 billion, but profit per share fell to $18.81 from $22.05, largely due to higher tariffs.
A big named risk: tariffs (import taxes). They expected about $2.6 billion of tariff costs in 2026, $800 million more than 2025.
Their own forecast (guidance) for 2026: sales growing near the top of a 5 to 7 percent yearly target, helped by data centers.
Investor Michael Burry closed bets against the stock (puts) after a nearly 4x gain; one headline says shares are down 46% from June.
Another headline says company insiders have been buying shares after the recent drop.
Other stories debate whether the stock is overvalued, and describe Cat as a way to tap into AI-driven demand for power.

takeaways: The latest quarter was strong: sales and profit both grew a lot, led by power equipment for data centers.
Not everything improved: rail sales fell, Asia sales slipped, and tariffs and freight keep pushing costs up.
The share price has fallen hard even while the business grew. A company's results and its stock price can move in different directions.

earnings.headline: Cboe had a strong quarter: net revenue rose 18 percent and profit per share hit a record $4.08, up 43 percent.
points: Net revenue (sales after trading costs) was $712.2 million, up 18 percent from a year ago, and every sales category grew.
Adjusted profit per share was $3.63, up 36 percent. Part of the reported $4.08 came from a one-time gain on selling Cboe Australia.
Guidance (their own forecast) improved: 2026 sales growth is now 'high teens', and costs are now $830 to $845 million, lower.
Weak spots: Futures sales fell 5 percent, and Cboe's share of trading slipped in options, U.S. stocks and European stocks.
Cboe runs stock, options and currency exchanges in North America, Europe and Asia Pacific. It earns fees on trades and sells market data.
In 2025, about 68% of net revenue came from options and futures, mostly S&P 500 (SPX) options and VIX 'fear gauge' products.
What changed: it began closing its Japan stock business, quit corporate listings, and moved to sell its Australia and Canada units.
Biggest risk they name: losing the exclusive right to list S&P 500 index options. That license now runs through 2051.
Cboe got SEC approval for new 'event contracts' tied to company results (KPIs), with a November launch planned.
A report says Cboe could list options on Anthropic shares as early as November 23.
Headlines say the VIX, the market 'fear gauge' that Cboe runs, is surging again.

takeaways: Cboe makes money when people trade, and trading was busy this quarter, with a record in options that expire the same day (0DTE).
Much of its business relies on one license from S&P. That deal now runs through 2051, which reduces a big risk.
Not everything grew: futures shrank, Cboe lost some market share, and part of the record profit was a one-time gain from a sale.

earnings.headline: Sales hit a record and the company raised its own forecast, but its losses grew much bigger than a year ago.
points: Sales (revenue) hit a record $210.8 million, up 55% from a year ago. Cloud sales jumped 265% to $141.9 million.
Hardware sales fell: 68,881 vs 96,794 a year ago (in thousands of dollars). Profit left after direct costs also shrank.
Losses got much bigger: a net loss of 161,218 vs 22,201 a year ago (thousands of dollars). Research spending about tripled.
Their own forecast (guidance): core sales of $310 to $330 million next quarter and $940 to $960 million for all of 2026.
News reports say the new big cloud deal is with Microsoft. The company's release only called it a top three cloud giant.
Several outlets reported the stock rose after sales beat expectations and the company raised its forecast.
Wedbush, a research firm, cut its price target on the stock by $100, according to Barchart.

takeaways: Sales are growing fast, mostly from renting out AI computing, and it has $26.1 billion in signed work still to deliver.
It is still losing a lot of money. Costs grew faster than sales this quarter.
It relies on a few big customers, including OpenAI, and on getting data centers built on time. The company names both as risks.

earnings.headline: Sales and profit fell from a year ago, but a cash-profit measure rose and the company nudged its full-year forecast up.
points: Sales from renting tower space fell to $966 million from $1,012 million a year ago, down 5%.
Profit fell 12% to $283 million. AFFO (a cash-profit measure) rose 8% to $530 million, helped by lower interest costs.
They raised their own forecast (guidance) for the year: Adjusted EBITDA up $25 million, AFFO up $5 million.
New leasing is heading to the bottom of their $60 million to $70 million range. Dividend stayed at $1.0625 a share.
They own about 40,000 U.S. cell towers and earn rent from phone carriers that put equipment on them.
Tower rent sales fell 5% in 2025 to $4,049 million, mostly from $204 million of lost leases after T-Mobile and Sprint merged networks.
Interest costs rose 4% to $972 million as they borrowed more to pay for spending.
Named risk: rising rates. A 1/4 point rise on their $3.9 billion of floating-rate debt adds about $10 million a year in interest.
Headlines say shares jumped 31% in a month on talk of SpaceX using towers; the company says it is talking to all parties.
Other stories point to customers leaving (tenant churn) and a possible growth rebound in 2027 from new wireless airwaves.
The company declared its regular quarterly dividend, per a GlobeNewswire release.

takeaways: This is a landlord for cell towers: it earns rent, and that rent shrank this year as some carriers left.
Its cash-profit measure is rising because it pays less interest and has fewer shares out after selling its fiber business.
New leasing is tracking at the low end of its own range, and interest rates still matter a lot for its costs.

earnings.headline: Carnival had its best quarter ever for sales and profit and beat its own forecast, but higher fuel prices pushed costs up.
points: Sales (revenue) hit an all-time high, and profit (net income) was a record $1.9 billion for the quarter.
Profit per share was $1.43 on their adjusted basis, about flat with last year. Fuel and currency moves cost $131 million.
Costs per passenger-day rose 4.2 percent, mostly from fuel. A key margin measure fell 1.3 percent.
They raised their own forecast (guidance) for the year. Customer deposits for future trips hit a record $7.6 billion.
They make money selling cruises on brands like Carnival, Princess, Cunard and Holland America, plus islands and hotels they own.
They paid no dividend (cash payout to owners) for the year ended November 30, 2025, then restarted it at $0.15 per share.
They owe a lot: $32,188 million in total debt payments, including interest, are scheduled over the coming years.
Risks they name: war, pandemics, bad weather, ship accidents or illness outbreaks, and people having less money to travel.
Most headlines are about the stock price, such as a 16% gain in a month and a 104% rise over three years.
Some stories note the stock lagged other cruise companies on certain days, and one points to unusual options trading.
One headline is about CCL Industries, a different company that shares the same letters, not Carnival.

takeaways: Carnival just had its best quarter ever, and people are booking future cruises at record levels and prices.
Fuel is a real cost problem: it pushed costs up and kept profit per share flat with last year.
The company still carries a lot of debt, but it is paying some down and S&P upgraded its credit rating.

earnings.headline: Sales grew 22% and the company raised its 2026 forecast, but its profit margin got thinner.
points: Sales (revenue) were $1.633 billion, up from $1.339 billion a year ago, a 22% jump.
Profit margin shrank: GAAP operating margin fell to 26.2% from 31.8%. GAAP profit per share was flat at $1.05.
Their own forecast (guidance) for 2026 sales is now $6.387 billion to $6.417 billion, about 21% growth.
Backlog (signed orders not yet counted as sales) hit a record $8.2 billion. They spent $400 million to repurchase shares.
They sell chip-design software, hardware and ready-made chip building blocks (IP) to chip and electronics makers.
In 2025 they acquired several businesses and agreed to acquire Hexagon's D&E design business, pending approvals.
China sales dropped in 2025 while US rules briefly required export licenses. The US could bring back limits.
They settled US charges over $45.3 million of past sales to a China customer without permission. Audits continue.
Recent headlines say the stock fell, one day down 3.2%, as investors rethink AI-linked design software names.
Some articles ask whether the stock is overvalued after its new AI design platform news.

takeaways: The business is growing fast: sales up 22% and a record $8.2 billion backlog of signed work.
It keeps a smaller slice of each sales dollar as profit than a year ago, partly due to deal and restructuring costs.
US-China trade rules are a real risk. Past limits already cut their China sales.

earnings.headline: CDW's third quarter sales jumped 17.7% and profit rose, but it kept a smaller cut of each sale than a year ago.
points: Sales (money from customers) were $6,755 million, up 17.7% from a year ago, led by storage, servers, laptops and software.
Net income (profit after all costs) rose 6.5% to $310 million, slower than sales because costs grew too.
Gross margin (the cut kept from each sale) slipped to 20.5% from 21.9%, and interest costs rose 19.8% to $66 million.
Financial services sales jumped 73.2%. Their goal: grow 200 to 300 basis points (hundredths of a %) faster than US IT spending.
CDW resells and sets up tech (laptops, software, cloud, security) from brands like Apple, Cisco and Dell for over 250,000 customers.
In 2025 sales rose 6.8% to $22,424.1 million, but net income fell 1.0% to $1,066.6 million as costs grew faster.
Education sales fell 1.8% in 2025, while Small Business sales grew 13.3%.
Risks they name: two distributors supply over 25% of purchases, vendor deals are short-term, a shaky economy, government shutdowns.
Most headlines are stock price pages and forecasts, not news about the business itself.
CDW's CEO and CFO will take questions at a UBS investor conference on Dec. 1.
Some coverage mentions the quarterly dividend (cash paid to shareholders) of $0.680 per share, paid December 10, 2026.

takeaways: Sales grew fast this quarter, but CDW kept a slightly smaller cut of each sale than last year.
Profit grew more slowly than sales, partly because interest, taxes and expenses all went up.
CDW depends on big tech brands and a few distributors, so changes on their side could hurt its business.

earnings.headline: Sales grew from a year ago and the company raised its yearly cash forecast, but profit fell from the quarter before.
points: Sales were $2.6 billion, up 6 percent from a year ago but down 7 percent from the quarter before.
Adjusted (one-offs removed) profit per share was $1.65, down from $2.45 last quarter, up from $1.34 a year ago.
Guidance (their own forecast): $6.00 to $6.25 profit per share this year; cash forecast raised to $750 to $800 million.
They expect a slower fourth quarter, and debt is still heavy: about 4.7x a year of operating earnings.
Two businesses: specialty plastics for cars, medical and electronics, and basic chemicals used in paints, glues and packaging.
In 2025, plastics sales fell 3.7% and chemicals sales fell 11.1%, mostly from lower prices and weaker demand.
Chemicals operating profit dropped 43.0% in 2025. To pay down debt they cut the dividend (cash paid to owners) by about 95%.
Biggest risks they name: their large debt, raw material and energy prices, and swings in the car and building industries.
Celanese agreed to sell more of its Nutrinova food-ingredients venture for about $152 million, keeping an 11% stake.
Headlines also cover Celanese growing production of liquid crystal polymer, a special plastic, in China.

takeaways: Sales are higher than a year ago, but this quarter was weaker than the last and they expect a slow year-end.
The company is focused on paying down a big debt by selling off pieces and cutting its dividend.
Cash coming in was strong this quarter: $461 million left after spending on plants and equipment.

earnings.headline: Record sales of $847.2 million, up 16.8%, but each sale kept less profit as aluminum (can) and fuel costs rose.
points: Sales (revenue) rose 16.8% to a record $847.2 million, led by Alani Nu, up about 24% to $410.1 million.
The flagship CELSIUS brand's sales fell about 6% to $356.8 million. Rockstar's store sales fell 13.2%.
Gross margin (what's left of each sale after making it) fell to 46.8% from 51.3%, hurt by aluminum and fuel costs.
Profit was $127.0 million vs a $61.0 million loss a year ago, but adjusted EPS (profit per share) dipped to $0.41 from $0.42.
They sell energy drinks under three brands, CELSIUS, Alani Nu and Rockstar, mostly made by outside bottlers (co-packers).
In 2025 they bought Alani Nu and Rockstar and made Pepsi the main distributor of those brands in the U.S. and Canada.
Big named risk: heavy reliance on Pepsi for delivery, a large share of sales, and much of the money owed to them.
Another named risk: their brand image could sour fast from quality problems, bad press or social media trends.
Headlines say the shares rose nearly 4% after the quarter, and S&P raised its outlook on the company.
Several stories focus on the shrinking margins and whether the new brand-led leadership setup will help.
Analyst write-ups point to Alani Nu as the brand doing the heavy lifting.

takeaways: Total sales are growing fast, but mostly from Alani Nu and Rockstar. The original CELSIUS brand is shrinking.
Can and fuel costs are eating into profit per sale. The company says cost projects should help over time.
Sales abroad jumped 78% to $41.0 million, still small next to $806.2 million in North America. No number forecast was given.

earnings.headline: Sales grew 22% to $81.4M, led by a 141% jump overseas, but the net loss grew by $35.7 million.
points: Sales hit $81.4M, up 22%. Overseas cannabis sales rose 141% to $12.3M, mostly in Germany and Poland.
They kept less from each sale: gross margin (share of sales left after making the product) fell to 29% from 33%.
Net loss grew by $35.7 million, mostly from $35.8 million in value charges tied to their Canopy USA holdings.
Their own goal: positive adjusted EBITDA (a rough profit measure) during fiscal 2027. That loss is now $2.9M.
Canopy sells cannabis in Canada and other countries, plus Storz & Bickel vaporizers. Amounts are in Canadian dollars.
They had to redo (restate) past reports. Some warrants (rights to get new shares) were wrongly counted as equity, not debts.
Management says its checks on financial reporting were not working well enough as of March 31, 2026.
Risks they name: possible shareholder lawsuits over the redo, more costs to fix it, and partners losing trust.
Headlines say the stock fell 26% in a month.
One report says Q2 sales came in below what analysts expected, and the quarter was a loss.
Some coverage raises questions about how much debt the company carries.

takeaways: Sales are growing fast, especially in Europe, but the company still loses money.
Profit per sale got thinner, partly because Canada cut what it pays for veterans' medical cannabis. Vaporizer sales also dipped.
Past reports had accounting errors and were redone; the company says it is still fixing the checks behind them.

earnings.headline: Sales grew 18% and losses shrank a lot, but the company still lost money and forecasts lower sales next quarter.
points: Sales (revenue) rose 18% to $116.1 million, up from $98.6 million a year ago, and beat their own forecast.
Still losing money: net loss was $35.6 million, smaller than the $66.2 million loss a year earlier.
Their own forecast for next quarter's sales is $105 million to $115 million, below this quarter's $116.1 million.
Gross margin (share of each sale kept after making it) was 36% vs 31%, but 4 percentage points came from tariff refunds.
They make money selling EV chargers, plus subscriptions to their charger software and repair plans (warranties).
They have lost money every year since starting in 2007; total past losses reached $2,111.6 million.
US EV sales fell after the $7,500 federal tax credit ended in September 2025, which can mean fewer chargers sold.
Other risks they name: tough competition, tariffs, relying on few suppliers, and maybe needing to raise more money.
Recent headlines are mostly stock-price pages and daily price moves, not news about the business itself.

takeaways: The business is growing and losing less money, but it is still not profitable.
Cash on hand was $95.7 million, and the company says it may need to raise more money in the future.
Its future depends heavily on how many people buy EVs, and US EV sales slowed after a tax credit ended.

earnings.headline: Sales rose 29.5% to $5.4 billion and profit grew, but cash coming in from the business fell.
points: Sales (revenue) rose 29.5% to $5.4 billion, mostly because they charged more for truck, ocean and air shipping.
Net income (profit) rose 21.8% to $198.5 million. Earnings per share rose 24.6% to $1.67.
Bad news: cash from day-to-day business fell by $151.3 million to $124.1 million, as higher freight rates tied up cash.
No number forecast is given. Truck costs per mile rose 33.5%, faster than prices at 31.5%. Customs profit fell 12.9%.
They arrange shipping by truck, rail, ocean and air, linking 75,000 customers with 450,000 contract carriers.
In 2025, sales fell 8.4 percent to $16.2 billion, partly from selling their Europe trucking unit.
Ocean volume fell 4.5 percent and air tonnage fell 11.5 percent in 2025, as weak world demand kept rates low.
Risks they name: a recession cutting freight, customers not paying, and carriers raising prices faster than they can.
Headlines mention a dividend raise (cash paid to owners) and an extended credit line (a standing loan they can tap).
One executive got a 7,430-unit stock award that becomes theirs in three equal parts over time.
Several articles are opinions on whether the stock is fairly priced. Those are views, not company facts.

takeaways: They are a shipping middleman: when trucking prices rise, their sales jump, but so do their costs.
Profit grew strongly, helped by fewer staff (average headcount down 10.4%) and more automation they call Lean AI.
Profit rose but cash from operations fell. They are also adding RXO, and the CEO's hopes for that deal are not results yet.

earnings.headline: Sales grew and Cigna raised its own yearly forecast, but reported profit fell from a year ago and its pharmacy unit earned less.
points: Sales (revenue) rose 6% to $73.7 billion, with growth in both the pharmacy unit (Evernorth) and the health insurance unit.
Net income (profit) fell to $1.4 billion, or $5.47 per share, from $1.9 billion, or $6.98, because last year had a one-time sale gain.
Profit from pharmacy benefits fell 22% after big client contract renewals. Specialty drugs and health insurance profits each rose 15%.
Their own forecast (guidance) for 2026 went up to at least $30.60 per share of adjusted profit, which leaves out one-time items.
Two main businesses: managing pharmacy benefits and specialty drugs (Evernorth), and selling health insurance (Cigna Healthcare).
About 67,700 workers serve more than 185 million customer relationships in more than 30 markets and jurisdictions.
Biggest named risk: medical costs coming in higher than they priced for. Small misses can swing results a lot.
Other risks: price fights for big pharmacy clients who can switch easily, and new laws on drug rebates and pricing.
Several articles ask whether the stock is cheap or fairly priced after the company raised its earnings forecast.
Other headlines track day-to-day stock moves compared with rival health companies.

takeaways: Sales grew and the company raised its own forecast, but reported profit was lower than a year ago.
Customer counts shrank: pharmacy customers fell 5% to 117.7 million, and behavioral care fell 19% after a lost government contract.
Medical customers grew 2% to 18.5 million, but Cigna plans to leave individual and family health plans on January 1, 2027.

earnings.headline: Cipher started collecting its first rent from AI data centers and grew its contracts, but it still lost money this quarter.
points: Sales (revenue) were $27 million. Adjusted EBITDA, a rough measure of cash profit, was negative $10 million, so it ran at a loss.
First rent came in from Black Pearl, a data center leased for HPC (powerful computers for AI). More data halls are due by year-end.
The Barber Lake lease grew to a 20-year term. Total contracted rent there is now about $9.1 billion, adding about $5.2 billion.
They borrowed $850 million at 0.000% interest, due 2032. These notes can turn into shares, which can spread out existing owners.
Cipher used to earn mostly from bitcoin mining. It is shifting to building data centers it rents to big tech and AI firms.
It reported 4.2 gigawatts of power capacity across 10 sites, with 600 MW of AI data centers being built for two tenants.
Biggest risk they name: the AI data center business may not become profitable and needs a lot of extra money.
New Texas power rules (SB 6) for sites using at least 75 MWs could raise costs or delay projects. Bitcoin prices are also very volatile.
Headlines swing both ways: some ask why the stock is surging, others why it is falling. One says it is down 55% this year.
Jefferies, a research firm, cut its price target (its guess at a fair price) on Cipher and similar AI data center companies.

takeaways: Cipher is changing from a bitcoin miner into a landlord for AI computers, and the first rent checks have started.
It has big long-term contracts on paper, but it is still losing money today and relies on borrowing to build.
The stock has been very bumpy this year, and new Texas power rules add real uncertainty to its growth plans.

earnings.headline: Total profit fell sharply because last year's big stock gains didn't repeat, while core insurance profit held about steady.
points: Insurance sales (earned premiums) rose 5% and investment income rose 10% versus the same quarter last year.
Total profit fell to $459 million from $1.122 billion, mostly from smaller stock gains. Core profit was flat at $443 million.
More disaster losses: costs ate 90.9% of premiums, up from 88.2%. Under 100% still means the insurance side made money.
New business sold through agents fell 12%, led by home and auto policies.
They sell business, home and auto insurance through independent agents in 46 states. Headquarters is in Fairfield, Ohio.
They also sell life insurance, specialty insurance, reinsurance (insuring other insurers) and run a Lloyd's unit in London.
The parent company holds its own investments, owns the headquarters and pays shareholder dividends. 2025 marked 75 years in business.
The company declared its regular quarterly cash dividend (a cash payment to shareholders).
CEO Stephen M. Spray was awarded 10 shares and now holds 17,741 shares directly.
Many headlines are stock forecasts and ratings from outside sites. Those are opinions, not company news.

takeaways: The big profit drop came mostly from smaller investment gains, not from the insurance business falling apart.
More storm and disaster claims made this quarter less profitable than last year, and fewer new customers signed up.
The dividend rose to $0.94 a share from $0.87. They say they have raised it for 66 years.

earnings.headline: Colgate grew sales and profit this quarter and raised its own profit forecast for 2026, though North America got weaker.
points: Sales rose 4.6% to $5,369 million. Organic sales (sales minus currency swings and deals) rose 3.6%.
Profit per share (EPS) rose 3% to $0.94. Leaving out one-off costs, it rose 7% to $0.97.
They raised their forecast: profit per share growth of 5% to 7% for 2026, with sales up 4% to 5%.
Weak spot: North America sales fell 1.7% and its operating profit dropped 11%. Asia Pacific profit slipped 1%.
They sell toothpaste, soap, cleaners and pet food in over 200 countries. Oral care was 44% of 2025 sales, pet food 23%.
About two-thirds of sales come from outside the U.S., so currency swings, tariffs and trade fights are named as big risks.
A new three-year cost-cutting program is expected to bring $200 to $300 million in charges, mostly by 2028.
They also name wars in Ukraine, the Middle East and Venezuela, plus rising costs, as risks to their business.
Most headlines are opinion pieces comparing Colgate's stock with other household-goods companies like Kimberly-Clark.
One headline claims the stock may be 21% below a 'fair value' estimate. That is an outside opinion, not company news.
Several 'CL' headlines are about other companies (Fox, CCL, Mineros) and say nothing about Colgate.

takeaways: The business grew this quarter: more sales, better profit, and a higher forecast from the company itself.
Not everywhere is strong. North America sales and profit went down, even as Latin America grew fast.
Selling in so many countries spreads risk, but it also exposes them to tariffs, wars and currency swings.

earnings.headline: Sales grew 10.1% to $294.1 million and the company turned a profit, as it agreed to be bought out for $7.75 per share.
points: Sales (money from customers) were $294.1 million, up 10.1% from $267.1 million a year earlier.
Profit after all costs was $30.2 million, versus a loss of $2.0 million a year ago.
Weaker spot: adjusted gross margin (share of sales left after direct costs) slipped to 76% from 78%.
No forecast: they stopped giving guidance (their own outlook) because of the pending buyout, and held no earnings call.
CCC sells cloud software that links car insurers, repair shops, automakers and parts suppliers to handle claims and repairs.
More than 300 insurers and more than 30,500 repair shops use its network. More insurers draw more shops, and vice versa.
Profit after all costs fell to $1,688 thousand in 2025 from $31,240 thousand in 2024.
Risks it names: a few big customers drive much of sales and can push prices down; lawsuits say its tool undervalued totaled cars.
A law firm is looking into whether the $7.75 per share buyout price is fair to shareholders.
Banks led by JPMorgan lowered the borrowing costs on a $2.85 billion loan to pay for the buyout.

takeaways: The business is growing: sales rose 10.1% and AI-related sales grew 40% from a year ago.
It is being bought: holders would get $7.75 cash per share and CCC would go private, if approvals come through.
It carries $1.28 billion of debt and stopped giving forecasts, so there is less outlook info to go on.

earnings.headline: Profit per share rose sharply from a year ago, and the company raised the middle of its own full-year forecast.
points: Total sales (revenue) were not given in this release, so it does not show how sales changed.
Profit was $5.19 per share, up from $2.97 a year ago. Their adjusted measure was $5.06, up from $3.04.
Guidance (their own forecast) for the full year is now $12.50 - $12.80 per share: a narrower range with a higher middle.
Downsides: interest costs and a nuclear tax credit hurt results, and wind/solar capture slipped to 96.4% from 96.8%.
They make money selling power from 55 gigawatts of nuclear, gas, hydro, wind and solar plants to about 2.5 million accounts.
A federal nuclear tax credit brought in $320 million in 2025 vs $2,080 million in 2024, down 84.6%, as power prices rose.
They plan to spend about $5.7 billion in 2026 and $4.7 billion in 2027 on plants, nuclear fuel and growth projects.
Named risks: a credit rating cut could require about $2.7 billion more collateral; market swings can shrink plant cleanup funds.
Headlines focus on the strong quarter. One says the stock jumped over 10%, another says it cooled after earnings.
Barron's notes that worries about limits on new data centers don't show up in the company's own forecast.

takeaways: Profit per share grew a lot from a year ago, and the company raised the middle of its own yearly forecast.
New long-term deals with Amazon and Google fund more nuclear power; the CEO says existing customers won't bear the cost.
Watch-outs: a key nuclear tax credit shrank, interest costs weighed on results, and a $715 million plant deal still needs approval.

earnings.headline: Sales jumped 33% to $1.91 billion and profit rose, but higher costs squeezed margins and they now expect results near the low end of their forecast.
points: Sales rose 33% to $1.91 billion. About 15 points of that came from the purchase of GOJO, the maker of Purell.
Adjusted EPS (profit per share, minus one-time items) rose 82% to $1.55 from $0.85, helped by cost savings and a lower tax rate.
Gross margin (cents kept per sales dollar) fell to 40.4% from 41.7% because materials, factory and shipping costs rose.
Guidance (their own forecast) held, but they now expect profit closer to the low end because cost pressures got worse.
Clorox sells cleaners, Glad bags, Fresh Step litter, Kingsford charcoal, Hidden Valley, Brita and Burt's Bees in about 95 markets.
Last fiscal year, sales were $6.7 billion. Sales and profit fell, and diluted EPS (profit per share) dropped 26%.
In April 2026 it acquired GOJO, maker of Purell, to grow with hospitals, offices and other business customers.
Problems they name: a shaky economy changing how people shop, slower categories, and disruption from a new computer system.
Several headlines report a long winning streak in the stock, with reported gains of 23% to 24%.
One report says the stock swung on talk of possible takeover interest. That is speculation, not a confirmed deal.
Clorox declared its regular quarterly dividend (cash paid to shareholders) of $1.25 per share.

takeaways: Much of the big sales jump came from the Purell purchase and an easy comparison to a weak quarter a year ago.
Costs are rising faster than expected, so Clorox keeps less of each sales dollar and expects results near the low end.
Last year was rough, with sales and profit down. This quarter looked better, but the full-year forecast is modest.

earnings.headline: CME had its best third quarter ever for sales, $1.7 billion, as trading jumped in all six of its main markets.
points: Sales hit $1.7 billion, up from 1,537.6 million a year ago. Data sales hit a record $243 million, up 20%.
Profit (net income) was $1.0 billion, or $2.89 per share. Leaving out some one-off items, it was $3.02 per share.
Costs rose too. Total expenses were 595.9 million, up from 565.0 million. Tech costs went from 71.4 to 80.9 million.
No forecast was given in this release. Cash fell to 2,198.5 million from 4,416.9 million at the end of 2025. Debt is $3.4 billion.
CME runs marketplaces for futures and options, which are deals on future prices for rates, stocks, oil, gold, crops and crypto.
Most of its money comes from small fees on each trade, plus selling market data. Sales rise and fall with how much people trade.
It is moving its systems to Google Cloud. It warns that running old and new systems at the same time adds costs.
Biggest risks it names: calm markets cutting trading, tougher rules or a trade tax, more competition, and tech or cyber failures.
Headlines say CME set a record for trading volume in October.
Some articles say the stock has already risen 69% and may be pricey, so a lot of good news could already be in the price.
Several articles compare CME with other financial companies. The rest are CME's own product pages.

takeaways: Busy, nervous markets help CME. More trading led to record third-quarter sales and higher profit.
The flip side: if markets calm down and trading slows, sales could shrink, because trade fees are its main income.
It paid nearly $1 billion to shareholders in one quarter through dividends and buybacks, but its cash pile fell this year.

earnings.headline: Sales grew 9.6% to $3.3 billion, but profit fell because costs rose faster than sales.
points: Sales (revenue) rose 9.6% to $3.3 billion, mostly from new restaurants. Sales at older stores grew only 2.1%.
Profit fell: net income was $339.9 million, down from $382.1 million. Per share it was $0.27, down from $0.29.
Costs rose: labor was 25.7% of sales (was 25.2%), and office costs rose to $185.2 million from $146.7 million.
Their own forecast (guidance): 350 to 370 new restaurants in 2026, and 340 to 360 new U.S. and Canada ones in 2027.
They make money by selling burritos, bowls, tacos and salads in restaurants they own and run themselves.
At the end of 2025 they owned 3,938 U.S. restaurants and 104 abroad, plus 14 abroad run by partners.
The biggest risk they name is food safety: an illness linked to their food could hurt the brand and sales.
Other risks they name: rising wages and food costs, tariffs, cyber attacks, and not growing as planned.
Several analyst articles argue the stock looks overpriced after profit slipped. These are opinions, not company facts.
A marketing stunt: a 'Sneak It In' hoodie designed to carry burritos into movie theaters.

takeaways: More restaurants mean more sales, but right now each dollar of sales turns into less profit.
Customers are visiting a little more: store visits rose 0.8%, the third quarter in a row of growth.
Costs are the thing to watch: wages, beef and office spending are rising faster than sales at older stores.

earnings.headline: Sales rose 13% to $9.4 billion and profit jumped, but Cummins trimmed its full-year sales forecast because pickup truck demand is weak.
points: Sales (revenue) were $9.4 billion, up 13% from a year ago, helped by big demand for power generators at data centers.
Profit was $1.14 billion, or $8.25 per share, vs $536 million a year ago, when $240 million of one-time charges hit.
Guidance (their own forecast) for full-year sales growth is now about 10%, down from 10% to 13%, due to weak pickup orders.
Not all good: the Accelera clean-energy unit's sales fell 15% to $103 million and it lost $56 million.
Cummins makes engines, truck parts and power generators, sold through about 640 distributor sites in about 190 countries.
In 2025 the company earned $2.8 billion on $33.7 billion in sales.
It is stopping new hydrogen electrolyzer sales; charges tied to its Accelera clean-energy unit were $458 million in 2025.
Biggest named risks: emissions rules and a past pickup engine settlement, tariffs and trade fights, and economic slowdowns.
Several headlines say sales came in below what Wall Street expected and the stock fell after the report.
Other coverage focuses on data center demand and supply limits shaping what comes next.
A filing shows CEO Jennifer Rumsey reported a stock transaction; the headline doesn't say if she bought or sold.

takeaways: Data centers need lots of backup power, and that is now Cummins' strongest business.
Weak pickup truck demand made them lower their sales forecast for the year, a real soft spot.
They raised the dividend (cash paid to shareholders) from $2.00 to $2.20 per share, a raise for 17 years in a row.

earnings.headline: CenterPoint earned $0.50 per share this quarter, up from $0.45 a year ago, and raised its own forecast for 2026.
points: Profit was $331 million, or $0.50 per share, vs $0.45 a year earlier. Sales (revenue) were not given in this release.
Main boost: growth and rate recovery (approved price increases) added $0.09 per share; weather and usage added $0.03.
Worse: higher borrowing costs and more shares cut $0.04 per share; losing last year's one-time tax benefit cut $0.05.
Guidance (their own forecast): 2026 now $1.90-$1.92 per share; 2027 set at $2.07-$2.09. They say it may not be met.
They deliver electricity and natural gas to more than seven million customers across four states.
Most money comes from moving power over wires and selling gas; regulators decide what prices they may charge.
They sold Louisiana and Mississippi gas units in 2025; the Ohio gas business sale was completed on October 1, 2026.
Risks they name: storm outages and lawsuits (as after the February 2021 storm), regulators blocking price hikes, costly borrowing.
An insider gave away 1,300 shares on Nov. 17, and Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Group sold 52,612 shares.
Several articles ask what analysts think and whether the new earnings change how the stock is valued.

takeaways: Profit per share rose from a year ago, and the company raised its own forecast for this year.
It plans to spend much more on its grid, now $70.7 billion over 10 years, paid partly with new debt and new shares.
Its forecasts depend on weather, regulators and interest rates, and the company itself says they may not be met.

earnings.headline: Coinbase won a bigger slice of crypto trading and record USDC balances, but crypto held on its platform fell from a year ago.
points: The slides give no total sales or profit numbers for the quarter, so we can't say from them how earnings changed.
Its share of world crypto trading rose to 10.7%, up from 5.6% a year ago. That is the fourth quarter in a row of gains.
Crypto held on Coinbase fell to $377 billion from $516 billion a year ago, though its share of all crypto held steady at 12.5%.
Next: two trading platforms (INTX/Deribit) just merged, and they warn volumes may be bumpy for a while. A new Coinbase Pro comes in Q4.
Sales come from trading fees ($4.1 billion in 2025) and services like stablecoin products and subscriptions ($2.8 billion).
Total sales (revenue) rose to $6.9 billion in 2025 from $6.3 billion, but profit (net income) fell to $1.3 billion from $2.6 billion.
In 2025 they added stocks, futures and prediction markets, and in August bought Deribit, a crypto derivatives exchange.
Biggest risks they name: wild crypto prices, drops in trading, new rules from regulators, and falling interest rates.
Headlines say the stock has fallen lately. One says it is down 23% in the past month, another asks what sent it down 6%.
Coinbase got news on a trust charter (a type of license). One writer says that news could make the stock look pricey.
Coinbase and others back the CFTC, a U.S. trading regulator, in a court fight over futures contracts tied to stocks.

takeaways: Coinbase's results rise and fall with crypto prices. The company says this plainly in its own report.
It is winning a bigger share of crypto trading and earning more from non-trading fees, like its stablecoin products.
Sales grew in 2025, but profit roughly halved, and the crypto customers keep there is down from a year ago.

earnings.headline: Sales grew, debt fell by $1.15 billion and the full-year forecast went up, but cash profit per share was flat.
points: Sales (revenue) were $691.6 million, up 4.2% from $663.7 million a year ago.
Profit jumped to $683.4 million, mostly from a one-time $714.1 million gain on the EQT deal, not normal business.
Adjusted FFO (a REIT's cash-profit measure) was flat at $0.35 per share. Core FFO fell to $0.23 from $0.29.
Their own forecast (guidance) for adjusted FFO rose to $1.31 to $1.33 per share, from $1.26 - $1.32 before.
They rent space in cold warehouses and move frozen and chilled food for farms, food makers, distributors and stores.
They ran 231 warehouses at the end of 2025. Now it is 208, after moving some sites into a deal where they keep a 30% stake.
Named risks include heavy debt, higher interest rates, labor shortages, tariffs and many short customer contracts.
As a REIT they must pay out 90% of taxable income, so they rely on borrowing and outside money to grow.
Headlines say the stock hit a 52-week high at 16.89 USD, its highest price in a year.
One big shareholder, Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Group, reduced its stake. One opinion article was upbeat on the business.

takeaways: Sales and warehouse profits grew, but cash profit per share stayed flat compared with last year.
The huge profit figure mostly came from a one-time gain on a deal. It is not everyday earnings that will repeat.
Debt is lower but still about $3.3 billion, and the company itself says business conditions remain challenging.

earnings.headline: Costco's sales and profit both grew in its fourth quarter, helped a little by a one-time tariff refund.
points: Sales rose 11.2 percent to $93.9 billion in the 16-week quarter, up from $84.4 billion a year ago.
Net income (profit) was $2.998 billion, or $6.75 per share, up from $2.610 billion, or $5.87, last year.
Part of that, $0.15 per share, was a one-time boost from tariff refunds, so the gain is a bit smaller than it looks.
Same-store sales grew 10.7% in the U.S. but 5.0% in Canada. No forecast (guidance) was given for next year.
Costco sells a short list of goods at low prices in members-only warehouses. It had 939 at year end, up from 914.
Yearly membership fees rose to $5,907 million from $5,323 million. Gas made up 11% of total net sales.
Debt due within a year jumped to $2,248 million from $75 million, while long-term debt fell to $3,914 million.
Biggest named risk: it relies on the U.S. and Canada (86% of sales), and California is 26% of U.S. sales.
Costco declared a $30 special dividend (a one-time extra cash payment to shareholders).
It also renewed a $4 billion buyback (money set aside to buy back its own shares).
Headlines say the stock is near a 52-week high; one Yahoo piece says it could be above fair value.

takeaways: Costco is selling more and earning more than a year ago, both in stores and online.
Some of the latest profit came from a one-time tariff refund that is not expected to repeat.
