It leans heavily on U.S. and Canadian shoppers, so a slowdown there would hurt it the most.

earnings.headline: Centuri had a record quarter: sales grew 40% and it kept more profit from each sales dollar, though a couple of units slipped.
points: Sales (revenue) hit a record $1.2 billion, up 40% from a year ago. All four business units grew.
Net income (profit after all costs) was $26.9 million, up from $2.1 million in the same quarter last year.
Profit kept per sales dollar (gross margin) rose to 9.5% from 9.2%, but Canada's fell to 19.6% from 21.9%.
Their own forecast (guidance) for 2026 sales is $3.8 to $3.9 billion. It assumes no storm repair work in the fourth quarter.
They build, fix and upgrade gas and power lines for utility companies across the U.S. and Canada, mostly under long-term contracts.
Their top 20 customers made up 65% of sales in fiscal 2025, so a lot depends on a few big utilities.
Former parent Southwest Gas Holdings sold all of its shares in 2025, so Centuri now runs fully on its own.
Risks they name: weather, cost overruns on fixed-price jobs, rising costs, labor shortages, and lawsuits like a City of Chicago case.
Insider trades: director Carl Icahn sold $33.7M of stock, while directors Patton and Mariucci bought shares.
Other headlines cover the Q3 earnings call and results that came in ahead of what analysts expected.

takeaways: The business grew fast this quarter, with record sales and more profit kept from each dollar of sales.
Debt is lighter compared to earnings: 2.6x now vs 3.8x a year ago. Lower means less strain from borrowing.
Forecasts are not promises. Storm work, costs and a few big customers can swing results either way.

earnings.headline: Carvana sold a record number of cars and made more total profit, but it earned less on each car than a year ago.
points: Sold 217,385 cars, up 39% from a year ago, while the overall car market stayed about flat.
Revenue (sales) was $8.040 billion, up 42%. Net income (profit after all costs) was $483 million.
Profit per car fell to $6,997, down $365. Higher fuel costs and rising interest rates cut about $200 per car.
Their own forecast (guidance): more cars sold next quarter, and Adjusted EBITDA (a profit measure) near the top of $2.7 to $3.0 billion.
They make money selling used cars online, giving car loans to buyers, and selling cars that miss their standards at wholesale.
Since 2012 they have sold 2.8 million cars and brought in $84.1 billion in total sales.
Big risks they name: heavy debt, needing to raise more money, and relying on selling car loans for much of their profit.
Other risks: a recession hurting car buying, high interest rates, and the Garcia family controlling the company.
An investor lawsuit claims Carvana misled people about title and registration (the paperwork to legally own a car).
Several articles debate whether the stock is priced too high and what weaker used-car demand could do to the business.
One research firm, Stifel, started covering the company with a positive view of its growth in cars sold.

takeaways: Carvana is growing fast and making more total profit, but it earns a bit less on each car than last year.
Starting with their next earnings call, they plan to stop giving quarterly or yearly forecasts and focus on long-term goals.
The company carries a lot of debt and faces an investor lawsuit about car paperwork. Both are real risks to keep in mind.

earnings.headline: Sales grew 40% and the company raised its forecast again, but it still lost money, mostly because of a one-time cost tied to its debt.
points: Sales (revenue) were $321 million, up 40% from a year ago. It was the fifth quarter in a row that growth sped up.
They lost $43 million overall. The main cause was a one-time $57 million cost of buying back some of their debt early.
Operating income (profit from day-to-day business) fell 27% to $33 million. Not every profit measure got better.
Their own forecast (guidance): Q4 sales of $348 to $351 million, up 44% to 45%, and 60%+ sales growth in 2027.
They rent out computing power over the internet (a "cloud"), including AI chips, mainly to growing tech companies.
They focus on smaller firms. A research firm expects that market to grow from $138 billion in 2025 to $251 billion in 2028.
They are pushing hard into AI, including tools for "agents" (AI programs that do tasks on their own).
Risks they name: results can swing a lot, profits may not last, and growth could slow as the business gets bigger.
Several headlines say the stock went up, including an 11% gain on a day when tech shares bounced back.
One investment fund opened a new $98.1M position in the stock.
Some articles give outside opinions on what the stock is worth. Those are guesses, not company facts.

takeaways: Sales are growing fast, up 40%, mostly from AI customers. The company's own forecast says growth will speed up even more.
On paper they lost money this quarter. Most of that loss came from a one-time cost of paying down debt.
Big customers (over $100,000 a year) now bring in 41% of sales. Growth depends on AI demand and on building data centers in time.

earnings.headline: Dover's sales and profit both grew in the third quarter, and it still expects double-digit adjusted profit growth per share for 2026.
points: Sales (revenue) were $2.2 billion, up 8% from a year ago. Not counting newly bought businesses, sales still grew 7%.
Profit per share was $2.50, up 14%. The adjusted version, which leaves out one-time items, was $2.88, up 10%.
Guidance (their own forecast) for 2026: profit per share of $8.93 to $9.08 and sales growth of 7% to 8%.
Orders rose in all five units and beat shipments. On the downside, restructuring costs and losses from sold businesses grew.
Dover makes equipment, parts and software in five units, from fueling gear and refrigeration to marking printers and pumps.
About 46% of sales come from outside the United States, which exposes Dover to tariffs, trade limits and political trouble abroad.
It sold its Environmental Solutions Group in 2024 for $2.0 billion, so those results are now counted separately.
Named risks: recessions, rising labor costs or strikes, worker shortages, and employee misconduct that could bring fines.
Most headlines are stock forecasts and price targets from finance sites, not news about the business itself.
Dover presented at an industrial conference, and one site says refinancing its debt could be a notable update.
Two board members each received 970 stock units, paid out as shares when their board service ends.

takeaways: Dover is growing: sales and profit both rose this quarter and so far this year.
Orders are stacking up, with much of the backlog (orders not yet shipped) set to ship in 2027.
It's not all smooth: restructuring costs rose, and tariffs, recessions and labor costs are real risks.

earnings.headline: Dow's sales and profit rose a lot from a weak year ago, mainly because prices went up, though it sold slightly less.
points: Sales were $11.3 billion, up 13% from a year ago, mostly because prices rose 14%. Volume (amount sold) fell 1%.
Profit (net income) was $525 million, up from $124 million. Earnings per share were $0.62, up from $0.08.
Bad spot: the Middle East conflict hurt sales in Asia Pacific, and one segment sold 7% less than a year ago.
Their own forecast: cost cuts and plant closures should add more than $1 billion of profit (EBITDA) in both 2026 and 2027.
Dow makes plastics and chemicals for packaging, buildings, cars and home goods. Sales were $40 billion in 2025.
2025 was rough: sales fell 7 percent and Dow lost $3.70 per share, after earning $1.57 per share in 2024.
They booked $1,856 million in charges for restructuring and write-downs, and cut about 1,500 jobs to save money.
Risks they name: asbestos lawsuits (7,158 claims open at end of 2025), wars, energy and raw material prices.
One headline says Dow's shares are up 41% so far this year.
Other articles weigh what analysts think of the stock; several headlines are about the Dow Jones index, not this company.

takeaways: Higher prices for their plastics lifted sales and profit sharply compared with a weak quarter a year ago.
They are selling slightly less, and the Middle East conflict is a real drag on parts of the business.
2025 was a loss year. This quarter shows recovery, but energy costs, raw materials and lawsuits remain risks.

earnings.headline: Domino's grew sales and profit this quarter, but sales at existing stores were nearly flat and cash left over fell.
points: Sales (revenue) rose 3.4% to $1,185.6 million, mostly from more food sold to stores and more franchise fees.
Profit (net income) rose 9.2% to $152.2 million. Profit per share was $4.60, up from $4.08 a year ago.
Sales at older U.S. stores barely grew, up 0.3% vs 5.2% a year ago. Older stores abroad were up just 0.2%.
Free cash flow (cash left after costs) fell 7.2% to $459.8 million so far this year, partly from the timing of ad payments.
About 99% of stores are run by franchise owners. Domino's earns fees (royalties) on their sales and sells them food.
It has more than 22,100 locations in over 90 markets and calls itself the largest pizza company in the world.
Its U.S. pizza market share rose to about 23.3% in 2025, up from about 22.5% the year before.
Biggest named risks: heavy debt, cheese and other food costs, labor, rivals and delivery apps, and weaker spending.
Analyst firm Baird raised its view, saying it sees a clearer path to better sales and franchisee profits.
Headlines note the stock is up 11.1% since the last earnings report.
A company officer plans to sell 370 shares received as part of their pay.

takeaways: Domino's is still growing, but slowly: more stores and more profit, while sales at existing stores were almost flat.
Profit grew faster than sales, helped by cheaper food buying and the company buying back its own shares.
The weak spots: cash coming in dropped this year, the company carries a lot of debt, and it gave no number forecast.

earnings.headline: Sales rose 5.1% to $3.2 billion, but profit per share fell to $2.05 from $2.19 a year ago.
points: Sales (money coming in) rose 5.1% to $3.2 billion. LongHorn Steakhouse led, with same-restaurant sales up 6.2%.
Profit per share was $2.05, down from $2.19. Last year included a one-time gain from selling Olive Garden Canada.
Leaving out one-time items, profit per share rose 4.1% from last year's $1.97. Olive Garden sales grew only 1.1%.
Their own forecast (guidance) is unchanged: $11.10 to $11.35 profit per share for the full year.
They make money running sit-down restaurants like Olive Garden and LongHorn: 2,202 owned in the US as of May 31, 2026.
Another 167 restaurants are run by other companies under franchise deals, using Darden's brand names.
This year they sold eight Olive Garden restaurants in Canada and started weighing options for Bahama Breeze.
Biggest risks they name: rising food, wage and energy costs, tariffs, and guests eating out less when money is tight.
Headlines say the stock hit an all-time high, and several track what Wall Street analysts think of it.
Darden plans to share its next results on Dec. 18 in a call with a webcast and Q&A.
Some stories cover higher dividends (cash paid to owners); the latest declared is $1.62 per share.

takeaways: More people are spending at Darden: sales grew and every group of brands had higher same-restaurant sales.
Profit per share was lower than a year ago on paper, mostly because last year had a one-time sale gain.
Costs rose too, and short-term debt grew to $979.7 million from $693.6 million, so that is worth watching.

earnings.headline: Sales were $3.578 billion, but profit fell from last quarter and cash flow fell from a year ago, while the low end of the forecast rose.
points: Sales (revenue) were $3.578 billion. Each treatment brought in $415.25, a bit less than $415.87 last quarter.
Profit fell to $3.40 per share from $4.02 last quarter, partly from a $62 million write-down (lower value) of its China unit.
Cash left after running costs (free cash flow) was $276 million, down from $604 million a year ago.
Their own forecast (guidance) for adjusted profit per share is now $14.30 to $15.20. The low end used to be $14.10.
DaVita makes most of its money running dialysis centers. Dialysis is a treatment that cleans the blood when kidneys fail.
It also runs care programs that try to slow kidney disease and lower total health costs. It has centers outside the U.S. too.
Biggest risk it names: profits lean on patients with private insurance, who pay more, and those payment rates keep getting squeezed.
Other named risks: Medicare payment cuts, rising worker pay, supply problems, its debt, and a 2025 cyberattack.
One headline says the company expects fewer dialysis treatments, which is seen as a possible weak spot.
DaVita says it now offers an advanced dialysis therapy at every U.S. center.
Several articles focus on how much cash the company makes and what analysts think of it.

takeaways: Sales held steady, but profit per share and cash flow came in lower than in the periods they were compared to.
This quarter, the cost of each treatment went up while the money earned per treatment dipped a little.
The company slightly raised the bottom of its own yearly forecast and keeps buying back its own shares.

earnings.headline: Devon made strong cash, cut debt and raised its merger savings goal, but a few areas came in weaker than planned.
points: Sales of oil, gas and NGL (natural gas liquids) were $5.9 billion. Profit was $1.0 billion, or $0.88 per share.
Cash from operations was $2.8 billion. After paying for drilling, $2.0 billion was left over (free cash flow).
Their own forecast (guidance) for 2026 is unchanged. For 2027, after a sale, they expect about 525,000 barrels of oil per day.
Weak spots: Eagle Ford oil came in below plan, and field running costs were slightly above their own forecast range.
Devon makes money by pumping and selling oil, natural gas and NGL (natural gas liquids), mostly in the U.S.
At the end of 2025, debt was $8.4 billion. $7.4 billion of it had fixed interest rates averaging 5.7%.
Big change: on February 1, 2026 Devon agreed to merge with Coterra. A named risk is not getting the hoped-for benefits.
Other named risks: swings in oil and gas prices, tariffs, pipeline limits, government and climate rules, and its debt.
Headlines cover the $8 billion buyback (the company buying its own shares) and the $4.2 billion asset sale.
Analysts disagree: JPMorgan raised its price target, while Raymond James cut its target on weaker oil prices.
One headline says the stock fell 19% over 5 straight down days. Activist shareholders want Devon to sell itself.

takeaways: Devon is making a lot of cash and using it to pay dividends ($0.32 a share), buy back shares and pay down debt.
It still owes $10.6 billion. It aims to get down to $9 billion in early 2027 using cash and the Eagle Ford sale money.
Results depend heavily on oil and gas prices, and the merger savings and the Eagle Ford sale still have to happen.

earnings.headline: Sales grew 11% and core profit improved, so Dexcom raised its own forecast for the year, though final profit dipped slightly.
points: Sales (revenue) grew 11% to $1.344 billion. U.S. sales grew 14%, but sales outside the U.S. grew only 5%.
Operating profit (profit from the core business) rose to $327.2 million, from $242.5 million a year ago.
Net income (final profit) dipped to $275.1 million from $283.8 million, because last year had more one-off other income.
They raised their full-year sales forecast (guidance) to $5.20 - $5.25 billion and OK'd up to $1.0 billion in share buybacks.
Dexcom makes money selling glucose sensors that help people with diabetes track their blood sugar, like Dexcom G7 and Stelo.
Risk they name: if prices for their products fall and they can't cut costs, profits could suffer.
Risk they name: insurers don't always cover their sensors, and getting paid can be a hassle, which could hurt sales.
Risk they name: they must answer an FDA (U.S. health regulator) warning letter, and making enough product could be a problem.
Some headlines ask whether a Medicare delay is the biggest risk for the company.
Dexcom marked the opening of its Athenry plant with a commercial production milestone.
Most other headlines are opinion pieces and forecasts about the stock, not news about the business itself.

takeaways: Sales and core profits are growing, and the company raised its own forecast for the year.
Final profit slipped a bit versus last year, and sales outside the U.S. are growing more slowly.
The risks they name are real: insurance coverage, falling prices, an FDA warning letter, and making enough product.

earnings.headline: Clean Harbors had a record quarter: sales rose 21% to $1.87 billion, profit jumped 75%, and it raised its own forecast for 2026.
points: Sales (revenue) rose 21% to a record $1.87 billion, up from $1.55 billion a year earlier. Both main businesses grew.
Profit (net income) rose 75% to $208.1 million, or $3.93 per share, compared with $118.8 million a year ago.
Guidance (their own forecast) went up. They now expect 2026 Adjusted EBITDA, a core profit measure, of $1.44 billion to $1.48 billion.
Caution: one big emergency cleanup brought in about $120 million. Jobs like that don't come every quarter. Refinery work stayed soft.
They collect, treat, recycle and dispose of hazardous waste at over 100 sites. They also turn used oil into new oil products.
In 2025, sales rose 2.4% to $6,030.8 million, but profit fell 2.8% to $391.0 million.
Sales at the used-oil unit fell $47.4 million in 2025. Prices for its oil products dropped and it sold less.
Biggest risks they name: accidents and spills at dangerous sites, tech failures or cyber attacks, and cheaper new ways to handle waste.
Investigators say an explosion at a Clean Harbors hazardous waste plant came after two earlier fires there.
Several articles debate whether the stock price is too high after the strong results and the CEO change.
A company director, Marcy L. Reed, gave away 350 shares as a gift, according to a required filing.

takeaways: Business was very strong this quarter: more sales, much more profit, and a higher forecast for the year.
Part of the jump came from one big emergency job and high oil prices. Those may not last.
Leadership is changing: Eric Gerstenberg becomes sole CEO on January 1. A plant explosion is also under investigation.

earnings.headline: Sales slipped and a $1,050.0 million write-down caused a big loss, but adjusted profit and cash flow held up and the dividend rose.
points: Sales (revenue) were $2,453.7 million, down (1.2)% from $2,483.3 million a year earlier.
A non-cash write-down of $1,050.0 million (an asset now valued lower) led to an operating loss of $(910.3) million.
Without that charge and other one-offs, operating profit edged up to $309.0 million from $305.1 million.
Their own forecast (guidance) for next quarter: sales of $2.410 billion to $2.460 billion, a (5.0)% to (3.0)% drop excluding currency.
They run customer service, sales and back-office work for more than 2,000 clients, paid mostly by staff hours or tasks handled.
About 455,000 staff work in 74 countries; about 89% of sales came from outside the U.S. in 2025, up from 88% in 2024.
Risks they name: cyberattacks, high staff turnover, currency swings and tariffs.
Clients can end contracts early for any reason, usually with 30 to 90 days' notice.
A law firm, Pomerantz, says it is investigating claims on behalf of Concentrix investors.
Several stories cover the company's launch of an AI migration tool.
Filings show large funds, including AQR, holding stakes in the company.

takeaways: Sales are shrinking a little, and the company expects more shrinking next quarter as AI changes its old business.
The huge loss was mostly an accounting write-down tied to a lower stock price, not cash out the door, but it is still bad news.
Cash keeps coming in ($268.2 million this quarter) and the dividend rose to $0.37, while a law firm is looking into investor claims.

earnings.headline: Crocs grew sales 4.6% to $1,043 million and raised its own full-year forecast for the third time this year.
points: Sales rose 4.6% to $1,043 million. The Crocs brand grew 4.4%, and HEYDUDE grew 6.1% after a weak 2025.
Profit per share was $4.52, up from $2.70. Without one-time items it was $3.69, up from $2.92: still solid, but smaller.
Their own forecast (guidance) for 2026 sales is now up about 3%, raised from up 1% to 2% before.
Weak spot: Crocs brand sales in North America fell 2.1%. The growth came from overseas, where sales rose 11.8%.
They sell Crocs and HEYDUDE shoes to other stores (wholesale) and straight to shoppers online and in their own shops.
In 2025, sales fell 1.5%. HEYDUDE sales dropped 13.3%, while the Crocs brand grew 1.5%.
They cut HEYDUDE's value on the books by $430.0 million (brand name) and $307.0 million (goodwill), so 2025 ended in a loss.
Risks they name: extra import taxes (duties) cut gross margin by 130 basis points, plus currency swings and limits from their debt.
Headlines say overseas sales rose 12% and ask whether that growth can last.
Several stories note the stock hit a new 52-week high after the earnings report.
A Crocs x Barkbox dog bed that sold out in minutes is back in stock.

takeaways: The business got better this year: sales and profit are up, and HEYDUDE is growing again after a rough 2025.
Part of the profit jump comes from one-time items like tariff refunds, so the adjusted numbers give a truer picture.
Growth now leans on buyers outside the US, where Crocs shoe sales slipped. Debt is still about $1.29 billion.

earnings.headline: NRG earned much more this quarter than a year ago, kept its 2026 forecast, and agreed to sell some power plants for $4 billion.
points: Profit was $561 million this quarter, up from $152 million a year ago, helped by power plants it bought from LS Power.
Its own forecast (guidance) for adjusted profit per share: $7.90 - $9.90 for 2026 (unchanged) and $8.05 - $10.05 for 2027.
Worse: total cash plus backup credit (liquidity) fell to $6.0 billion, $3.6 billion lower than at the end of 2025, after the big purchase.
Interest costs rose on debt from the purchase, and Texas earnings for the first nine months were $3 million lower than last year.
WSJ covers the $4 billion deal to sell six gas-fired power plants, plus the higher quarterly earnings.
Investor's Business Daily says NRG's buyback plans (the company buying back its own shares) drew attention after the results.

takeaways: Earnings jumped mainly because NRG bought more power plants and Texas had favorable summer weather.
NRG plans to use the $4 billion sale to buy back shares and cut debt, and plans to raise its dividend 8% to $2.05 per share.
The trade-off: more debt and interest, far less cash than at the start of 2026, and the sale still needs regulators to approve it.

earnings.headline: Intellia says it is getting ready to launch lonvo-z, its one-time treatment for HAE, which the FDA is reviewing with a March 10, 2027 goal date.
points: This release is a drug-launch update, not a sales report. It gives no new sales or profit numbers.
Their main drug, lonvo-z, is a one-time treatment for HAE, a rare genetic disease that causes painful swelling attacks.
The FDA (U.S. drug regulator) is reviewing it on a fast track. Its decision goal date is March 10, 2027.
It is not approved yet. The FDA said it does not plan an outside expert panel meeting, but approval is still not certain.
Today their sales come from partners like Regeneron: $67.7 million in 2025, up from $57.9 million. They have no drug for sale yet.
They still lose a lot of money: a 2025 loss of 412,694 thousand dollars, smaller than 519,021 thousand in 2024.
Research spending fell $77.5 million to $388.9 million, partly from job cuts in January 2025. Interest income also fell.
Risks they name: no approval, failed trials, needing more money to keep running, and relying on partners like Regeneron.
Intellia shared more positive trial and patient-reported data for lonvo-z at the ACAAI 2026 medical meeting.
Headlines note the FDA gave lonvo-z priority review (a faster review) and that the March 2027 decision is the big event.
A filing shows State Street, a big fund manager, now passively holds more than 5% of the company's shares.

takeaways: Intellia does not sell any medicine yet. Its future depends heavily on whether the FDA approves lonvo-z.
Its losses got smaller in 2025, but it still spends far more money than it brings in.
Approval is not certain. Good trial results so far do not mean the FDA will say yes.

earnings.headline: Sales jumped 34.1% to $794.0 million and Natera raised its yearly forecast, but it still lost money this quarter.
points: Revenue (sales) was $794.0 million, up 34.1% from $592.2 million a year ago, from more tests and better prices.
Still a loss: $59.9 million, smaller than the $87.5 million loss a year ago. Costs rose 19.5% to $576.1 million.
Guidance (their own forecast) for 2026 sales rose to $3.005 billion to $3.035 billion, up $140 million at the midpoint.
Cancer tests grew 60.9% to about 339,500. Gross margin (share of sales left after test costs) slipped to 64.7% from 64.9%.
Natera makes blood-based DNA tests for cancer, pregnancy and women's health, and checks for organ transplant rejection.
Sales were $2,306.1 million in 2025, up from $1,696.9 million in 2024. About 3.5 million tests were run in 2025.
Losses grew: the net loss was $208.2 million in 2025, up from $190.4 million in 2024.
Risks they name: more losses ahead, insurers may pay less or want refunds, tough rivals, and reliance on few suppliers.
Several headlines say the stock fell after the report, with one saying it was down 16% in a day.
A weekly recap mentions a $6B sales target for 2029 and over $3B expected in 2026.
A co-founder sold $478,944 of company stock, according to Investing.com.

takeaways: The business is growing fast: more tests, higher sales, and a higher forecast for the year.
It still loses money every quarter, though the loss shrank compared with last year.
A boost from updating past payment estimates is getting smaller, and the stock fell after the report.

earnings.headline: Sales dipped slightly and the company still lost money, but losses shrank and a big Sanofi payment lifted the yearly forecast.
points: Sales (revenue) were $68 million, down 3% from $70 million a year ago. Sanofi payments fell; product sales rose 91%.
They still lost money, but much less: a net loss of $31 million vs. $202 million a year ago, helped by big cost cuts.
They raised their own full-year forecast (guidance) to $385 - $415 million in adjusted sales, up from $235 - $275 million.
The raise leans on a one-time $125 million Sanofi payment. Cash fell to $627 million from $751 million at the end of 2025.
Novavax makes a COVID vaccine and an immune-boosting ingredient (Matrix-M), and earns fees and royalties from partners like Sanofi.
2025 sales jumped to $1.1 billion from $682.2 million, mostly one-time money when Canada ended its vaccine deal ($575.7 million).
Costs fell as they shrank their sales and office setup, but they took a $97.8 million write-down (lost value) on their headquarters.
A risk they name: hacks or IT breakdowns could expose data and cause costs. They also now depend on Sanofi to sell the vaccine.
Headlines focus on the $125 million Sanofi payment that raised the forecast and on the smaller quarterly loss.
Stock moves were mixed: some stories said shares rose after the report, another said they fell 8% despite beating estimates.

takeaways: The company is losing money more slowly because it cut costs hard, but it is still not profitable.
Much of this year's boost comes from one-time partner payments, not steady sales, and its cash pile is shrinking.
Future money depends a lot on Sanofi: more payments come only if partner trials, approvals and sales succeed.

earnings.headline: Novocure had record quarterly sales and raised its forecast for the year, but it still posted a small loss.
points: Sales hit a record $193.4 million, up 16% from a year ago, as 19% more patients used their devices.
They still lost money: a $10.4 million loss, or $0.09 per share. That loss is much smaller than a year ago.
Guidance (their own forecast) for 2026 sales rose to $736 million - $743 million, up from $710 million - $725 million.
Note: $4.4 million of sales came from one-time catch-up payments after insurers approved more claims, so it may not repeat.
They sell devices that send electric fields into the body to kill cancer cells: Optune Gio, Optune Lua and Optune Pax.
Most money comes from Optune Gio for brain cancer (glioblastoma), mainly in the U.S., Germany, France and Japan.
New: Optune Pax won U.S. approval for pancreatic cancer, and they sought approval for lung cancer that spread to the brain.
Risks they name: a long history of losses, relying heavily on one product, single-source suppliers, and getting insurers to pay.
The FDA said no to Optune Mya, their device for lung cancer that spread to the brain. That is a setback for growth plans.
Headlines also covered the raised sales forecast, and one analyst firm lowered its price target for the stock.

takeaways: The main business is growing: more patients, record sales, and a higher forecast for the year.
It is still not profitable, though losses shrank and it holds $463.5 million in cash and short-term investments.
The FDA rejection of a planned new use is a real setback. Future growth depends on new approvals and insurers paying.

earnings.headline: NVR earned $248.6 million in the third quarter, down 27% from a year ago, as it sold fewer homes at lower prices.
points: Sales (revenue) were $2.40 billion, down from $2.61 billion a year ago. Homes handed to buyers fell 7% to 5,268.
Profit kept per home fell to 18.3% from 21.0%, hurt by pricier land, price cuts and $24.8 million in land deposit write-downs.
New orders fell 7% to 4,391 homes, and 21% of buyers canceled, up from 19% a year ago.
Bright spot: homes sold but not yet delivered (backlog) rose 10% to 10,121, and mortgage profit grew 7% to $35.0 million.
NVR builds and sells homes (Ryan Homes, NVHomes, Heartland Homes) and runs a mortgage business that lends to its own buyers.
It mostly buys ready lots with deposits of up to 10% instead of owning land, so it can walk away and lose only the deposit.
In 2025 profit fell 20%, new orders fell 10%, and profit kept per home slipped to 21.2% from 23.7%.
Biggest risks it names: high interest rates, buyers unable to get mortgages, weak jobs and confidence, and a slowing economy.
Most headlines are stock price pages and daily share moves, not news about the business itself.
One headline says the shares extended a rally; another says the stock looks fully priced on cash flow estimates.

takeaways: Fewer people are buying new homes right now, and NVR is cutting prices to win them, which squeezes its profit.
The company itself warned that weak demand may keep weighing on home sales, prices and margins during 2026.
It still has some cushion: a bigger backlog of sold homes, a land plan that limits losses, and a mortgage arm that grew profit.

earnings.headline: Sales rose 19 percent from a year ago to $3.79 billion, and profit grew even faster.
points: Sales (money from customers) were $3.79 billion, up 19 percent from a year ago and 8 percent from last quarter.
Profit per share was $3.48 by standard rules ($4.20 by the company's adjusted count), up from $2.48 a year ago.
Their own forecast (guidance) for next quarter: sales of $3,750 to $3,950 million, from 1% lower to 4% higher.
Weak spot: phone-chip sales fell from a year ago, to $411 million from $430 million. Car-chip sales grew 13%.
NXP makes chips for cars, factories and smart devices, phones, and network gear. Car chips are its biggest business.
2025 sales were $12,269 million, down 2.7% from $12,614 million in 2024. Profit per share fell to $7.95 from $9.73.
Its gross margin (profit left after making the chips) fell to 54.7% from 56.4%. The company said lower prices and selling fewer high-profit products caused it.
It bought three companies in 2025, including TTTech Auto for $766 million. Rafael Sotomayor took over as CEO.
A cash dividend (a payout to shareholders) is due Jan. 7 to people who held shares on the Dec. 9 record date.
Most other headlines are stock-price pages or opinions on whether the stock is cheap or pricey. They are not new company facts.

takeaways: Business picked up strongly this year after sales slipped in 2025.
The company approved buying back up to $5 billion more of its own shares, on top of $1.3 billion left from before.
Forecasts are only estimates. The company itself says actual results may differ a lot.

earnings.headline: Sales and profit rose, nearly all buildings stayed rented, and the company raised its own forecast for the year.
points: Sales (revenue) were $1,621.6 million, up from $1,470.6 million a year earlier.
Profit for shareholders was $403.9 million, or $0.43 per share, up from $315.8 million, or $0.35.
They raised their own 2026 forecast (guidance) for cash profit per share (AFFO) to $4.45–$4.46.
Weak spot: rent from the same buildings as last year grew only 1.1%, and the monthly dividend rose just 0.7%.
They buy buildings and rent them long-term to businesses. Tenants pay most costs like taxes, insurance and repairs (a net lease).
They own over 15,500 properties across all 50 U.S. states, the U.K. and eight other countries in Europe.
In 2025 they invested $6.3 billion and sold 425 properties. Their top 20 tenants paid about 35.8% of the rent.
Risks they name: tenants who can't pay or go bankrupt, interest rate changes, competition for buildings, property that is slow to sell.
The company declared its 137th monthly dividend increase.
It announced a change in top leadership (an executive transition), along with severance pay terms.
Some commentary says the company's growth is slowing.

takeaways: Sales and profit grew this quarter, and the company raised its own forecast for the year.
Almost all buildings are rented (98.8%), but rent growth on existing buildings is slow, at 1.1%.
It relies on borrowing and selling new shares to grow, so interest rates and new share sales matter to owners.

earnings.headline: Income and profit dipped from last quarter, and the value behind each share slipped to $15.63.
points: Total investment income (their sales, mostly interest on loans) was $68.2 million, down from $69.4 million last quarter.
Net investment income (profit from lending after costs) fell to $0.34 per share from $0.37, as fees rose and income dropped.
Net asset value (what each share's holdings are worth) fell to $15.63 from $15.70 in June and $16.64 a year earlier.
They will pay $0.30 per share plus a $0.02 extra on December 31, 2026. Loans that stopped paying fell to 6 from 10 a year ago.
They lend to companies that can't easily borrow from banks or bond markets, and earn interest. Most loans are rated risky ("junk").
Full-year net investment income was $133.4 million, down from $152.6 million, mainly from lower interest rates and a smaller portfolio.
They borrowed $299.9 million by selling new bonds and paid down their credit line. Total debt is $1,416.0 million.
Risks they name: tariffs, inflation, high interest rates, wars, and AI shaking up some industries, especially software.
Profit per share matched what analysts expected, but sales came in below their estimates.
Keefe Bruyette and Wells Fargo lowered their price targets, pointing to credit quality and a lower earnings outlook.

takeaways: Income and profit both shrank this year, mostly because interest rates fell and they hold fewer loans.
Losses on some loans and stakes ($92.1 million this year) pushed down what each share is worth.
Fewer of their loans have stopped paying than a year ago, which is a real improvement.

earnings.headline: Old Dominion's sales rose 13.1% and profit per share jumped 28.9%, even though it moved slightly fewer shipments.
points: Sales rose 13.1% vs. a year ago, mostly because they earned 13.3% more per hundred pounds of freight they carried.
Profit per share was $1.65, up 28.9% from $1.28. Costs ate a smaller slice of sales: 71.5% vs 74.3%.
Bad news: shipments per day fell 2.0%, and fuel and supply costs grew as a share of sales.
Their own plan: about $380 million of spending on buildings, trucks and tech in 2026. Demand picked up in September.
They haul smaller loads that share a truck (called LTL). That has historically been more than 98% of their revenue.
2025 was weaker: sales fell 5.5%, net income (profit) fell 13.7%, and profit per share dropped to $4.84 from $5.48.
Freight volume shrank: tons hauled fell 9.1% in 2025, which they tie to a soft U.S. economy.
Risks they name: a weak economy, rising costs they can't pass on, losing big customers, and costly accident claims.
Susquehanna, a Wall Street firm, cut its price target (its own guess at a fair stock price).
A fund reported opening a new $24.8M position in the stock.
Most other headlines are about daily stock moves and options trading, not the business itself.

takeaways: The latest quarter was much stronger than a year ago, after a weak 2025.
They are earning more per shipment but moving fewer shipments, so growth leans on pricing.
They keep returning cash: $400.6 million on buying back shares and $180.7 million in dividends in nine months.

earnings.headline: ONEOK earned more this quarter, moved more fuel through its pipes, and raised its own forecast for 2026 again.
points: No total sales figure was given. Adjusted EBITDA (a cash-profit measure) was $2.24 billion, up 6% from a year ago.
Profit was $1.35 billion, or $2.13 per share, but $336 million of that is a one-time tax benefit, not from daily business.
Guidance (their own forecast) went up: 2026 profit is now expected around $3.985 billion, or $6.30 per share.
Not all good: operating costs rose, and the natural gas liquids unit earned less than it did a year ago.
ONEOK moves and processes natural gas, gas liquids, fuel and crude oil. Most of its money comes from fees, like a toll road.
It plans to hedge (lock in prices) on about 75% of its own monthly gas volumes over time, to soften price swings.
In 2025 it grew by acquiring EnLink, paying with 41 million new shares worth $4.0 billion, and a Delaware Basin JV for $941 million.
Biggest risks it names: less drilling near its pipes, swinging energy prices, inflation, tariffs and higher interest rates.
Headlines discuss ONEOK's Brazos Permian purchase and a deal involving Apollo.
Several big funds, including Invesco and Goldman Sachs, reported opening new positions in the stock.
Some headlines say the stock lagged similar companies on certain days, and analysts updated their coverage.

takeaways: The business had a strong quarter: more volume moved through its system and it raised its full-year forecast.
Part of the profit jump is a one-time tax item, so the everyday business grew less than headline profit suggests.
It paid off nearly $5.5 billion of debt and got better credit ratings, but still faces energy-price and drilling risks.

earnings.headline: Oklo, which has no sales yet, went public in 2024, grew customer interest to 14 GW, and spent less cash than it forecast.
points: No sales yet: Oklo is still building its first nuclear plant, in Idaho, and aims to deliver power by the end of 2027.
It used $38.4 million in cash to run the business, below its own forecast (guidance) of $40-50 million.
Going public brought in $276 million in cash after fees.
Customer interest hit 14 GW, led by a 12 GW deal with Switch, but these deals are non-binding (not final contracts).
Oklo plans to make money by building small nuclear plants on customer sites and selling them the power. It has no plant running yet.
Lost $105.7 million in 2025. Cash used to run the business was $82.2 million, up from $38.4 million the year before.
Costs jumped as staff grew: research spending rose $32.1 million and office and admin costs rose $54.4 million.
Risks they name: no plant built, no binding power deals, and the special fuel (HALEU) is not yet available at scale.
Headlines say the stock has swung hard: some note it is far below its high, others report big one-day jumps.
Headlines mention Q3 results: a loss, and sales below what analysts expected.
One headline links Oklo to a Meta reactor. The filings here do not explain that deal.

takeaways: Oklo is still building its first plant. It has no sales and loses money every year.
There is a lot of customer interest, but most deals are not final, and customers can walk away.
It holds a large cash cushion, but costs are rising fast and first power is still years away.

earnings.headline: Okta grew sales 11% and earned much more profit than a year ago, but its own forecast shows slightly slower growth ahead.
points: Sales (revenue) were $805 million, up 11% from a year ago. Most of it, $793 million, came from subscriptions.
Profit under standard accounting rules was $116 million, up from $67 million a year earlier.
Their own forecast (guidance) for next quarter: sales of $813 million to $817 million, growth of 10%, a bit slower.
They paid off $350 million of old debt in cash and still held $2.299 billion in cash and short-term investments.
Okta sells subscriptions to software that controls who can log in to which apps. Subscriptions were about 98% of sales.
Sales for the year were $2,919 million, up 12%. They earned $235 million, up from $28 million the year before.
Customers paying over $100,000 a year grew to 5,100 from 4,800. They are also building tools to secure AI agents.
Risks they name: hackers (they had breaches, including October 2023), tough rivals, slower deals, and a weak economy.
Several headlines tie Okta to concerns about a DHS data leak. The filings here do not describe that event.
Most other headlines are stock-price chatter and comparisons with other companies, not news about the business.

takeaways: The business is still growing and now makes a real profit, after losing money in fiscal 2024.
Growth is slowing a little: their own forecast for the full year is 10% to 11%, versus 12% last year.
Security is the core risk: Okta protects logins, so any breach can hurt trust and sales, as past ones did.

earnings.headline: Sales grew 9.1% and profit jumped, but sales at older stores fell 1.8% and Ollie's lowered its full-year sales forecast.
points: Sales rose 9.1% to $741.3 million from new stores, but sales at older stores fell 1.8% as shoppers spent less per trip.
Profit per share rose 43.4% to $1.42, helped a lot by tariff refunds (money back on import taxes) of $28.3 million.
Their own forecast (guidance) for yearly sales was cut to $2.928 to $2.941 billion, from $2.980 to $3.000 billion.
They spent $84.0 million buying back their own shares and now plan about $175 million for the year, up from $125 million.
Ollie's buys leftover and extra brand-name goods cheap and sells them in stores at prices up to 70% below normal stores.
Opening new stores is their main way to grow. They had 645 stores in 34 states as of January 31, 2026.
Risks they name: weaker shopper spending, tariffs (import taxes), bad weather, and trouble at their warehouses.
They sell only in stores, with no online shopping, which they say could make it harder to win and keep customers.
Ollie's own survey says 78% of shoppers want earlier holiday discounts or are bargain hunting before Black Friday.
Analysts are split after the second-quarter results. Some headlines call the stock cheap, others call it overvalued.

takeaways: The company keeps growing by opening more stores, but shoppers at existing stores are spending less.
Much of the profit jump came from tariff refunds, which they plan to spend on lowering prices.
They lowered their sales forecast but raised their profit forecast, so the picture is mixed.

earnings.headline: Omnicom's sales and profit grew this quarter, helped by its merger with rival Interpublic (IPG) and the cost cuts that came with it.
points: Core sales (revenue) were $6.0 billion, up 7.2% from real growth, not from buying firms or currency swings.
Adjusted profit per share was $2.73, up 22%. The official figure was $2.38, up from $1.75 a year ago.
They say they're on track for $900 million in merger cost savings in 2026. That helped lift margin to 18.2% from 16.2%.
Bad news: interest on debt rose $61.0 million to $104.2 million, mostly from debt that came with the IPG deal.
Omnicom owns ad, media, PR and marketing agencies. Big companies pay them to plan, make and place their ads.
Big change: it bought rival IPG on November 26, 2025. Old Omnicom owners now hold about 60.6% of the combined firm.
Biggest risk they name: a weak economy. Clients may cut or delay ad spending, which would cut Omnicom's sales.
Other risks: inflation raising their costs, and getting stuck with media bills if a client doesn't pay.
Recent headlines are mostly stock-chart and analyst-opinion pieces, not new news from the company itself.
A couple of opinion articles argue Omnicom is doing better than others in its industry.

takeaways: The big merger is showing up in the results: more sales, a bigger profit margin, and large planned cost savings.
The deal also brought more debt, so the company now pays a lot more in interest.
Omnicom does well when companies spend on ads. A weaker economy is the main thing that could hurt it.

earnings.headline: Sales rose 9% to $5.12 billion and profit per share rose 14% to $0.97, helped partly by a $39 million tariff refund.
points: Revenue (sales) grew 9% to $5.12 billion, from $4.71 billion a year ago. Sales at stores open a year or more rose 7.2%.
Net income (profit) rose 8% to $786 million. But they kept a slightly smaller slice of each sales dollar: 15.3% vs 15.4%.
Profit per share rose 14% to $0.97, partly because they repurchased stock: 812 million shares now vs 853 million a year ago.
Guidance (their own forecast) went up: full-year sales of $19.0 billion to $19.3 billion, profit per share $3.25 to $3.35.
They sell car parts, tools and supplies to do-it-yourself drivers and to repair shops. They call this their dual market strategy.
At the end of 2025 they had 6,447 stores in 48 states and Puerto Rico, 112 in Mexico and 26 in Canada.
Older cars help them. The average U.S. car age rose from 11.4 years in 2014 to 12.6 years in 2024, and old cars need more repairs.
Risks they name: a weaker economy, tough rivals incl. cheaper online sellers, tariffs, more debt, and new car tech needing fewer repairs.
Several analyst sites debate whether the stock is priced too high for its growth. One firm started coverage with a positive rating.
A company insider sold shares worth $1,269,078, per an SEC filing. Insider sales happen for many reasons.

takeaways: The business got bigger: more sales and more stores, and the company raised its own forecast for the year.
Part of the profit jump came from a one-time tariff refund and fewer shares, not only from selling more parts.
Share repurchases cost $3.47 billion in 2026 so far, while rising debt is one of the risks the company names.

earnings.headline: Sales rose 6% to $3.9 billion, but adjusted profit (leaving out one-time items) slipped and adjusted EPS of $1.05 was flat.
points: Sales up 6% to $3.9 billion. Service (upkeep, repairs, upgrades) sales grew 8%. New Equipment (new elevators) sales grew 3%.
Adjusted operating profit (business profit, minus one-offs) fell $6 million to $626 million versus a year ago.
New Equipment profit dropped $17 million to $42 million. New-elevator sales in China fell by more than 20%.
Their own forecast (guidance) for the year: sales of $15.1 to $15.3 billion and adjusted EPS of $4.01 to $4.05.
Two parts: Service gave 65% of 2025 sales and 91% of segment profit. New Equipment gave 35% of sales and 9%.
About 71% of 2025 sales came from outside the U.S., so currency swings can raise or lower their reported results.
UpLift, a cost-cutting overhaul begun in 2023, saves about $200 million a year. Its costs so far total $282 million.
Risks they name: slower building activity, tariffs and trade rules, China policy, inflation, wars and natural disasters.
Some analysts raised their price targets for the stock. These are opinions, not facts and not advice.
Several articles point to Otis's recurring revenue: service contract income that comes back year after year.
A headline says Guinness named two elevators in a building in China the tallest of their kind.

takeaways: Most of Otis's money and profit comes from looking after elevators, and that part keeps growing.
Selling new elevators is getting harder, especially in China, and that part earns little profit.
Sales grew, but profit after one-offs did not. The company still expects roughly the year it forecast.

earnings.headline: Paycom's sales and profit both grew in the third quarter, and it raised its own forecast for the full year.
points: Sales (revenue) were $544 million, up 10% from the same quarter a year ago.
Profit (net income) was $133.2 million, or $2.99 per share, up from $110.7 million a year ago.
Their own forecast (guidance) for 2026 sales is $2.213 billion to $2.218 billion, about 8% growth.
Cash on hand fell to $193.9 million, down from $370.0 million at the end of 2025.
Paycom sells cloud software that runs payroll and HR (people management) tasks for businesses of all sizes.
Most sales repeat (recurring): clients keep paying for the software over time, not just once.
Profit (net income) fell to $453.4 million in 2025, down from $502.0 million in 2024.
Big risks they name: hackers and data leaks, privacy laws, tough rivals, and new tech like AI changing the field.
Several articles debate whether the stock price is fair after the company raised its 2026 forecast.
Filings show company officers, including the COO (chief operating officer), selling or planning to sell shares.

takeaways: The latest quarter was strong: sales and profit grew, and the company raised its own forecast.
Not everything improved: cash on hand dropped a lot this year, and full-year profit fell in 2025.
Clients pay again and again, but the company says its results are sensitive to the job market.

earnings.headline: Paychex grew sales 6% and profit per share 14% last quarter, and raised part of its forecast for the year.
points: Sales rose 6% to $1.6 billion. Payroll and HR software sales grew 4%; outsourced HR and insurance sales grew 12%.
Profit per share rose 14% to $1.21, from $1.06. Lower costs tied to a past acquisition helped.
Guidance (their own forecast): yearly sales growth of 5% to 6%, unchanged. HR and insurance forecast raised to 7% to 8%.
Weak spots: 'other income' fell 54% and taxes rose 19%. Long-term debt is $4.6 billion vs $1.0 billion in cash and investments.
Paychex runs payroll, HR help, benefits and insurance for about 840,000 customers; about 800,000 use its payroll service.
Over 60% of its sales come from things other than payroll, like HR advice, benefits and insurance.
In April 2025 it bought Paycor, a payroll and HR software maker, to reach bigger businesses.
Risks it names: AI mistakes, hacks and data leaks, rising health insurance costs, and a weak economy hurting small clients.
Bank of America restarted coverage of Paychex with a neutral rating; other analysts' views are mixed.
Several articles compare Paychex with rival ADP, mostly on the dividends (cash paid to owners) each one pays.

takeaways: The business grew: more sales and more profit than a year ago, with outsourced HR and insurance growing fastest.
Last quarter it paid $424.1 million in dividends, a bit more than the $413.5 million in cash its operations brought in.
Its forecast is only its own guess, and the company itself warns a changing economy could alter it.

earnings.headline: PACCAR's sales and profit grew strongly from a year ago, helped by better truck profit margins and record parts sales.
points: Sales (revenue) rose 19% to $7.94 billion, up from $6.67 billion in the same quarter last year.
Profit (net income) jumped 44% to $847.5 million, from $590.0 million a year earlier.
Parts hit record sales of $1.78 billion, but parts profit dipped to $404.4 million from $410.0 million.
Their forecast: 2027 U.S./Canada big-truck sales of 240,000–280,000, versus 240,000–260,000 expected for 2026.
They build Kenworth, Peterbilt and DAF trucks (68% of 2025 sales), and also sell parts and lend money to truck buyers.
2025 was a weaker year: sales fell to $28.44 billion from $33.66 billion as truck deliveries dropped 22%.
Profit fell to $2.38 billion in 2025 from $4.16 billion in 2024, including a $264.5 million Europe lawsuit charge.
Risks they name: U.S. import tariffs hurting orders and margins, and more unpaid truck loans if the economy weakens.
Several articles argue the stock looks undervalued after a 113% rise; these are outside opinions, not company facts.
Some big investment funds reported opening or adding to PACCAR share positions.
One article looks at the parts business growth and the company's 2026 sales forecast.

takeaways: Truck demand is recovering after a weak 2025, and profit grew faster than sales this quarter.
The parts business set a sales record, but its profit was a little lower than last year.
Tariffs and the economy are the big swing factors, and the company's own forecasts can change.

earnings.headline: Sales grew 19% to $402 million and beat the company's own forecast, but it still lost money under strict accounting rules.
points: Revenue (sales) was $402 million, up 19% from a year ago. About 2 percentage points of that came from buying DroneDeploy.
Under strict accounting rules (GAAP) they still lost money. Leaving out costs like stock pay, profit was 23% of sales.
Cash grew slower than sales: free cash flow (cash left after spending) was $73 million, up 8% from a year ago.
They raised their full-year forecast (guidance). For the fourth quarter they expect $420 million to $422 million in sales.
They sell subscriptions to construction software, priced by the products used and the dollar value of building work run on it.
Sales grew to $1.3 billion in 2025 from $1.2 billion in 2024, but they warn the growth rate has slowed and may keep slowing.
They lost $100.8 million in 2025 and have a history of losses. They say they are not sure when, or if, they will stay profitable.
Big risks they name: a shaky mood in construction, the wider economy, and whether new spending on sales teams pays off.
Several insiders, including a director and the chief legal officer, sold shares, some under preset trading plans.
Investment firm ICONIQ handed its Procore shares out to its own partners for no money in return, not a sale for cash.
Most other headlines are stock price pages and forecasts, which say little about how the business itself is doing.

takeaways: The business is growing and beat its own forecast, partly helped by buying another company, DroneDeploy.
It shows solid profit on an adjusted basis, but under strict accounting rules it still loses money.
Customers mostly stay: they kept 95% of revenue from existing customers, and big customers grew 14%.

points: PDD (owner of the Temu shopping app) earned more profit than experts expected, but sales came in below forecasts.
Headlines say the profit beat ended a string of declines, and shares jumped 8% after the report.
Bad news too: shares fell after bank Morgan Stanley downgraded the stock, and one headline notes a 42% slump.

takeaways: The latest quarter was mixed: profit (what's left after costs) beat expectations, but sales (revenue) missed.
Opinions are split. Some headlines call the stock cheap, while a big bank lowered its rating.
These are only headlines, not the company's own report, so details on sales, profit and its forecast are missing here.

earnings.headline: Official profit dropped sharply, but adjusted profit rose slightly and the full-year forecast held.
points: Official profit fell to $376 million ($0.76 a share) from $622 million ($1.24) a year ago.
Adjusted profit (skips one-off items and market swings) edged up to $1.15 a share from $1.13.
They kept their own 2026 forecast (guidance) for adjusted profit: $4.28 to $4.40 a share.
Power-plant arm lost $130 million vs a $107 million profit, partly from market-value swings left out of adjusted profit.
Mostly a regulated utility: NJ's largest power-line and gas network, plus nuclear plants selling power to the grid.
Rate base (assets regulators let them earn on) grew from about $34 billion to about $36 billion in 2025.
Plans to spend $24 billion to $28 billion in total over 2026-2030 on the grid, gas pipes and energy-saving programs.
Risks they name: a new summer no-shutoff rule raised unpaid bills, plus interest rates, unclear tax rules and tariffs.
One analysis says the bull case could change after weaker quarterly earnings.
PSEG Long Island warned customers about utility scams on Scam Awareness Day.
Other headlines are general stock ratings and trading recaps, not company news.

takeaways: The big drop in official profit came mostly from items the company treats as one-offs or market swings.
Their utility arm earned a bit less ($506 million vs $515 million) as wear-and-tear and interest costs rose.
Their own forecast for 2026 did not change.

earnings.headline: Sales grew solidly, but underlying profit barely rose and PepsiCo lowered its own profit forecast for the year.
points: Sales (revenue) rose 5.6% to $25,274 million. Without deals and currency swings, sales grew 3.1%.
Profit per share (EPS) rose 17%, but core EPS, which strips out one-off items, grew only 2%.
They cut their own forecast (guidance): core EPS growth now +2.5% to +3.5%, down from the low end of +5% to +7%.
North America snacks sold at lower prices. A 4-percentage-point profit boost came from tariff refunds, which may not repeat.
PepsiCo makes money selling snacks and drinks under many brands it built or bought.
Discounts and payments to stores, like paying for shelf space, are taken out of sales, so they cut into revenue.
Their tax rate (share of profit paid as tax) was 19.0% in 2025, a little lower than 19.4% in 2024.
Risks they name: unstable world politics, high interest rates and rising costs, which affect what their brands are worth.
Headlines say about 1,000 job cuts are coming as PepsiCo tries to lower costs.
Bernstein lowered its rating on the stock, worried about weak results in North America.
Some articles note PepsiCo has raised its dividend (cash paid to owners) 54 straight years.

takeaways: Sales are growing, helped by international markets and companies it bought, but North America is still struggling.
The company itself now expects less profit growth this year than it said before. That is a step back.
Planned cash back to shareholders stays at $8.9 billion, mostly dividends of $7.9 billion.

earnings.headline: Sales held about flat at $16.6 billion and reported profit fell, but Pfizer raised its own forecast for 2026.
points: Sales were $16.6 billion, about flat vs a year ago. Leaving out COVID products, sales grew 7%.
Profit fell. Reported profit per share was $0.56 vs $0.62 a year ago. The 'adjusted' figure stayed at $0.87.
They raised their 2026 sales forecast (guidance) to $62.0 to $64.0 billion, up from $60.5 to $62.5 billion.
COVID pill Paxlovid sales fell 63% and vaccine Comirnaty fell 29%, while Eliquis rose 25% and Padcev rose 55%.
Pfizer makes money by discovering, making and selling medicines around the world.
Since 2025, 40% of the finance-linked bonus pool depends on 'adjusted income', a profit number that leaves out some costs.
They warn 'adjusted' numbers have no standard meaning and may not match how other companies count.
Risks named include currency, interest rate and stock price swings; they say a 10% dollar move would not hit profit much.
Pfizer and Blackstone signed a deal to share the cost of developing a drug called berobenatide.
Several articles cover the raised 2026 forecast and the 5.9% dividend yield. These are opinions, not company facts.

takeaways: COVID sales are shrinking fast, but newer drugs are growing and filling much of that gap.
Pfizer expects a better 2026 than it did before, yet reported profit for the first nine months fell 40%.
They paid $7.3 billion in dividends (cash paid to owners) so far this year and plan no share buybacks in 2026.

earnings.headline: Core profit per share grew and the dividend went up, but clients pulled money out and several units earned less.
points: Operating earnings per share (a cleaner profit measure) were $2.22, up 6% from a year ago.
Net income jumped to $2.91 a share from $0.95, but another profit measure fell 20% to $1.64.
Clients took out $10.7 billion more than they put in. International Pension profit fell 38% on weak reserve-fund returns.
Dividend (cash paid to owners) rises to $0.85 a share, up 8% from a year ago. The CEO said they are confident in their 2026 outlook.
They earn fees running retirement plans like 401(k)s, managing investments, and selling workplace insurance.
They oversaw $1,814.6 billion in assets at the end of 2025, including $781.0 billion they manage directly.
Rising markets lifted account values in 2025. Fees depend on those values, so market drops can cut their sales.
Risks they name: market downturns, interest rate changes, credit rating downgrades, and job cuts at client firms.
Several articles cover the third-quarter results and the dividend increase.
Some reports say the stock lagged similar companies on certain days. Others look at the retirement business.

takeaways: Core profit grew a little, and the company raised its cash payment to shareholders.
Clients took out more money than they put in, which can shrink the fees the company earns later.
Results move with markets. Weak investment returns hurt several parts of the business this quarter.

earnings.headline: Sales and profit grew in the first quarter, and the company kept its full-year forecast, though one unit's profit slipped.
points: Sales rose 5.5% to $18.0 billion, helped by new customers, acquisitions, and higher prices from inflation.
Profit (net income) jumped 38.4% to $129.5 million. Costs to run the business also rose 6.9% to $1.9 billion.
Guidance (their own forecast): full-year sales of about $72.5 billion to $73.0 billion, unchanged from before.
Weak spot: the Specialty unit's core profit fell 4.8% to $89.5 million as its operating costs rose 9.0%.
They buy food and related products and deliver them to over 350,000 places like restaurants, schools and stores.
Risks they name: a weaker economy, inflation, fuel prices, supply chain problems and labor shortages.
Over five years, $100 in their stock grew to $230, versus $182 for the S&P 500. Past results don't predict the future.
Buybacks: $498.5 million of a $500 million plan to buy back their own shares was still unused.
Several articles review the first-quarter results and what they mean for long-term owners of the stock.
Filings show directors got stock awards, such as 2,990 deferred stock units for director Barbara Beck.
Some analysts and sites published price views. These are opinions, not facts from the company.

takeaways: The company sold more and kept more profit per sale this quarter, led by independent restaurant customers.
Free cash flow (cash left after costs and investment) was negative $143.2 million, less negative than $224.1 million.
Worker and fuel costs keep rising, and the company itself says the economy remains challenging.

earnings.headline: Sales grew 4.0% to $23.3 billion, but profit per share rose only 1% because costs went up.
points: Sales (money from selling products) rose 4.0% to $23.3 billion, and people bought more items than a year ago.
Profit per share (EPS) was $1.97, up just 1%, because higher operating costs ate most of the sales gain.
Gross margin (profit kept from each sale) fell 160 basis points (hundredths of a percent), mostly from pricier raw materials.
Their own forecast (guidance) holds: core profit per share of $6.89 to $7.11 this year, despite a $1.4 billion cost hit.
P&G sells everyday items like hair care, razors, toothpaste, detergent and diapers in about 180 countries.
Walmart is about 16% of sales and the top ten customers about 43%, so a few big stores matter a lot.
More than 50% of sales come from outside the U.S., so currency swings can shrink what they earn in dollars.
Other named risks: tariffs, rising material and energy costs, weak economies, and a large amount of debt.
Many headlines focus on P&G's dividend (cash paid to shareholders) and how steady it has been.
One says the stock hit a 52-week high; others ask whether this 'safe' stock is riskier than it looks.
Wells Fargo raised its price target citing easing inflation; that is one analyst's opinion, not a fact.

takeaways: Sales are growing, but higher costs mean profit is barely growing.
P&G plans to pay over $10 billion in dividends and buy back about $5 billion of its own shares this year.
The main worries are costly raw materials, tariffs, currency swings and heavy reliance on Walmart.

earnings.headline: Sales grew and the insurance business stayed profitable, but quarterly profit dipped slightly as investments lost money.
points: Sales (premiums from customers) for the quarter were $22,301 million, up 4% from $21,384 million a year ago.
Quarterly profit slipped 3% to $2,542 million from $2,615 million, partly due to a $170 million loss on investments.
Insurance stayed profitable: claims plus costs took 88.7 cents of each premium dollar (combined ratio), vs 89.5 a year ago.
No forecast (guidance) was given. Policies in force rose 6% to 40,489 thousand, but home policies were flat.
Progressive makes most of its money selling car insurance. It also covers motorcycles, boats, RVs, homes and small businesses.
Personal lines (cars, bikes, boats, homes) were 87% of 2025 premiums, up from 85% in 2024.
It ranks second in U.S. car insurance by market share, among about 230 competitors.
Biggest named risk: pricing policies right. Bad guesses on claims, storms, inflation or tariffs can hurt results.
Analysts called Q3 results mixed, and the stock fell 3.58% on Nov 18, the day October results were due.
Several stories cover its dividends (cash paid to owners), including $13.90 per share paid this year.
Other headlines mention a new Snapshot Pro launch and a 190% rise in the stock over five years.

takeaways: More people are buying Progressive insurance: total policies grew 6% and sales rose, though home policies did not grow.
The core insurance business made money. The weak spot was investments, as bond values fell in September.
The company gave no forecast. It reports monthly, and October results came out November 18, 2026, not covered here.

earnings.headline: Pulte sold fewer homes and earned less than a year ago as rising mortgage rates pushed more buyers to the sidelines.
points: Sales from homes fell 9% to $3.9 billion, down from $4.2 billion a year ago. They closed on 6,876 homes.
Profit dropped to $476 million, or $2.53 per share, down from $586 million, or $2.96 per share, a year earlier.
They kept less per home: gross margin (what's left after building costs) fell to 24.8% from 26.2%.
New orders fell 6% to 6,208 homes, but the list of sold homes not yet built (backlog) rose 4% to 10,298.
The annual report section here covers one named risk: computer failures or data breaches could hurt the business and cost a lot.
Tech and security chiefs update the board's audit committee every quarter, and the full board at least once a year.
Both the tech chief and the security chief have over 30 years of experience.
Pulte says it knows of no major cyberattack in the last three years.
Pulte raised its quarterly dividend (cash paid to owners) 3.8% to $0.27, its ninth straight year of raises.
One headline says homebuilder confidence just fell to its lowest since 2012.
Other headlines are stock-price chatter; one says analysts cut their growth views.

takeaways: The business is slowing: fewer homes sold, lower sales and lower profit than last year.
The CEO names higher mortgage rates as the big problem. Homes are harder for people to afford.
It is still on solid footing: $1.4 billion in cash, a bigger backlog, and $350 million spent buying back its own shares.

earnings.headline: Sales and profit rose from a year ago and beat their own forecast, but they expect a weaker next quarter as costs climb.
points: Sales (money taken in) were $2.6 billion, up from $2.3 billion a year ago, helped by the Greif box business they bought.
Profit was $262 million, or $2.93 per share, up from $2.51. Without one-off costs it was $3.04, above their $2.91 forecast.
Weak spots: older box plants shipped 0.5% less, paper sales volume fell 2.5%, and freight, fiber and labor costs rose.
Their forecast (guidance) for next quarter is $2.81 per share, below this quarter, due to mill repair shutdowns and higher costs.
They make cardboard boxes and the heavy paper used to build them, plus office paper. They run ten mills in North America.
In 2025 sales rose to $9.0 billion from $8.4 billion, but profit dipped to $774 million from $805 million.
They bought Greif's box-paper business for $1.8 billion in cash. A risk they name: it may underperform or be hard to fold in.
Other risks they name: rising costs, strikes at a mostly union workforce, hacking, and stricter environmental rules.
CEO Mark Kowlzan sold shares at $254 each, and his trust filed to sell 9,378 more shares.
Most other headlines are general stock commentary and fund holdings, not news about the business itself.

takeaways: Growth came mostly from buying another company's mills. Their older box business was about flat.
Profit so far this year is $625.3 million, below $672.3 million at this point last year, so the full year is not all up.
Price increases are helping, but shipping, fiber and worker costs keep rising, and they expect next quarter to earn less.

earnings.headline: Record sales and higher adjusted profit, but reported profit per share fell and costs from energy and Ukraine are rising.
points: Sales (revenue) rose 5.5% to $11.4 billion, a record quarter. Smoke-free products made up more than 40% of sales.
Profit per share fell 4.9% to $2.12 as reported, mostly from an investment value change. Adjusted, it rose 5.4% to $2.36.
U.S. ZYN pouch profit fell 3.3% due to heavy marketing spend. They plan to spend even more in the fourth quarter.
Energy costs from the Middle East conflict are rising and Ukraine strikes disrupted supply. They expect more cost pressure ahead.
They sell cigarettes (like Marlboro) and smoke-free products: IQOS heated tobacco, ZYN nicotine pouches and VEEV vapes.
Sales rose to 40,648 million dollars in 2025 from 37,878 million. Profit for owners was 11,348 million vs 7,057 million.
Debt grew to $48.8 billion from $45.7 billion. On paper they owe more than they own (a 'stockholders' deficit').
Risks they name: money rules in places like Russia and Argentina. $2.3 billion of their cash was held in Russia.
Headlines are mostly about daily stock moves and big funds buying or trimming shares, not new business news.

takeaways: The business is growing: record sales, and smoke-free products are a bigger slice of sales.
Not all good: reported profit per share fell, U.S. ZYN profit dipped, and energy costs are rising.
They raised the quarterly dividend (cash paid to shareholders) by 8.8% to $1.60 per share, but carry a lot of debt.

earnings.headline: PNC made more profit as loans grew and costs fell, but total sales dipped from last quarter and bad loans rose.
points: Sales (revenue) were $6.6 billion, down 5% from last quarter but up 11% from a year ago.
Profit (net income) rose to $2.1 billion, or $4.97 per share, up from $4.81 last quarter.
Fees fell 6% after a busy second quarter for deal advice. Problem loans (nonperforming) rose 8% to $2.2 billion.
Their own forecast: share buybacks in the fourth quarter should be about the same as in the third quarter.
PNC is a bank. It mostly earns money by taking deposits and making loans, keeping the gap between interest earned and paid.
Biggest named risk is interest rates: a sharp rate drop (200 basis points) could cut first-year interest income about 2.9%.
Other market risks named: swings in credit spreads, foreign currencies, commodity prices and stock prices.
Outside auditors said the 2025 financial statements are fairly presented and internal controls worked.
PNC Bank started stablecoin (digital dollar) payments for its corporate and institutional clients.
Most other headlines are stock ratings, forecasts and dividend comparisons, not new company events.

takeaways: Profit went up and costs went down, but total sales slipped compared with last quarter.
Loans grew, but loans not being paid back as agreed (nonperforming) rose 8%. That part got worse.
The quarterly dividend (cash paid to owners) went up to $2.00 per share from $1.70.

earnings.headline: Pentair's sales and profit fell this quarter, mostly because its Pool business slumped, but it kept its full-year forecast.
points: Sales were $976 million, down 4 percent from a year ago. Pool sales fell 18 percent; Flow and Water Solutions grew a little.
Profit per share (EPS) was $0.91, down from $1.12. Adjusted EPS, which skips one-off items, was $1.18 vs $1.24.
Their own forecast (guidance): full-year adjusted EPS about $4.70, and fourth-quarter sales up 7 percent to 9 percent.
Surprising: about $8 million came from tariff refunds. Cash left after spending (free cash flow) fell to $153 million from $179 million.
Pentair sells water gear: pumps, filters and valves (Flow), home water systems (Water Solutions) and pool equipment (Pool).
In 2025 Pool made up 38% of sales, Flow 37%, Water Solutions 25%. For 2026, home and irrigation flow moved to Water Solutions.
Risks they name: a weaker economy or housing market, tough price competition, and tariffs that push up their costs.
They also flag a new global minimum tax (Pillar Two) that is raising the share of profit they pay in taxes.
A Morningstar headline says the stock is up 25% in a month.
A law firm notice is looking for shareholders who lost money, which can be an early step toward a lawsuit.
Filings show the head of the Pool business received 14,245 stock units that only become theirs over time.

takeaways: This was a weaker quarter: sales and profit both fell, and the Pool business was the main drag.
Two of their three businesses earned more, and the company kept its full-year profit forecast.
The dividend (cash paid to owners) went up again; this is the 50th year in a row they raised it.

earnings.headline: Profit rose about $21 million from a year ago, helped by more customers, more power use and a hot summer.
points: Profit (what's left after costs) was $434.2 million, or $3.49 per share, up from $413.2 million and $3.39 a year ago.
Sales to businesses and factories rose 14.5% and to homes 4.5%. Customers set a record peak use of 9,166 megawatts.
They raised their guidance (their own forecast) for 2026 to $5.05 to $5.25 per share.
The bad side: higher costs for wear on equipment (depreciation) and for interest on debt ate into the gains.
Nearly all money comes from APS, Arizona's biggest power company, serving about 1.4 million customers in 11 of 15 counties.
About 58% of its power in 2025 came from clean sources like nuclear, sun and wind.
Gas pipelines into Arizona are 100% full, so APS signed for a new one and plans up to 2,000 MW of new gas power.
Risks they name: wildfires, extreme heat, tariffs, rising interest rates, and whether regulators let them pass costs to bills.
Headlines say the latest profit came in better than Wall Street expected.
An investment firm, Barrow Hanley, now owns over 5% of the company as a passive (hands-off) holder.
The company presented at an industry finance conference (EEI).

takeaways: Arizona is growing fast, and more people and businesses using power has lifted profit.
The company now expects a better 2026 than it did before, but costs and debt interest are rising too.
Big new users like data centers must pay for their own hookups, and typical home bills get about a $14 credit in November.

earnings.headline: Sales rose 19.2% to $842 million and profit jumped, slightly above the company's own forecast.
points: Sales (revenue) were $842 million, up 19.2%. U.S. Pod sales grew 14.7%; overseas grew faster, 31.7%.
Profit was $141.1 million, or $2.03 per share, up from $87.6 million, or $1.24 per share, a year ago.
Own forecast (guidance) raised: 2026 sales growth now 21% - 22%. Small Drug Delivery unit still seen falling about 40%.
Surprise: a $1 billion plan to buy back its own shares, with about $400 million spent this quarter from cash on hand.
They mainly sell Omnipod, a tubeless insulin pump worn on the body. Used Pods get replaced, so sales keep repeating.
2025 sales were $2,708.1 million, up 30.7%. They had more than 600,000 users worldwide at year end.
Not all good: a $123.9 million loss from paying off debt early, and interest costs rose to $59.4 million.
Risks they name: relying on one main product, rivals, tariffs, insurance payment rules, and supply problems.
Stifel, a Wall Street research firm, lowered its rating on the stock, citing worries about U.S. momentum.
At the same time, Stifel raised its rating on Tandem, a rival insulin pump maker.
Jefferies kept its rating, pointing to Insulet's strong edge over rivals (its 'moat').

takeaways: The business grew fast and got more profitable this quarter, and it raised its own forecast for the year.
Growth in the U.S. is slower than overseas, and at least one analyst firm is worried about U.S. momentum.
It depends mostly on one product, so rivals, tariffs or supply trouble could hurt; it is using cash to buy back shares.

earnings.headline: PPG grew sales 7% to $4.4 billion and set a third-quarter profit record, but its factory-coatings unit earned less.
points: Sales (money from customers) were $4.4 billion, up 7% from a year ago, helped more by higher prices than by selling more paint.
Profit per share was $2.12, or $2.25 on their adjusted basis (leaving out one-time items), up 6% on that view.
Bad news: the factory-coatings unit (cars, packaging) earned 11% less, as raw material costs rose faster than its prices.
Guidance (their own forecast) for full-year adjusted profit per share is now $7.90 to $8.10, with a higher middle than before.
PPG makes paints and coatings for homes, cars, planes, ships and packaging, and sells in more than 50 countries.
2025 sales were about $15.9 billion, flat versus 2024; price and volume gains were offset by businesses it let go.
In October 2024 it began a cost-cutting plan, mostly in Europe, and took a $239 million charge, mainly worker severance.
Biggest risks it names: raw material costs (its largest cost), a weak economy, tariffs, wars, and currency swings.
Most headlines are analyst opinions and fund trades in PPG shares, not news about the business itself.
One headline says a PPG vice president sold 2,500 shares of company stock.
A PPG survey looked at how paint-buying habits differ between European countries.

takeaways: Sales and profit grew, driven mostly by higher prices and strong demand for airplane coatings.
Rising material costs still bite: the car and packaging coatings unit made less money than a year ago.
The company raised the middle of its own yearly profit forecast, but forecasts can turn out wrong.

earnings.headline: Sales grew 18% to $98.3 million, but the company lost more money than a year ago and kept its full-year forecast unchanged.
