points: Sales (revenue) were $98.3 million, up 18% from a year ago. U.S. procedures rose about 22% to over 13,400.
Net loss grew to $26.5 million from $21.4 million. Operating costs rose to $92.5 million from $77.2 million.
Guidance (their own forecast) is unchanged: full-year 2026 sales of $390 million to $410 million.
U.S. robot system sales were flat at $24.7 million, while sales outside the U.S. jumped 32% to $12.5 million.
They sell surgical robots plus a one-use handpiece needed for each treatment of an enlarged prostate (BPH).
Sales for 2025 were $308.1 million, up from $224.5 million in 2024.
They have lost money every period since starting: $95.6 million lost in 2025, $641.6 million lost in total so far.
Risks they name: they rely on one product line, insurance payment rules can change, and results can swing a lot.
Two company insiders sold shares, including a $92,852 sale by the strategy and marketing chief.
Analyst and research sites posted opinions on the stock after the results; those are views, not company facts.
Management will speak at a New York healthcare conference on Dec. 2.

takeaways: More people are getting this treatment: sales and procedures both grew by double digits.
The company still loses money, and the loss got bigger this quarter, not smaller.
It has about $221.4 million in cash, and a key trial result (WATER IV) is due in the first half of 2027.

earnings.headline: Sales and profit fell, the yearly forecast was cut, and Perrigo agreed to sell its Infant Formula business.
points: Sales fell. Total sales were $989 million, down 5.2%. Core sales (the business they're keeping) were $908 million, down 1.7%.
Profit fell. Adjusted profit per share (their own measure) dropped 25.0% to $0.60. On standard rules, it was a loss of $(0.10).
Guidance (their own forecast) was cut: Core profit per share now $2.15 to $2.35, down from $2.25 to $2.55.
Bright spot: they won market share in U.S. store-brand medicine and key European brands. Women's Health grew strongly.
They sell over-the-counter health products (no prescription needed), mostly store brands in North America and brands in Europe.
No one product is more than 5% of sales, so they don't depend on a single item.
Their 'Three-S' plan aims to stabilize, streamline and strengthen the business. In 2026 they began reporting by product type.
Risks they name: tariffs (about $30 million to $40 million in extra costs a year), inflation, interest rates, currency swings, wars.
Several headlines cover the lowered 2026 forecast and the Infant Formula sale.
Some articles debate whether the stock is cheap. Those are opinions, not facts from the company.
One headline says the stock hit a new 12-month high.

takeaways: Sales and profit both fell this quarter, and the company lowered its own forecast for the year.
Infant Formula is being sold for up to $175 million; they expect a one-time loss of $275.0 million to $375.0 million.
Debt is high: $3.3 billion owed versus $437 million in cash.

earnings.headline: PTC's quarterly sales and profit fell sharply from last year, but its subscription base kept growing as it waits to be bought by Schneider Electric.
points: Sales (revenue) fell 25% for the quarter, to $673 million from $894 million a year earlier.
Profit per share fell 50%, to $1.44 from $2.88. Free cash (cash left after spending) dropped to $38 million from $100 million.
Yearly subscription value (ARR) rose 8% to $2,508 million from $2,320 million. That counts contracts, not booked sales.
No forecast: PTC agreed to be bought by Schneider Electric, so it stopped giving guidance (its own forecast) and earnings calls.
PTC sells design and factory software, mostly by subscription, to companies that build physical products.
Last full year (FY'25), sales grew 19%. PTC also agreed to sell its Kepware and ThingWorx units to TPG for up to $725 million.
Risk they name: about 50% of sales come in foreign money, so currency swings change their reported results.
Risk they name: accounting rules book some contract sales up front, so sales can jump or drop a lot from one period to the next.
The stock hit a 52-week high of $196.06 after the buyout news.
A law firm, Halper Sadeh, is looking into whether shareholders are getting a fair price in the sale.
Most other headlines are opinion pieces and price forecasts, not company news.

takeaways: The big story is the sale: Schneider Electric agreed to buy PTC, so PTC no longer shares forecasts.
This quarter looked weak: sales, profit, and free cash all fell clearly from a year ago.
Part of the drop came from one-time costs and taxes tied to selling two units, while the subscription base still grew.
